p: How the Exam Tests This Unit · Commercial Law
x: Exam pattern (verify against the latest NTA notification): UGC NET Law Paper 2 has 100 objective questions of 2 marks each (200 marks). The syllabus has 10 units, so each unit carries roughly 10 questions. Commercial Law (Unit VI) is a high-scoring, factual unit, and a well-prepared candidate can expect 8–12 questions from it.

p: How the Exam Tests This Unit · Commercial Law
x: Statement-based: Statements I and II, choose the correct option. This is the most common format. Match the following: sections with topics (for example s.73 – compensation, s.74 – liquidated damages), or cases with principles. Assertion–Reason: common for doctrines such as frustration, privity, and the Turquand rule. Sequence/chronology: order of company incorporation steps, or the order of discharge of a surety. Numeric/fact recall: time limits, thresholds, and minimum numbers (for example the minimum members of a public company, or the CSR thresholds). Which-is-NOT-correct: negative questions that test exceptions.

p: How the Exam Tests This Unit · Commercial Law
x: Questions increasingly test section numbers and statutory definitions , not only case law. Amendments are favourites: Companies (Amendment) Acts 2015, 2017, 2019, 2020; the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act 2023; the LLP (Amendment) Act 2021 and LLP Rules; NI Act amendments of 2015 and 2018; the Specific Relief (Amendment) Act 2018. E-contract questions combine the IT Act 2000 with the Contract Act and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (the replacement of the Evidence Act). CSR questions test the exact rules: Section 135, Schedule VII, and the CSR Rules 2014 as amended in 2021. Landmark Supreme Court cases are repeated across years, so learn the principle attached to each case.

p: How the Exam Tests This Unit · Commercial Law
x: Study tip: For every topic, memorise (a) definition section, (b) key sections and numbers, (c) two to four landmark cases with the one-line principle, and (d) the common exceptions.

t: 1.1 Background of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
p: Essential Elements of Contract and E-Contract · Commercial Law
x: The Act came into force on 1 September 1872 . It is based largely on English common law principles. Originally it also covered sale of goods and partnership, but these were carved out: Sale of Goods: formerly ss.76–123, now the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 . Partnership: formerly ss.239–266, now the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 . Remaining structure: ss.1–75 (general principles), ss.124–147 (indemnity and guarantee), ss.148–181 (bailment and pledge), and ss.182–238 (agency). The Act is not exhaustive . Section 1 saves usages and customs of trade, and other statutes apply alongside it.

p: Essential Elements of Contract and E-Contract · Commercial Law
x: s.2(a) Proposal (offer): a person signifies to another his willingness to do or abstain from doing anything, with a view to obtaining the other’s assent. s.2(b) Promise: a proposal when accepted. s.2(c) Promisor and promisee: the person making the proposal is the promisor, and the person accepting is the promisee. s.2(d) Consideration: when, at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains, or promises to do or abstain, something. That something is a consideration for the promise. s.2(e) Agreement: every promise and every set of promises forming the consideration for each other. s.2(f) Reciprocal promises: promises which form the consideration or part of the consideration for each other. s.2(g) Void agreement: an agreement not enforceable by law. s.2(h) Contract: an agreement enforceable by law. s.2(i) Voidable contract: an agreement enforceable by law at the option of one or more of the parties, but not at the option of the other or others. s.2(j) Void contract: a contract which ceases to be enforceable by law. Formula to remember: Agreement + Enforceability = Contract. All contracts are agreements, but not all agreements are contracts.

t: 1.3 Section 10: Essentials of a Valid Contract
p: Essential Elements of Contract and E-Contract · Commercial Law
x: Section 10 says all agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract , for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object , and are not expressly declared void . Writing and registration are required only where a statute demands them. The full checklist is: Two or more parties (offer and acceptance). Intention to create legal relations. Free consent. Capacity of parties. Lawful consideration. Lawful object. Certainty and possibility of performance. Not declared void. Legal formalities, where required.

p: Essential Elements of Contract and E-Contract · Commercial Law
x: Kinds of offer: express or implied; general (to the world, as in Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. ), specific, cross-offers, counter-offers, and standing (continuing) offers (for example tenders: Great Northern Railway v Witham ). Rules: The offer must be capable of creating legal relations and be clear and definite. It must be communicated to the offeree. In Lalman Shukla v Gauri Dutt (1913), the servant who found the missing nephew could not claim the reward, because he did not know of the offer when he acted. (Contrast Carlill, where performance after knowledge sufficed.) An offer is different from an invitation to treat . Examples: price lists, advertisements, goods displayed in shops ( Pharmaceutical Society v Boots ), catalogues, auction bids, and the statement in Harvey v Facey (“lowest price for Bumper Hall Pen”), which was only information. In an auction, the bid is the offer and the fall of the hammer is acceptance (s.64 Sale of Goods Act). A counter-offer destroys the original offer ( Hyde v Wrench ). A mere request for information is not a counter-offer ( Stevenson v McLean ). Revocation of an offer (ss.5 and 6): may be revoked at any time before acceptance is complete as against the proposer. Modes (s.6): by communication of notice of revocation; by lapse of time (stipulated or reasonable); by failure to fulfil a condition precedent; by death or insanity of the proposer (if the acceptor comes to know of it before acceptance); by counter-offer; by rejection.

p: Essential Elements of Contract and E-Contract · Commercial Law
x: Acceptance must be absolute and unqualified , and expressed in the manner prescribed ; if no manner is prescribed, in a usual and reasonable manner. Silence is not acceptance ( Felthouse v Bindley ). The offeror cannot impose acceptance by silence. Only the person to whom the offer is made can accept it, except in a general offer. Acceptance by conduct (s.8): performing the conditions of a proposal, or accepting consideration for a reciprocal promise, is acceptance. Acceptance must be given before the offer lapses or is revoked , and within a reasonable time. Communication (s.4): the communication of a proposal is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made. Acceptance is complete as against the proposer when put in a course of transmission to him, so as to be out of the power of the acceptor to withdraw it. As against the acceptor it is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer. The same logic applies to revocation. Postal rule: Adams v Lindsell and Household Fire Insurance v Grant : acceptance by post is complete on posting. Instantaneous communication (telephone, telex, e-mail): the contract is made where and when the acceptance is received , per Entores Ltd v Miles Far East Corp. (English Court of Appeal) and followed by the Supreme Court in Bhagwandas Goverdhandas Kedia v Girdharilal Parshottamdas (1966).

p: Essential Elements of Contract and E-Contract · Commercial Law
x: The statute does not mention it expressly, but courts apply the English presumptions. Social and domestic agreements are presumed not to be intended as legal ( Balfour v Balfour ), though the presumption can be rebutted ( Merritt v Merritt ). Commercial agreements are presumed legal, unless there is an “honour clause” ( Rose and Frank Co. v Crompton Bros. ). Advertisements with mere puffery are not contracts, but those with a serious promise are ( Carlill ).

p: Essential Elements of Contract and E-Contract · Commercial Law
x: Section 11: every person is competent to contract who (a) is of the age of majority under the law to which he is subject, (b) is of sound mind , and (c) is not disqualified by any law. Minor (Indian Majority Act 1875): below 18 years, or below 21 where a guardian of the person or property has been appointed by a court or the minor’s property is under the Court of Wards. Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose (Privy Council, 1903): a minor’s agreement is void ab initio . Hence it cannot be ratified after majority. There is no estoppel against a minor, and a minor cannot be made liable even if he misrepresented his age. Restitution may be ordered only where the minor himself seeks relief and has obtained property by fraud (Specific Relief Act 1963, s.33, and equitable restitution). A minor may be a promisee or beneficiary ( Raghava Chariar v Srinivasa Raghava ). A minor’s estate is liable for necessaries supplied (s.68). The minor is not personally liable. Guardian’s contracts for the minor’s benefit are enforceable ( Mir Sarwarjan v Fakhruddin ). A minor cannot be a partner , but may be admitted to the benefits of partnership (s.30, Partnership Act). A minor may be an agent, and the principal is liable (s.184), but the minor is not personally liable. Sound mind (s.12): capable of understanding the contract and forming a rational judgment of its effect on his interests at the time of making it. A person usually of unsound mind may contract during lucid intervals. A usually sound person cannot contract when delirious, drunk, or so ill that he cannot understand. Disqualified persons: alien enemies, foreign sovereigns and ambassadors (partly), convicts (during sentence), insolvents, and corporations beyond their objects (ultra vires).

p: Essential Elements of Contract and E-Contract · Commercial Law
x: s.13: two or more persons consent when they agree upon the same thing in the same sense ( consensus ad idem ). s.14: consent is free when it is not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake. s.19: an agreement caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation is voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused. s.19A: same for undue influence (with power of court to set aside on terms). Mistake, by contrast, renders an agreement void (bilateral) or has no effect (unilateral). Coercion (s.15): committing or threatening to commit any act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code (now the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023), or unlawfully detaining or threatening to detain any property, with the intention of causing any person to enter into an agreement. It is irrelevant whether the IPC/BNS is in force where coercion is employed. Coercion may come from a stranger to the contract and be directed at any person ( Ranganayakamma v Alwar Setti : a widow was forced to adopt a boy by threatening to prevent the husband’s cremation). A threat to commit suicide is coercion ( Chikham Amiraju v Chikham Seshama ). A threat to file a civil suit is not coercion. Undue influence (s.16): a contract is induced by undue influence where the relations between the parties are such that one is in a position to dominate the will of the other and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage . Presumed relationships: parent and child, guru and disciple, doctor and patient, solicitor and client, trustee and beneficiary, fiancé and fiancée (not husband and wife by default). Where the dominant party holds a real or apparent authority, or the other is weak by age, illness or mental distress, the burden is on the dominant party to prove the contract was not induced by undue influence (s.16(3)). In an unconscionable bargain , the burden is on the stronger party. Cases: Lloyds Bank v Bundy ; Raghunath Prasad v Sarju Prasad (moneylender, unconscionable interest); Subhas Chandra Das Mushib v Ganga Prasad Das (1967); Ladli Prasad Jaiswal v Karnal Distillery (1963). Pardanashin women: the contract must be proved to have been explained to and understood by them. Fraud (s.17): includes any of the following acts committed by a party, or with his connivance, or by his agent, with intent to deceive another party or to induce him to enter into the contract: (1) suggestion as a fact of that which is not true by one who does not believe it true, (2) active concealment of a fact by one having knowledge or belief of it, (3) a promise made without any intention of performing it, (4) any other act fitted to deceive, and (5) any such act or omission as the law specially declares to be fraudulent. Mere silence is not fraud unless there is a duty to speak or the silence is equivalent to speech (Explanation to s.17). Contracts uberrimae fidei (insurance, family settlements, partnership, company prospectus, guarantee) require full disclosure. Derry v Peek : fraud is a false statement made knowingly, without belief in its truth, or recklessly. The defrauded party may rescind and claim damages. Under s.19, a party induced by misrepresentation cannot avoid the contract if he had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence, but this exception does not protect a fraudster. Misrepresentation (s.18): (1) a positive assertion in a manner not warranted by the information of the person making it, though he believes it true; (2) any breach of duty which gains an advantage to the person committing it without intent to deceive; (3) causing, however innocently, a party to make a mistake as to the substance of the thing which is the subject of the agreement. Mistake (ss.20–22): s.20 (bilateral mistake of fact essential to the agreement): the agreement is void . Examples: Raffles v Wichelhaus (the Peerless case, two ships of the same name), Couturier v Hastie (non-existent goods), Cooper v Phibbs (mistaken ownership), Cundy v Lindsay (mistake as to identity). s.21: mistake as to a law not in force in India is treated as mistake of fact. A mistake as to a law in force in India has the same effect as ignorance of law and does not make the contract voidable. s.22: a contract is not voidable merely because it was caused by one party’s unilateral mistake as to a matter of fact. Tarsem Singh v Sukhminder Singh (1998): the mistake must be as to a fact essential to the agreement.

p: Essential Elements of Contract and E-Contract · Commercial Law
x: Features of Indian consideration (s.2(d)): Moves at the desire of the promisor . May move from the promisee or any other person . Thus a stranger to consideration may sue ( Chinnaya v Ramayya , Madras HC, 1882; Durga Prasad v Baldeo ), but a stranger to the contract cannot (privity). Past consideration is good consideration in India (“has done or abstained”), unlike England. Cases: Sindha v Abraham ; Kedarnath v Gorie Mohamed . Consideration must be real , not illusory, but need not be adequate (Explanation 2 to s.25). Inadequacy may be relevant to free consent. Consideration must not be an already existing legal duty (pre-existing duty rule, partly relaxed in Williams v Roffey Bros ). s.25 (agreement without consideration is void), with three exceptions: A written and registered agreement made on account of natural love and affection between parties standing in a near relation to each other. A promise to compensate for something done voluntarily (past voluntary service) for the promisor. A written, signed promise to pay a time-barred debt (s.25(3)). Other cases needing no consideration: completed gift (Transfer of Property Act), gratuitous bailment , agency (s.185), charitable subscriptions (when acted upon), and remission/accord (s.63). Privity of contract: only parties to a contract can sue or be sued ( Tweddle v Guest ; Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre v Selfridge ). In India: Jamna Das v Ram Autar (Privy Council). Exceptions: trust, marriage settlements, family arrangements and partition, acknowledgment/estoppel, assignment, covenants running with land, agency, statutory rights (insurance beneficiary), and M.C. Chacko v State Bank of Travancore (1969), where a beneficiary was allowed to enforce a contract because of a trust-like arrangement. Unlawful consideration/object (s.23): forbidden by law; of such a nature that, if permitted, it would defeat the provisions of any law; fraudulent; involving or implying injury to the person or property of another; or the court regards it as immoral or opposed to public policy . Such agreements are void . Gherulal Parakh v Mahadeodas Maiya (1959): public policy should be applied narrowly, and wagering agreements are void but not illegal. Central Inland Water Transport Corp. v Brojo Nath Ganguly (1986): unconscionable and unreasonable contract terms are opposed to public policy. ONGC v Saw Pipes Ltd. (2003): “patent illegality” as a ground to set aside an award under public policy; later narrowed in Associate Builders v DDA (2015), and now governed by s.34(2A) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. Examples of immoral: marriage brokerage contracts, sexual immorality. Public policy: stifling prosecution, trafficking in public offices, champerty and maintenance (limited). Void by express provision (ss.24–30): s.24: consideration or object partly unlawful. If the lawful part is separable ( severability ), it is enforceable; otherwise the whole is void. s.26: agreements in restraint of marriage (except of minors). s.27: agreements in restraint of trade are void, with the sole statutory exception of sale of goodwill within specified local limits. Cases: Madhub Chunder v Raj Coomar Dass ; Nordenfelt v Maxim Nordenfelt Guns (English); Niranjan Shankar Golikari v Century Spinning (1967: a negative covenant during the term of employment is valid); Percept D’Mark v Zaheer Khan (2006: post-term restraint void); Superintendence Co. of India v Krishan Murgai (1981). s.28: agreements in restraint of legal proceedings (absolutely restricting remedies, or curtailing limitation periods). Exceptions: arbitration agreements and agreements to refer existing disputes. Courts uphold exclusive jurisdiction clauses where more than one court has jurisdiction ( Hakam Singh v Gammon (India) Ltd. , 1971; ABC Laminart v A.P. Agencies , 1989). Section 28 was amended in 1997. s.29: agreements whose meaning is uncertain. s.30: wagering agreements are void; collateral transactions are not void ( Gherulal Parakh ). Exception: prizes for horse races above Rs. 500 (s.294A IPC, now covered under BNS). Some states (e.g., Maharashtra, Gujarat) have stricter amendments making wagers illegal.

p: Essential Elements of Contract and E-Contract · Commercial Law
x: A contingent contract depends on an event collateral to the contract (s.31). Enforcement: on the happening of the event (s.32), on its non-happening (s.35), and a contract contingent on an impossible event is void (s.36). s.33 deals with events happening in a certain way, and s.34 with the conduct of a living person. Certainty (s.29) and possibility (s.56) are separate requirements. Insurance and indemnity are classic contingent contracts, while a wager is not contingent because the event is not collateral.

p: Essential Elements of Contract and E-Contract · Commercial Law
x: No general requirement of writing or registration. Specific statutory requirements: s.25(1) registration; arbitration agreements in writing (Arbitration Act s.7); Registration Act 1908, s.17 (immovable property above Rs. 100); Transfer of Property Act (sale, mortgage, lease, gift); Negotiable Instruments Act (written and signed).

p: Essential Elements of Contract and E-Contract · Commercial Law
x: An e-contract is a contract formed and executed through electronic means (the internet, e-mail, apps, EDI) rather than on paper. The general law of contract applies equally to it. Types: click-wrap (the user clicks ‘I agree’), browse-wrap (terms linked on the site, weakest enforceability), shrink-wrap (terms inside software packaging), e-mail contracts , EDI (electronic data interchange), and smart contracts on a blockchain. Information Technology Act, 2000 (amended 2008) is based on the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Commerce, 1996 . Key provisions: s.2(1)(t): definition of ‘electronic record’. s.3 and s.3A: authentication by digital signature and electronic signature. s.4: legal recognition of electronic records. s.5: legal recognition of electronic signatures. s.10A (inserted in 2008): contracts formed through electronic means are not unenforceable solely because electronic form or means were used for the proposal, acceptance or revocation. s.11–13: attribution, acknowledgment and the time and place of dispatch and receipt . Dispatch occurs when the record enters a computer resource outside the originator’s control. Receipt occurs when it enters the designated computer resource of the addressee, or if none is designated, when the addressee retrieves it. Place is the place of business of the originator (dispatch) and the addressee (receipt). First Schedule (s.1(4)): the Act does not apply to negotiable instruments (other than cheques), powers of attorney, trusts, wills, and contracts for the sale or conveyance of immovable property. s.75: extra-territorial application. Evidentiary position: earlier s.65B of the Evidence Act governed electronic evidence ( Anvar P.V. v P.K. Basheer , 2014; Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal , 2020, which held that the s.65B certificate is mandatory). Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (in force from 1 July 2024) the corresponding provision is s.63 . Key cases: Trimex International FZE Ltd. v Vedanta Aluminium Ltd. (2010): a contract may be concluded through e-mail exchange even without a formal signed document. Shakti Bhog Foods v Kola Shipping (2009): an arbitration agreement can be concluded by electronic communication. P.R. Transport Agency v Union of India (Allahabad HC, 2006): an e-mail acceptance concludes the contract at the place where it is received. Bhagwandas Kedia (1966): the rule for instantaneous communication. Related legislation: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020; Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; UN Convention on the Use of Electronic Communications in International Contracts (2005); UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Signatures (2001).

t: 2.1 Void Agreement, Void Contract, Voidable Contract and Illegal Agreement
p: Breach, Frustration, Void and Voidable Agreements · Commercial Law
x: Feature Void agreement Void contract Voidable contract Illegal agreement Definition s.2(g): not enforceable by law from the start s.2(j): contract that ceases to be enforceable s.2(i): enforceable at the option of one party Forbidden by law or against public policy Legal effect No legal effect from inception Valid at first, later void Valid until avoided Void, with penal consequences Examples Minor’s agreement, wager, restraint of trade Frustration under s.56, contingent event fails Consent by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation Contract to commit a crime Collateral transactions Enforceable, with some exceptions n/a n/a Collateral transactions generally tainted Agreements declared void by the Act: s.11 (incompetent party), s.20 (bilateral mistake), s.23 (unlawful object/consideration), s.24 (partly unlawful and inseparable), s.25 (no consideration), s.26 (restraint of marriage), s.27 (restraint of trade), s.28 (restraint of legal proceedings), s.29 (uncertainty), s.30 (wager), s.36 (contingent on impossible event), s.56 para 1 (agreement to do an impossible act). Voidable by statute: s.19 and 19A (consent not free), s.39 (repudiation by a party), s.53 (prevention of performance by one party), s.55 (failure to perform at a time fixed when time is of the essence). Consequences: s.64: a party rescinding a voidable contract must restore any benefit received to the other party. s.65: when an agreement is discovered to be void, or a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage must restore it or make compensation . See Kuju Collieries Ltd. v Jharkhand Mines Ltd. (1974). Note that in Mohori Bibee restitution under s.65 was refused, because s.65 applies to persons competent to contract. Rights of third parties: a bona fide purchaser for value without notice acquires good title before rescission. Rescission may be lost by affirmation, lapse of time, intervention of third-party rights, or impossibility of restitutio in integrum.

p: Breach, Frustration, Void and Voidable Agreements · Commercial Law
x: By performance (ss.37–67): both parties must perform or offer to perform. Tender (s.38): an offer of performance that is unconditional, made at the proper time and place, with a reasonable opportunity to inspect the goods. A valid tender of performance, if refused, relieves the promisor of liability for non-performance but not of the promise itself. A valid tender of money does not discharge the debt. Joint promisors (ss.42–45). Appropriation of payments (ss.59–61): the debtor can direct the appropriation; if not, the creditor; if neither, in the order of time. Reciprocal promises (ss.51–54): performance in the order specified; where one is dependent on the other, the party at fault must compensate. s.55 (time as the essence): if time is of the essence and the promisor fails, the contract is voidable at the promisee’s option. If not of the essence, the promisee can claim compensation only. In contracts for sale of immovable property, time is presumed not to be of the essence ( Hind Construction Contractors v State of Maharashtra , 1979; Gomathinayagam Pillai v Palaniswami Nadar , 1967). By mutual agreement (ss.62–63): novation (substitution of a new contract), rescission (cancellation), alteration , remission (acceptance of lesser performance or satisfaction), waiver , accord and satisfaction . By impossibility (s.56), discussed below. By lapse of time , under the Limitation Act, 1963. By operation of law: death (in personal contracts), insolvency, merger, and material alteration of a written document. By breach (s.39 and following).

p: Breach, Frustration, Void and Voidable Agreements · Commercial Law
x: Text of s.56: Para 1: An agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void . Para 2: A contract to do an act which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible , or, by reason of some event which the promisor could not prevent, unlawful , becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful. Para 3: Where one person has promised to do something which he knew, or with reasonable diligence might have known, and which the promisee did not know, to be impossible or unlawful, such promisor must compensate the promisee for any loss through the non-performance. Indian position: the doctrine is a rule of positive law under s.56, not a rule based on an implied term. Unlike English law (where frustration was developed by the courts and is regulated by the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act, 1943 ), the Indian statute governs, and s.65 provides restitution. Leading cases: Taylor v Caldwell (1863): music hall destroyed by fire before the concerts. Origin of the doctrine. Krell v Henry (1903): rooms hired for viewing the coronation procession, which was cancelled. The foundation of the contract was frustrated. Herne Bay Steam Boat Co. v Hutton (1903): hire of a boat to see the naval review. Not frustrated as the boat could still cruise. Satyabrata Ghose v Mugneeram Bangur & Co. (1954): Supreme Court: s.56 is wider than the English rule; ‘impossible’ includes impracticable and useless from the point of view of the object and purpose of the parties. The test is the destruction of the foundation of the contract. Naihati Jute Mills v Khyaliram Jagannath (1968): mere commercial hardship or difficulty is not frustration. Alopi Parshad & Sons v Union of India (1960): increase in cost does not frustrate a contract. Sushila Devi v Hari Singh (1971): migration after Partition made performance impossible. Energy Watchdog v CERC (2017): a rise in coal prices and a change in Indonesian regulation did not frustrate the power purchase agreement; force majeure clauses are dealt with under s.32 and are distinct from s.56. Halliburton Offshore Services v Vedanta Ltd. (Delhi HC, 2020): Covid-19 force majeure claims are examined on the contract wording and cannot excuse non-performance that occurred before the event. Grounds for frustration: destruction of the subject-matter; non-occurrence of a contemplated event; death or incapacity of a party in personal-service contracts; change of law or governmental intervention; outbreak of war. Where the doctrine does NOT apply: self-induced frustration; mere hardship, delay or increased cost; a contract expressly providing for the risk (force majeure clauses); leases (a transfer of property, per Raja Dhruv Dev Chand v Raja Harmohinder Singh , 1968); and where the event was foreseeable. Initial vs supervening impossibility: initial impossibility (para 1) renders the agreement void from the start; supervening impossibility (para 2) makes a valid contract void later .

p: Breach, Frustration, Void and Voidable Agreements · Commercial Law
x: Meaning: failure or refusal to perform contractual obligations without lawful excuse. Kinds: Actual breach: on the due date of performance, or during performance. Anticipatory breach (s.39): a party, before the due date, refuses wholly to perform or disables himself. The promisee may treat the contract as repudiated and sue at once, or wait until the due date (affirm) and keep the contract alive ( Hochster v De La Tour , 1853; Frost v Knight , 1872). By electing to wait, the promisee risks supervening events and still has the duty to mitigate. Remedies for breach: Rescission (s.39, s.75): the injured party may rescind and claim compensation (s.75). Damages (s.73): compensation for any loss or damage caused which naturally arose in the usual course of things or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result. Compensation is not given for remote and indirect loss. The rule in Hadley v Baxendale (1854) underlies this: damages are limited to (a) those arising naturally and (b) those within the reasonable contemplation of both parties at the time of contract. The injured party has a duty to mitigate (Explanation). Liquidated damages and penalty (s.74): where a sum is named as payable on breach, or a penalty is stipulated, the party complaining is entitled to reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount named , whether or not actual damage is proved. The English distinction between penalty and liquidated damages is not followed. Fateh Chand v Balkishan Dass (1963): s.74 applies to both; the court awards reasonable compensation; forfeiture of earnest money beyond a reasonable amount is a penalty. Maula Bux v Union of India (1969): forfeiture of earnest money/security deposit. ONGC v Saw Pipes (2003): the party claiming must prove the loss unless the loss is impossible to prove. Kailash Nath Associates v DDA (2015): the Supreme Court summarised the s.74 principles. Specific performance: governed by the Specific Relief Act, 1963 , as amended by the Specific Relief (Amendment) Act, 2018 (in force 1 October 2018). Specific performance is now a general rule rather than a discretionary remedy . New s.20 provides substituted performance ; s.20A sets out special provisions for infrastructure projects (courts cannot grant injunctions that obstruct them); s.20B designates special courts. Injunction: preventing a breach of a negative covenant (Specific Relief Act, Chapter VII). Quantum meruit (‘as much as he has earned’): a claim for reasonable remuneration for work done where the contract is discharged by breach or is incomplete ( Alopi Parshad ; s.70 as a quasi-contract). Restitution (ss.64, 65, 72). Types of damages: nominal (breach with no loss), ordinary or general , special (foreseeable by the parties), exemplary/vindictive (generally not awarded in contract except for breach of promise to marry and wrongful dishonour of a cheque by a bank), and damages for mental agony (rare). Remoteness: Hadley v Baxendale (mill-shaft case), Victoria Laundry v Newman , Czarnikow v Koufos (The Heron II) . In India: Murlidhar Chiranjilal v Harishchandra Dwarkadas (1962).

p: Standard Form of Contract and Quasi-Contract · Commercial Law
x: Meaning: a contract whose terms are drafted in advance by one party (usually the stronger, such as a corporation, bank, insurer, airline, telecom operator or website) and offered on a ‘take it or leave it’ basis. The other party can only adhere and has no real chance to negotiate. Examples: railway tickets, insurance policies, bank loan forms, bills of lading, airline tickets, software licences, app terms and conditions. Features: pre-printed or digital; uniform; non-negotiable; often contain exemption/exclusion clauses; unequal bargaining power; efficient for mass transactions. Advantages: saves time and cost, uniformity, certainty, ease of administration, standard risk allocation. Disadvantages: unfair and one-sided terms, hidden clauses, limitation of liability, unequal bargaining power, no meaningful consent. Judicial control: Notice rule: the terms must be brought to the notice of the other party before or at the time of contract ( Parker v South Eastern Railway ; Thornton v Shoe Lane Parking ; Olley v Marlborough Court ). Signature rule: a person who signs is bound, even if he has not read ( L’Estrange v Graucob ), unless there is fraud or misrepresentation ( Curtis v Chemical Cleaning ). Contra proferentem: ambiguities are construed against the party who drafted them. Doctrine of fundamental breach: attempted by Lord Denning, but the House of Lords held in Suisse Atlantique (1967) and Photo Production v Securicor (1980) that it is a rule of construction, not of law. Unreasonable and unconscionable terms: Central Inland Water Transport Corp. v Brojo Nath Ganguly (1986) applied Article 14 to a standard-form service rule and declared it unconscionable and void under s.23 as against public policy. Also Delhi Transport Corporation v DTC Mazdoor Congress (1991) and LIC of India v Consumer Education and Research Centre (1995). Bharathi Knitting Co. v DHL Worldwide Express Courier (1996): a party who signs a standard form is bound by its terms. Lily White v Munuswami (Madras HC, 1966): a laundry’s limitation of liability on a ticket was held reasonable. Statutory control in India: Indian Contract Act: ss.16, 23, 28 and 74. Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (in force 20 July 2020): s.2(46) defines ‘ unfair contract ’ (terms causing significant change in the rights of consumers, such as excessive security deposits, disproportionate penalty, refusing to accept early repayment, unilateral termination without reasonable cause, or assignment to a third party to the consumer’s detriment). The State Commission and National Commission may declare unfair terms null and void (ss.49(2) and 59(2)). Unfair trade practice (s.2(47)) and Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 . Law Commission of India, 199th Report (2006) on ‘Unfair (Procedural and Substantive) Terms in Contract’ recommended a separate statute (not enacted).

t: 3.2 Quasi-Contract (Sections 68–72): ‘Certain Relations Resembling Those Created by Contract’
p: Standard Form of Contract and Quasi-Contract · Commercial Law
x: Concept: a quasi-contract is not a real contract. There is no offer, acceptance or agreement; the law imposes an obligation to prevent unjust enrichment (no person should be enriched at the expense of another). The Act places it in Chapter V. Section Situation Rule s.68 Supply of necessaries to a person incapable of contracting (minor, person of unsound mind) or to one whom he is legally bound to support Supplier is entitled to be reimbursed from the property of the incapable person; no personal liability s.69 Payment by a person interested in the payment of money which another is bound by law to pay Entitled to be reimbursed by the other s.70 Non-gratuitous act done lawfully for another, who enjoys the benefit The enjoyer must compensate or restore s.71 Finder of goods Subject to the same responsibility as a bailee s.72 Money paid or thing delivered by mistake or under coercion Must be repaid or returned Section 70, conditions (very frequently tested): A person must lawfully do something for another or deliver something to him. He must not do so gratuitously . The other person must enjoy the benefit of it. Cases: State of West Bengal v B.K. Mondal & Sons (1962: the benefit must be accepted voluntarily, not forced); Mulamchand v State of Madhya Pradesh (1968); Damodara Mudaliar v Secretary of State ; Alopi Parshad . Section 72 cases: Sales Tax Officer v Kanhaiya Lal Makund Lal Saraf (1959: tax paid under mistake of law is recoverable, and the State can be made to refund); Mafatlal Industries v Union of India (1997: refund of excise duty is subject to the principle of unjust enrichment , and where the burden has been passed on to consumers the claim fails). s.71 (finder of goods): the finder takes on a bailee’s obligations (ss.151–152, 154). He may retain the goods against the owner until lawful charges are paid, and may sue for a reward if one was publicly offered (s.168). If the owner cannot be found, the finder may sell only if the goods are perishable or the lawful charges amount to two-thirds of their value (s.169). Contract vs quasi-contract: A contract arises from consent; a quasi-contract arises by operation of law. A contract requires competent parties and an agreement; a quasi-contract does not. In a contract, damages are measured by the loss; in a quasi-contract the claim is limited to the value of the benefit conferred. Related doctrines: unjust enrichment ( Lipkin Gorman v Karpnale Ltd. ), quantum meruit (reasonable payment for work done), and total failure of consideration ( Fibrosa Spolka Akcyjna v Fairbairn Lawson Combe Barbour Ltd. , 1943).

p: Specific Contracts: Bailment, Pledge, Indemnity, Guarantee and Agency · Commercial Law
x: Definition (s.148): the delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that they shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them. The delivering person is the bailor ; the person to whom goods are delivered is the bailee . Essentials: (1) a contract (express or implied), (2) delivery of possession (not ownership), (3) goods only (movable property; not money meant to be spent, not immovables), (4) for a purpose, and (5) the obligation to return or dispose according to directions. Delivery (s.149) may be actual or constructive (doing anything with the effect of putting the goods in possession of the bailee or any person authorised to hold them on his behalf). Kinds: gratuitous bailment (no reward) and bailment for reward; also bailment for the benefit of the bailor, of the bailee, or of both. Examples: loan for use, deposit, hire, pawn, carriage, repair. Duties of the bailor: s.150: disclose known faults in the goods that materially interfere with their use or expose the bailee to risk. In gratuitous bailment the bailor is liable for damage if he knew of the faults and did not disclose them. In bailment for hire, the bailor is liable whether or not he knew of the faults. s.158: to repay necessary expenses (gratuitous bailment) and extraordinary expenses. s.164: to indemnify the bailee for loss arising from the bailor’s defective title. Duties of the bailee: s.151: take as much care of the goods as a man of ordinary prudence would take of his own goods of the same bulk, quality and value. s.152: the bailee who takes such care is not liable for loss, destruction or deterioration, in the absence of a special contract. s.153: the bailor may terminate the bailment if the bailee does an act inconsistent with its terms. s.154: the bailee who makes unauthorised use is liable for damage arising from it. ss.155–157 (mixture of goods): with consent, the parties share in proportion; without consent but separable, the bailee bears the expense of separation and any damage; without consent and inseparable, the bailee must compensate the bailor for the loss. s.160: return or deliver according to the bailor’s directions when the time has expired or the purpose has been accomplished. s.161: if the bailee fails to return on time, he is responsible for loss even without negligence. s.163: deliver any increase or profit accruing from the goods (accretions), unless otherwise agreed. s.165–166: bailee’s delivery to one of several joint owners, and to the bailor without title. Termination: s.153 (inconsistent act), s.162 (death of bailor or bailee in gratuitous bailment), and completion of purpose or expiry of time. Rights of the bailee: s.168 (finder’s rights to compensation and to sue for reward offered), s.170 particular lien (retain goods bailed to him for work done on them till he is paid), s.171 general lien (bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of High Court and policy-brokers may retain goods bailed to them as a security for a general balance of account, unless there is a contract to the contrary). s.169: the finder may sell if the owner cannot be found with reasonable diligence, if the goods are perishable, or if the lawful charges equal two-thirds of the value. Special bailees: carriers (Carriers Act, 1865: a common carrier is liable as an insurer subject to statutory exceptions); railways (Railways Act, 1989); innkeepers; banks keeping lockers. Bailment vs sale: in bailment ownership remains with the bailor and the same goods must be returned; in sale ownership passes to the buyer. Bailment vs pledge: a pledge is a bailment made as security for a debt.

p: Specific Contracts: Bailment, Pledge, Indemnity, Guarantee and Agency · Commercial Law
x: Definition (s.172): the bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise . The bailor is the pawnor (pledgor) and the bailee is the pawnee (pledgee) . Essentials: goods (movable), delivery of possession (actual or constructive), a debt or promise to be secured, and a contract. Rights of the pawnee: s.173: retain the goods for payment of the debt, interest, and necessary expenses. s.174: no right to retain for any debt other than the one pledged, unless there is a contract to the contrary (but presumed for subsequent advances). s.175: claim extraordinary expenses incurred for preservation. s.176: on default, the pawnee may (a) sue on the debt and retain the goods as collateral, or (b) sell the goods after giving the pawnor reasonable notice . If the proceeds are less than the debt, the pawnor remains liable for the balance; any surplus must be paid to the pawnor. Right of the pawnor (s.177): to redeem at any time before actual sale, on payment of the debt, interest and expenses incurred owing to the default. Cases: Lallan Prasad v Rahmat Ali (1967: the pawnee’s sale without notice is not valid); Bank of Bihar v Damodar Prasad (1969). Pledge by non-owners (exceptions to the rule nemo dat ): s.178: by a mercantile agent in possession of goods or documents of title with the owner’s consent, acting in the ordinary course of business, if the pawnee acts in good faith without notice. s.178A: by a person in possession under a voidable contract (if the contract has not been rescinded before the pledge and the pawnee acts in good faith without notice). s.179: by a pawnor having a limited interest (to the extent of that interest). A pledge by a co-owner in possession with the consent of the others, and by a seller in possession after sale. Pledge vs mortgage, hypothecation and lien: Feature Pledge Mortgage Hypothecation Lien Subject Movable goods Immovable property Movables, possession stays with debtor Goods in the possession of the lienholder Possession Transferred Not necessarily Not transferred Retained Nature Security Transfer of interest Charge/equitable security Bare right to retain Governing law Contract Act Transfer of Property Act SARFAESI/contract Contract Act, Sale of Goods Act

p: Specific Contracts: Bailment, Pledge, Indemnity, Guarantee and Agency · Commercial Law
x: Definition (s.124): a contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss caused to him by the conduct of the promisor himself, or by the conduct of any other person . The promisor is the indemnifier and the promisee is the indemnified (indemnity-holder) . Nature: two parties; a contingent contract; the liability arises on the loss. The Act’s definition is narrower than the English one because it covers only losses caused by human conduct ; losses from fire, accident or other events not caused by human agency are not within the strict statutory definition. In Gajanan Moreshwar v Moreshwar Madan (Bombay HC, 1942), the court held that the Act’s provisions are not exhaustive and that equitable principles of indemnity apply, so the indemnifier must pay even before the indemnity-holder has actually paid, if the liability has become absolute. Insurance contracts (fire, marine, motor) are contracts of indemnity, but life and personal accident insurance are not (the loss cannot be measured). Rights of the indemnity-holder (s.125), when sued: (1) all damages he is compelled to pay in a suit in respect of any matter covered by the promise; (2) all costs he is compelled to pay in bringing or defending the suit, if he acted as prudently as in his own case or under the promisor’s authority; and (3) all sums paid under the terms of a compromise of the suit, if not contrary to the promisor’s orders and if prudent or authorised.

p: Specific Contracts: Bailment, Pledge, Indemnity, Guarantee and Agency · Commercial Law
x: Definition (s.126): a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default . The person giving the guarantee is the surety ; the person in respect of whose default it is given is the principal debtor ; the person to whom it is given is the creditor . A guarantee may be oral or written . Essentials: three parties (principal debtor, creditor, surety); a liability which is existing or likely to arise; a promise by the surety; consideration (s.127: anything done or any promise made for the benefit of the principal debtor is sufficient consideration; the surety need not benefit directly); free consent, and no misrepresentation or concealment (ss.142–143). A guarantee obtained by misrepresentation or concealment of a material part of the circumstances is invalid (but contracts of guarantee are not contracts uberrimae fidei in the strict insurance sense; the creditor must disclose facts that would affect the surety’s willingness). Kinds: specific (a single debt or transaction) and continuing (s.129: extends to a series of transactions, such as a bank overdraft). Revocation of a continuing guarantee: by notice to the creditor as to future transactions (s.130), and by the death of the surety as to future transactions in the absence of a contract to the contrary (s.131). Extent of liability (s.128): the surety’s liability is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless the contract provides otherwise. It is immediate , and the creditor need not first proceed against the principal debtor or realise other securities ( Bank of Bihar v Damodar Prasad , 1969; State Bank of India v Indexport Registered , 1992). Discharge of the surety (ss.133–139): Section Mode of discharge s.133 Variance in the terms of the contract between creditor and principal debtor without the surety’s consent s.134 Release or discharge of the principal debtor by the creditor’s contract, or by the creditor’s act or omission that legally discharges him s.135 Creditor’s composition with, giving time to, or promise not to sue the principal debtor, without the surety’s consent s.139 Creditor’s act or omission impairing the surety’s eventual remedy against the principal debtor s.141 Loss or parting with security by the creditor (the surety is discharged to the extent of its value) Not discharging the surety: s.136 (agreement by the creditor with a third person to give time to the principal debtor), s.137 (mere forbearance to sue), s.138 (release of one co-surety does not discharge the others, nor free him from liability to contribute), and the principal debtor’s insolvency (a discharge by operation of law). Rights of the surety: Against the principal debtor: subrogation and indemnity on payment (s.140, s.145), the right to the benefit of the creditor’s securities (s.141). Against the creditor: to have the securities handed over on payment. Against co-sureties: contribution (s.146: equally, in the absence of a contract; s.147: where co-sureties are bound in different sums, equally, subject to the limit of the maximum). Bank guarantees and letters of credit: a performance or bank guarantee is an independent contract between bank and beneficiary and generally must be honoured on demand. Courts restrain payment only for fraud or irretrievable injury/special equity ( U.P. Co-operative Federation v Singh Consultants , 1988; Svenska Handelsbanken v Indian Charge Chrome , 1994; Standard Chartered Bank v Heavy Engineering Corporation , 2020). Indemnity vs guarantee: Basis Indemnity Guarantee Parties Two (indemnifier and indemnified) Three (creditor, principal debtor, surety) Contracts One Three (principal debt, creditor–surety, surety–debtor implied indemnity) Liability Primary and independent Secondary (arises on default) Right to sue third party Indemnifier cannot ordinarily sue the third party Surety can sue the principal debtor after payment Nature Contingent Conditional on default

p: Specific Contracts: Bailment, Pledge, Indemnity, Guarantee and Agency · Commercial Law
x: Definition (s.182): an agent is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in dealings with third persons. The person for whom the act is done is the principal . Capacity: the principal must have attained majority and be of sound mind (s.183). Any person may be an agent, but a minor or person of unsound mind cannot be made responsible to the principal (s.184). No consideration is necessary (s.185). Kinds of agents: general, special and universal; mercantile agents (factor, broker, commission agent, auctioneer, del credere agent, banker); sub-agents (s.191) and substituted agents (s.194). Del credere agent: for an extra commission guarantees the solvency of third parties. Creation of agency: express or implied (s.187); by necessity (s.189, emergency, Great Northern Railway v Swaffield ); by ratification (ss.196–200); by estoppel/holding out (s.237); by operation of law (partnership, s.18 Partnership Act); and by prior relationship (husband and wife in the matter of household necessities). Authority of agent: s.188 (an agent having authority to do an act has authority to do every lawful thing necessary); s.189 (emergency); s.190 (delegation) : delegatus non potest delegare , but sub-agency is allowed where ordinary business custom, the nature of the agency requires, or purely ministerial acts. Ratification (ss.196–200): where acts are done by one person on behalf of another without authority, the principal may ratify them, expressly or impliedly. The agent must have purported to act for the principal ; the principal must have been in existence at the time of the act ( Kelner v Baxter : a promoter cannot bind a company not yet in existence) and competent at ratification. The principal must have full knowledge of material facts (s.198). The whole transaction must be ratified (s.199). Ratification cannot be used to injure a third person (s.200), and it cannot be made after the time for performance has passed. Ratification has retrospective effect (relation back; Bolton Partners v Lambert ). Duties of an agent: follow the principal’s directions (s.211); act with reasonable skill and diligence (s.212); render accounts (s.213); communicate with the principal in difficulty (s.214); no secret profit and no dealing on his own account without disclosure (ss.215–216); pay sums received (s.218). Rights: remuneration (s.219), retainer (s.217), lien (s.221), indemnity for lawful acts (s.222), and indemnity for acts done in good faith (s.223). Termination (s.201): by revocation by the principal, renunciation by the agent, completion of the business, death or unsoundness of mind of either, insolvency of the principal, and expiry of time. Agency coupled with interest (s.202): the agent has an interest in the property that is the subject matter; it cannot be terminated to the prejudice of that interest in the absence of an express contract. Revocation is not allowed after the authority has been partly exercised (s.204), and reasonable notice is needed (s.206). Liability to third parties: Disclosed principal: the principal is bound, the agent is not personally liable (s.226 and s.230). s.230 exceptions (agent personally liable): contract for goods to be bought from abroad, where the agent does not disclose the principal’s name, and where the principal cannot be sued. Undisclosed principal (s.231): the third party may hold either the agent or the principal liable once the principal is discovered. s.235: a pretended agent is liable for breach of the warranty of authority . s.237: the principal is bound where he induced the third party to believe the agent’s acts were authorised (estoppel). s.238: misrepresentation or fraud by an agent affects the contract as if made by the principal. s.229: notice to the agent is notice to the principal.

t: Overview: Specific Contracts: Bailment, Pledge, Indemnity, Guarantee and Agency
p: Specific Contracts: Bailment, Pledge, Indemnity, Guarantee and Agency · Commercial Law
x: Where they sit in the Indian Contract Act, 1872: Indemnity and Guarantee = ss.124–147; Bailment = ss.148–171; Pledge = ss.172–179; Agency = ss.182–238. (Chapter VIII covers bailment and pledge; Chapter X covers agency.)

p: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 · Commercial Law
x: Buyer s.2(1); delivery s.2(2): voluntary transfer of possession from one person to another; deliverable state s.2(3); document of title s.2(4); fault s.2(5); future goods s.2(6): goods to be manufactured, produced or acquired by the seller after making the contract. Goods s.2(7): every kind of movable property other than actionable claims and money ; includes stock and shares, growing crops, grass, and things attached to or forming part of the land which are agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale . Insolvent s.2(8); mercantile agent s.2(9); price s.2(10): money consideration for a sale of goods; property s.2(11): the general property (ownership) in goods, not merely a special property; quality of goods s.2(12); seller s.2(13); specific goods s.2(14): goods identified and agreed upon at the time the contract of sale is made. Classification of goods (s.6): existing (owned or possessed by the seller) or future ; specific, ascertained, unascertained ; and contingent goods (future goods the acquisition of which depends on a contingency).

p: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 · Commercial Law
x: s.4(1): a contract whereby the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price . It may be absolute or conditional. s.4(3): sale is when property in goods is transferred at the time of the contract (an executed contract); s.4(4): agreement to sell is when the transfer takes place at a future time or subject to a condition later to be fulfilled (an executory contract). An agreement to sell becomes a sale when the time elapses or the conditions are fulfilled. Essentials: two parties (buyer and seller, different persons); goods; a price in money; transfer of property; and the usual elements of a valid contract. s.5: no particular form required, and the contract may be oral or written, or implied from conduct. s.7: if the contract is for specific goods which, without the knowledge of the seller, have perished at the time of the agreement, the agreement is void . s.8: where specific goods perish after the agreement to sell but before the risk passes to the buyer, without fault of either party, the agreement is avoided . Sale vs agreement to sell: Basis Sale Agreement to sell Nature Executed; a conveyance Executory contract Transfer of property Immediate At a future time or on a condition Remedy on breach by buyer Seller can sue for the price Seller can sue only for damages Risk Passes to the buyer ( res perit domino ) Remains with the seller Insolvency of buyer Seller must deliver and has only a claim for the price Seller can refuse to deliver Sale vs other transactions: vs bailment (no transfer of ownership); vs barter/exchange (no price in money); vs gift (no price); vs hire-purchase (the hirer has only an option to buy; see K.L. Johar & Co. v Deputy Commercial Tax Officer , 1965); vs pledge (security, not transfer of ownership); vs contract for work and labour (the substance is skill and labour, not sale of goods). Price (ss.9–10): fixed by the contract, or left to be fixed in a manner agreed, or determined by the course of dealing; otherwise the buyer must pay a reasonable price (s.9(2)). s.10: where the price is to be fixed by a third-party valuer who fails, the agreement is void, but the buyer who has taken goods must pay a reasonable price. s.11: unless otherwise agreed, stipulations as to time of payment are not the essence of the contract.

p: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 · Commercial Law
x: Condition (s.12(2)): a stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract, the breach of which gives the buyer the right to repudiate the contract (and claim damages). Warranty (s.12(3)): a stipulation collateral to the main purpose, the breach of which gives a right to damages only , not to reject the goods. s.12(4): whether a stipulation is a condition or warranty depends on the construction of the contract. A stipulation may be a condition though called a warranty. s.13: a condition may be treated as a warranty where the buyer waives the condition, elects to treat the breach as a breach of warranty, or accepts the goods (in a non-severable contract, where specific goods are involved). Implied conditions and warranties: s.14(a): Condition as to title. The seller has a right to sell the goods (or will have a right at the time property is to pass). Case: Rowland v Divall (the buyer recovers the full price although he used the car, because there was a total failure of consideration). s.14(b): Warranty of quiet possession. s.14(c): Warranty that goods are free from any charge or encumbrance in favour of a third party not declared or known to the buyer. s.15: Sale by description. The goods must correspond with the description ( Varley v Whipp ; Beale v Taylor ). If the sale is by sample as well as description, the bulk must correspond with both (s.17). s.16(1): Fitness for purpose. Where the buyer expressly or by implication makes known to the seller the particular purpose and relies on the seller’s skill or judgment , there is an implied condition that the goods are reasonably fit for that purpose ( Priest v Last ; Grant v Australian Knitting Mills ). The proviso: in the case of a specified article under its patent or trade name , there is no implied condition of fitness. s.16(2): Merchantable quality. Where goods are bought by description from a seller who deals in goods of that description , there is an implied condition that goods are of merchantable quality. If the buyer has examined the goods, there is no implied condition regarding defects which such examination ought to have revealed ( Wallis v Pratt ). The doctrine of caveat emptor (let the buyer beware) is the general rule, subject to these exceptions. s.16(3): implied conditions annexed by usage of trade. s.16(4): an express warranty does not negate an implied condition unless inconsistent. s.17: Sale by sample: the bulk must correspond with the sample in quality; the buyer must have a reasonable opportunity to compare; the goods must be free from defect not apparent on reasonable examination of the sample.

p: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 · Commercial Law
x: s.18: where there is a contract for the sale of unascertained goods , no property in the goods is transferred until the goods are ascertained . ( Specific goods: s.19.) s.19(1)–(2): in specific or ascertained goods, property passes at the time the parties intend it to pass, judged by the terms of the contract, the conduct of the parties and the circumstances. Rules for ascertaining intention (ss.20–24): s.20: specific goods in a deliverable state : property passes at the time of the contract, even if payment or delivery is postponed. s.21: specific goods to be put into a deliverable state by the seller: property passes when the seller does so and the buyer has notice . s.22: specific goods in a deliverable state, but the seller has to weigh, measure or test them to ascertain the price: property passes when the act is done and the buyer has notice. s.23: unascertained or future goods by description: property passes when goods of that description and in a deliverable state are unconditionally appropriated to the contract, with the assent (express or implied) of the other party. s.24: Goods sent on approval or ‘on sale or return’: property passes (a) when the buyer signifies approval or acceptance, (b) when he does any act adopting the transaction (for example pledging or selling the goods), or (c) when he retains the goods beyond the time fixed (or a reasonable time) without giving notice of rejection. s.25: Reservation of the right of disposal (until conditions are fulfilled). Where goods are shipped and the bill of lading makes the goods deliverable to the seller or his agent, the seller is prima facie reserving the right of disposal. s.26: Risk prima facie follows property ( res perit domino ), whether delivery has been made or not. If delivery is delayed by the fault of either party, the goods are at the risk of the party in fault as regards any loss that might not have occurred but for such fault.

t: 5.5 Transfer of Title: Sale by Non-Owners (ss.27–30)
p: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 · Commercial Law
x: General rule: nemo dat quod non habet : no one can give a better title than he himself has. Exceptions: s.27 (Estoppel): where the owner, by conduct or words, leads the buyer to believe that the seller is the owner or has authority to sell, the owner is estopped from denying the seller’s authority. Also sale by a mercantile agent in possession of goods or documents of title with the owner’s consent, in the ordinary course of business, and where the buyer acts in good faith without notice. s.28 (Joint owners): sale by one of several joint owners in sole possession with the consent of the others. s.29 (Voidable title): a person in possession under a contract voidable on grounds such as fraud sells before the contract is rescinded, and the buyer acts in good faith without notice. s.30(1) (Seller in possession after sale): the seller, continuing in possession, delivers or transfers the goods to a person who takes in good faith without notice. s.30(2) (Buyer in possession): the buyer, having obtained possession with the seller’s consent, delivers or transfers the goods to a person who takes in good faith without notice. Other exceptions: a sale by a finder of lost goods (s.169 ICA), by a pawnee (s.176 ICA), by an unpaid seller exercising his right of resale (s.54), under an order of court or an execution sale, and sale by an official assignee or insolvency official . Cases: Eastern Distributors v Goldring ; Lickbarrow v Mason (documents of title).

p: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 · Commercial Law
x: s.31: the duty of the seller is to deliver the goods and of the buyer to accept and pay for them. s.32: delivery and payment are concurrent conditions unless otherwise agreed. Modes of delivery (s.33): actual (physical handing over), constructive (the person in possession acknowledges that he holds on behalf of the buyer), and symbolic (the means of control, such as the keys of a warehouse or a bill of lading). s.34: part delivery is a delivery of the whole if made with the intent to deliver the whole. s.35: the seller is not bound to deliver unless the buyer applies for delivery. s.36: place of delivery; the cost of putting goods in a deliverable state is borne by the seller; the buyer must pay for the cost of taking delivery . s.37: delivery of the wrong quantity (less: the buyer may reject; more: the buyer may accept the contracted quantity and reject the excess, or reject the whole). s.38: instalment deliveries (no obligation to accept in instalments unless agreed). s.39: delivery to a carrier is prima facie delivery to the buyer. s.40: deterioration in transit. s.41: the buyer’s right to examine the goods. s.42: acceptance occurs when the buyer intimates acceptance, does an act inconsistent with the seller’s ownership, or retains the goods beyond a reasonable time. s.43: a buyer who rightfully refuses is not bound to return the goods. s.44: liability of the buyer for neglecting or refusing delivery.

p: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 · Commercial Law
x: Who is an unpaid seller (s.45): one to whom the whole of the price has not been paid or tendered, or who has received a bill of exchange or negotiable instrument as conditional payment that is dishonoured. Rights (s.46): Rights against the goods (even where property has passed): Lien (ss.47–49): to retain possession until payment or tender, where the goods were sold without any stipulation as to credit, or the credit term has expired, or the buyer has become insolvent . s.49: the lien is lost by delivery to a carrier without reserving the right of disposal, by the buyer lawfully obtaining possession, or by waiver. A part delivery does not by itself lose the lien (s.48). Stoppage in transit (ss.50–52): the right to resume possession of goods in transit when the buyer becomes insolvent . Transit begins when the goods are delivered to a carrier and ends when the buyer or his agent takes delivery (s.51). The stoppage is effected by taking actual possession or by giving notice to the carrier (s.52). Resale (s.54): by an unpaid seller who has exercised a right of lien or stoppage, where the goods are perishable, or where he gives notice to the buyer of his intention to resell and the buyer does not pay within a reasonable time. If there is a loss on resale, the seller may recover it from the buyer; the surplus belongs to the seller where there was no condition about resale and the buyer was in default. Rights against the buyer personally: s.55 suit for the price (where property has passed and the buyer wrongfully neglects to pay, or where the price is payable on a certain day irrespective of delivery); s.56 damages for non-acceptance ; s.61 interest and special damages.

p: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 · Commercial Law
x: s.57: damages for non-delivery . s.58: specific performance (for specific or ascertained goods), now to be read with the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as amended in 2018. s.59: remedy for breach of warranty : set off the loss against the price or sue for damages. s.60: repudiation of the contract before the date of delivery (anticipatory breach). s.61: interest and special damages. s.62: exclusion of implied terms by express agreement or custom. s.63: reasonable time is a question of fact.

p: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 · Commercial Law
x: The sale is divided into lots; each lot is a separate contract unless otherwise agreed. The sale is complete on the fall of the hammer (or other customary announcement); until then, a bidder may withdraw his bid. The right to bid may be reserved expressly ; if not, the seller or any person on his behalf may not bid, and any sale in contravention is voidable at the buyer’s option . A reserve price may be stipulated. Pretended bidding to raise the price makes the sale voidable (s.64(6)).

p: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 · Commercial Law
x: Basics: in force from 1 July 1930 ; ss.1–66; carved out of the Contract Act (old ss.76–123). The general Contract Act principles apply unless inconsistent (s.3). It does not apply to sale of immovable property.

t: Memory Capsule: Sale of Goods Act, 1930
p: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 · Commercial Law
x: Be able to match: s.4 (definition), s.12 (condition and warranty), s.14 (title), s.16 (fitness and merchantable quality), s.18–26 (property and risk), s.27–30 (title by non-owners), s.45–54 (unpaid seller), s.55–61 (suits), s.64 (auction) . Remember the insolvency link: lien and stoppage in transit are tied to buyer’s insolvency; resale needs notice (except perishables). Consumer law now overlays SOGA: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (product liability, defective goods, unfair contracts).

p: Partnership and Limited Liability Partnership · Commercial Law
x: Basics: in force from 1 October 1932 (except s.69, effective 1 October 1933); ss.1–69 (original structure), replacing Chapter XI of the Contract Act (ss.239–266). Partnership is governed by the principles of contract (s.5: it arises from contract, not from status; members of a Hindu undivided family carrying on business are not partners merely by status). Definition (s.4): the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all . Persons are individually partners and collectively a firm ; the name is the firm name . Essentials: An agreement between two or more persons (contractual capacity required). A business (a continuous activity for profit). Sharing of profits (sharing of losses is not essential; sharing of gross receipts is not partnership). Mutual agency : the business is carried on by all or any of them acting for all. This is the real test ( Cox v Hickman , 1860: mere sharing of profits is not conclusive; Mollwo March & Co. v Court of Wards , 1872). s.6 (Mode of determining existence): regard must be had to the real relation between the parties, as shown by all relevant facts taken together. Sharing of profits or gross returns, or receipt of a share of profits, does not by itself make a person a partner. Maximum number of partners: 50 (Companies Act, 2013, s.464, read with Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014); 10 for banking business. An association exceeding the limit is an illegal association. Firm is not a legal person (it is not distinct from partners in civil law), although for income tax and certain other purposes it is treated as a unit. Kinds of partners: active (working), sleeping/dormant, nominal, partner by estoppel/holding out (s.28), partner in profits only, sub-partner, and a minor admitted to the benefits (s.30). Kinds of partnership: at will (s.7: no fixed duration; any partner may dissolve by notice, s.43) and particular (s.8: for a particular venture or adventure).

t: 6.2 Relations of Partners to One Another (ss.9–17)
p: Partnership and Limited Liability Partnership · Commercial Law
x: s.9: partners must carry on the business to the greatest common advantage, be just and faithful to each other, and render true accounts and full information. s.10: duty to indemnify for loss caused by fraud. s.11: the mutual rights and duties may be determined by contract, and may be varied by consent. s.12: rights of partners: every partner has the right to take part in the conduct of the business; to be consulted and heard (a decision in the ordinary course of business is by majority, but a change in the nature of the business requires consent of all); to have access to books; and the duty to act diligently. s.13: unless otherwise agreed: no remuneration; profits shared equally and losses in the profit ratio; interest on capital: none ; interest on advances beyond capital: 6% per annum ; right to be indemnified for expenses incurred and liabilities in an emergency or in the ordinary conduct of business; liability for wilful neglect. s.14: property of the firm: all property originally brought in or acquired in the course of business, including goodwill. s.15: application of firm property exclusively for the firm’s business. s.16: personal profits earned by a partner from firm’s business or use of its property or name; competing business (the partner must account for and pay over the profit). s.17: rights and duties after change in the constitution of the firm (on a continuing basis); the partner’s rights after the firm’s dissolution.

t: 6.3 Relations of Partners to Third Parties (ss.18–30)
p: Partnership and Limited Liability Partnership · Commercial Law
x: s.18: a partner is the agent of the firm for the purposes of its business. s.19: implied authority to bind the firm in acts done in the usual way of business. Exceptions (not allowed unless there is a contract to the contrary): submit a dispute to arbitration; open a bank account in his own name; compromise or relinquish a claim; withdraw a suit; admit liability in a suit; acquire immovable property on behalf of the firm; transfer immovable property belonging to the firm; enter into partnership on behalf of the firm . s.20: express restriction of implied authority is effective against third parties with notice. s.21: emergency authority. s.22: mode of binding the firm (an act done in the firm name or in any manner expressing intention to bind). s.23: admissions by a partner concerning the affairs of the firm are evidence against the firm. s.24: notice to the acting partner is notice to the firm. s.25: Liability of every partner for all acts of the firm done while he is a partner is joint and several . s.26–27: the firm is liable for wrongs and misapplication of money by a partner acting in the ordinary course of business ( Hamlyn v Houston , an English authority). s.28/29: Holding out: a person who represents himself, or knowingly lets himself be represented, as a partner is liable to those who have given credit on that faith. A partner by estoppel . s.30: Minors: a minor cannot be a partner but may be admitted to the benefits with the consent of all. He has a share of profits and property, may inspect accounts, and cannot sue the firm for his share except for dissolution. He is not personally liable. On attaining majority (or on knowing he was admitted), within six months he must give public notice electing whether to become or not become a partner. If he elects to become a partner, he becomes personally liable to third parties for acts of the firm since he was admitted to the benefits; if he elects not to, his share is not liable for acts after the date of the notice.

p: Partnership and Limited Liability Partnership · Commercial Law
x: s.31: a new partner can be introduced only with the consent of all the partners, unless otherwise agreed. An incoming partner is not liable for acts before joining (s.31(2)). s.32: Retirement: with the consent of all, by agreement, or by notice in the case of a partnership at will. A retiring partner remains liable for acts before retirement, and also for subsequent acts until public notice is given (s.32(3)). His liability can be discharged by an agreement with the third party and the continuing partners. s.33: Expulsion: only in good faith, by a power conferred by contract and exercised by a majority. s.34: insolvency of a partner. s.35: death of a partner (the estate is not liable for subsequent acts). s.36: rights of an outgoing partner to carry on a competing business (permitted, unless restrained by contract, but he cannot use the firm name or represent himself as carrying on the firm’s business). s.37: an outgoing partner (where the business continues without final settlement) has the right to a share in subsequent profits or to 6% interest on his share at his option.

p: Partnership and Limited Liability Partnership · Commercial Law
x: Dissolution of the firm differs from dissolution of partnership : the former ends the whole firm, while the latter means the relationship between some partners changes (for example, by retirement) and the firm continues. Modes: s.40: by agreement. s.41: Compulsory dissolution: on insolvency of all partners, or all but one, or on any event that makes the business or partnership unlawful. s.42: By contingencies (subject to contract): expiry of term; completion of the adventure; death of a partner; insolvency of a partner. s.43: by notice in partnerships at will. s.44: By the court on grounds: unsound mind; permanent incapacity of a partner; misconduct likely to prejudicially affect the business; persistent breach of agreement; transfer of the whole interest of a partner to a third party; the business can only be carried on at a loss; and any other just and equitable ground . Consequences: s.45: continued liability for acts after dissolution until public notice (not for the estate of a deceased, insolvent or retired partner’s apparent liability). s.46: right of partners to have the business wound up and property applied in payment of debts. s.47: authority to continue for winding up. s.48: Mode of settlement of accounts in the absence of agreement: (a) losses , including deficiencies of capital, are paid first out of profits , next out of capital , and lastly, if necessary, by the partners individually in the proportion in which they were entitled to share profits ( Garner v Murray : a solvent partner need not make up the deficiency of an insolvent partner’s capital); (b) assets are applied in the following order: debts to third parties , then advances (loans) by partners (rateably), then capital of each partner, and the residue (if any) is shared in the profit ratio. s.49: the right to personal profits earned after dissolution. s.51: return of premium on premature dissolution. s.52: where a partnership is rescinded for fraud, the party defrauded has a lien and rights. s.53: restraining use of the firm name or property after dissolution. s.54–55: agreements in restraint of trade and goodwill (the goodwill is sold with the business, and the selling partner may be restrained from carrying on a competing business).

p: Partnership and Limited Liability Partnership · Commercial Law
x: Registration is optional , not compulsory. Procedure: an application to the Registrar of Firms, with the prescribed fee, signed by all partners, with the details of firm name, place of business, date of joining, names and addresses, and duration (s.58). Effects of non-registration (s.69): (1) No suit by a partner (or his representative) against the firm or other partners to enforce a right arising from the contract or conferred by the Act. (2) No suit by or on behalf of an unregistered firm against any third party to enforce a right arising from a contract. (3) No set-off or other proceeding claimed by or on behalf of the firm. Exceptions (s.69(3)–(4)): suits for the dissolution of a firm or for accounts, and the realisation of the property of a dissolved firm or an insolvent partner; the right to sue for claims under Rs. 100 ; suits that do not arise out of a contract (torts, statutory rights); firms with no place of business in the territories where the Act applies; third parties can sue an unregistered firm.

p: Partnership and Limited Liability Partnership · Commercial Law
x: Background: Enacted to provide a hybrid form combining limited liability and flexible organisation. It was in force from 31 March 2009 . The LLP Rules, 2009 and the LLP (Amendment) Act, 2021 (and the LLP Rules 2022 after) added reforms.
