Key features: Body corporate and a separate legal entity distinct from its partners (s.3), with perpetual succession (continuity despite changes in partners) and a common seal (optional). Minimum two partners; no upper limit (s.6). If the number falls below two for more than six months , the surviving partner who carries on business with knowledge is personally liable for obligations incurred after that period. Partners: any individual or body corporate (s.5). An individual is not capable of being a partner if he is of unsound mind (declared by a competent court), an undischarged insolvent, or has applied to be adjudicated insolvent. Designated partners (s.7): at least two (individuals) and at least one resident in India (resident means present in India for not less than 120 days in the preceding one year). Each must obtain a Director Identification Number (DIN) . They are responsible for compliance. LLP Agreement (s.23): governs mutual rights and duties; in the absence of agreement, the First Schedule governs (for example, equal profit sharing, no remuneration; each partner has equal rights in management). Partners are agents of the LLP only , not of other partners (s.26). The LLP is not bound by acts of a partner done without authority where the other party knows this (s.27). The LLP is liable for wrongful acts of its partners in the course of business (s.27). Limited liability: the liability of a partner is limited to his agreed contribution . A partner is not personally liable for the wrongful acts of other partners (s.28), but remains liable for his own wrongful act (s.28(2)). s.30: Fraud: where an act is carried out with intent to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose, the LLP and any partner knowingly party to it have unlimited liability for the LLP’s liabilities, and are liable to penal consequences (imprisonment 6 months to 5 years, and a fine). Contributions: may be tangible or intangible property, movable or immovable, or any other benefit (including cash, promissory notes, services). Incorporation (ss.11–15): an incorporation document (and a statement of compliance) is filed online with the Registrar of Companies (through form FiLLiP); the Registrar issues a certificate of incorporation (s.11, 12, 13) which is conclusive evidence. The LLP’s name must end with ‘LLP’ or ‘Limited Liability Partnership’ (s.15). Accounts and compliance: statement of accounts and solvency ( Form 8 ) and annual return ( Form 11 ) are filed every year (ss.34–35). Audit is required if turnover exceeds Rs. 40 lakh or contribution exceeds Rs. 25 lakh (LLP Rules, 2009, Rule 24). Maintenance of proper books for each year. LLP (Amendment) Act, 2021 (notified in 2022): key reforms: Introduced the concept of a ‘small LLP’ (contribution up to Rs. 25 lakh, turnover up to Rs. 40 lakh, as prescribed) with lower penalties for default. Decriminalised and rationalised several offences; introduced compounding and adjudication of penalties. Allowed Indian LLPs to raise funds by way of ECB and allowed conversion and foreign LLP reforms. Provisions on ‘Foreign LLPs’ , appeals to the NCLT and NCLAT , LLP Rules for conversion of firms, private companies and unlisted public companies (Schedules II–IV) into LLPs, and Authority for Adjudicating Officers . Now Central Government-appointed Adjudicating Officers and Special Courts deal with penalties. Conversion: from a partnership firm (Second Schedule), a private company (Third Schedule), or an unlisted public company (Fourth Schedule). LLPs can also convert to a company under the Companies Act, 2013 (Chapter XXI). Winding up (ss.63–64): voluntary or by the Tribunal (NCLT) . The grounds for winding up by the Tribunal include: the LLP decides it should be wound up by the Tribunal; the LLP is unable to pay its debts; the LLP has acted against the sovereignty and integrity of India or the security of the State; the LLP has defaulted in filing the statement of accounts and annual returns for five consecutive financial years ; and the Tribunal considers it just and equitable . The Companies Act provisions apply in so far as they relate to winding up. t: 7.1 Meaning and Kinds of Negotiable Instruments
p: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 · Commercial Law
x: s.13(a): a negotiable instrument means a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque payable either to order or to bearer . The essential idea is free transferability , with the right to give a good title to a holder in due course free from the defects of earlier holders. Features: (1) freely transferable by delivery (bearer) or endorsement and delivery (order); (2) the holder takes in his own name and may sue in his own name; (3) a holder in due course gets a better title than the transferor (an exception to the nemo dat rule); (4) notice of transfer is not required; (5) there is a presumption as to consideration, date, acceptance, transfer, endorsement and stamp (s.118). Instrument Section Definition (short) Parties Promissory note s.4 A written, unconditional undertaking , signed by the maker, to pay a certain sum of money only to, or to the order of, a certain person or to the bearer. Not a bank note or a currency note. Maker (promisor) and payee Bill of exchange s.5 A written, unconditional order , signed by the maker, directing a certain person to pay a certain sum only to, or to the order of, a certain person or to the bearer. Drawer, drawee (acceptor on acceptance), payee Cheque s.6 A bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker and not expressed to be payable otherwise than on demand . It includes the electronic image of a truncated cheque and a cheque in electronic form (added by the 2002 amendment). Drawer, drawee bank, payee Differences: A promissory note has two parties , a bill has three . A promissory note is a promise to pay, a bill is an order. A promissory note needs no acceptance; a bill (except one payable on demand) needs acceptance by the drawee . A cheque is always payable on demand and drawn on a banker . A promissory note cannot be made payable to bearer on demand (s.31 RBI Act reserved the issue of such notes to the RBI). Kinds of bills: inland or foreign; time or demand; trade or accommodation bills. Maturity (s.21–25): an instrument payable at a fixed period matures on the due date after three days of grace (s.22); if the last day is a public holiday, the instrument is due on the preceding business day (s.25). Instruments payable on demand or at sight carry no days of grace. Other key definitions: s.8: holder (entitled in his own name to the possession and to recover the amount); s.9: holder in due course (HDC): (i) takes the instrument for consideration , (ii) before maturity , (iii) without notice of any defect in the title of the transferor, and (iv) it is a negotiable instrument in complete and regular form (s.9 says: becomes the possessor of a cheque payable to bearer or the payee/endorsee of an order instrument). s.10: payment in due course : in accordance with the apparent tenor, in good faith and without negligence, to the person in possession, and under circumstances which do not afford a reasonable ground for believing he is not entitled to receive the payment.

p: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 · Commercial Law
x: s.14: negotiation is the transfer to any person so as to constitute him the holder. A bearer instrument is negotiated by delivery (s.47); an order instrument by endorsement and delivery (s.48). Endorsement (ss.15–16): the signature of the maker or holder on the instrument, on the back or face, for the purpose of negotiation. Kinds: in blank (signature only; then becomes payable to bearer), in full (name of the endorsee), restrictive (prohibits further negotiation: ‘pay D only’), conditional , partial (invalid: s.56), sans recours , and facultative . s.118: presumptions until the contrary is proved: (a) consideration ; (b) date ; (c) time of acceptance ; (d) time of transfer ; (e) order of endorsements ; (f) stamp ; (g) that the holder is a holder in due course . s.139: it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder received the cheque for the discharge, in whole or in part, of a debt or other liability. s.53: a holder in due course gets a good title free from the defects of the transferor’s title, and even if the transferor obtained it by fraud, unless the holder himself was a party to the fraud. s.58: an instrument obtained by unlawful means or for unlawful consideration cannot be recovered by the person who obtained it unless he is a HDC. Liability of parties: s.30 the drawer of a bill or cheque is bound to compensate the holder if the instrument is dishonoured; s.32 the acceptor is primarily liable ; s.35 the endorser is liable to subsequent holders; s.37 the maker of a promissory note is primarily liable . s.38: as between prior and subsequent parties, the prior parties are liable to the later. s.41–42: acceptance for honour ( s.108 onwards ). Capacity (s.26): every person capable of contracting may bind himself as a maker, drawer, acceptor, endorser etc. A minor may draw, endorse, deliver and negotiate so as to bind all parties except himself . Material alteration (s.87): a material alteration without the consent of the parties avoids the instrument, except against a party who made or authorised or consented to the alteration (and subsequent parties). A holder in due course can recover as it originally stood (s.88 and s.89).

p: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 · Commercial Law
x: Presentment for acceptance (ss.61–75): a bill payable after sight must be presented for acceptance. Presentment for payment is required (s.64) to charge the parties, within a reasonable time, during business hours, at the proper place. A cheque must be presented within its validity period ( three months from the date of the cheque, per RBI direction effective 1 April 2012, and within the period of its validity under s.138). Dishonour: by non-acceptance or non-payment. Notice of dishonour (ss.93–98) must be given to parties sought to be held liable. Noting and protest (ss.99–104): noting by a notary public, and protest for foreign bills. Discharge (ss.77–82): by payment in due course (s.78), by cancellation, release, material alteration, or merger. The drawer and endorsers are discharged by delay in presentment, by the holder’s default, and by novation.

p: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 · Commercial Law
x: General crossing (s.123): two parallel transverse lines, with or without the words ‘& Co.’, ‘not negotiable’; the cheque is payable only through a bank account, not over the counter. Special crossing (s.124): the name of a particular banker is written across the face; the drawee bank must pay only to that banker or his agent. s.125: the holder may cross an uncrossed cheque, or a generally crossed cheque specially. s.126: payment in due course of a crossed cheque. s.128: payment in due course of a crossed cheque protects the paying banker. s.129: a banker who pays a crossed cheque otherwise than as directed is liable to the true owner. s.130: the effect of the words ‘not negotiable’ : the holder cannot give a better title than he himself has. s.131: protection to a collecting banker who in good faith and without negligence receives payment for a customer. s.131A: extension to drafts.

p: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 · Commercial Law
x: Chapter XVII was inserted in 1988 to ensure the credibility of cheques as payment instruments. It makes the dishonour of a cheque for insufficiency of funds (or because it exceeds the arrangement with the bank) a criminal offence . Ingredients of s.138: A cheque is drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker, in favour of another person. It is issued for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability that is legally enforceable . The cheque is presented to the bank within three months (or within its validity period, whichever is earlier). The cheque is returned unpaid because the money standing to the credit of the account is insufficient , or exceeds the arrangement with the bank. The payee or holder in due course gives a written demand notice within 30 days of receiving information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque. The drawer fails to pay within 15 days of receipt of the notice. The cause of action arises on the expiry of the 15-day period. Complaint must be filed within one month from the date on which the cause of action arises (s.142(1)(b)), though the court may condone delay for sufficient cause. Punishment: imprisonment up to two years , or a fine up to twice the amount of the cheque , or both (2002 amendment). Related provisions: s.139: statutory presumption that the cheque was issued for a legally enforceable debt. The accused can rebut it on the preponderance of probabilities , not beyond reasonable doubt ( Rangappa v Sri Mohan , 2010; Bir Singh v Mukesh Kumar , 2019: even a signed blank cheque voluntarily given attracts the presumption). s.140: it is not a defence that the drawer had no reason to believe the cheque would be dishonoured. s.141: Offences by companies: every person who, at the time of the offence, was in charge of and responsible to the company for the conduct of its business is deemed guilty. The company must be arraigned as an accused ( Aneeta Hada v Godfather Travels & Tours , 2012). A director is liable only if in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business ( S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals v Neeta Bhalla , 2005); a signatory of the cheque is automatically liable. s.142: Cognizance: only on a written complaint by the payee or holder in due course. s.142(2) (inserted by the 2015 amendment): the court within whose local jurisdiction the branch of the bank where the payee or holder maintains the account is situated has jurisdiction (in case of a cheque delivered for collection through an account). This overruled Dashrath Rupsingh Rathod v State of Maharashtra (2014), which had held that the drawer’s bank branch alone determines jurisdiction. Earlier, K. Bhaskaran v Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan (1999) held that the five acts constituting the offence give multiple venues. s.143: Summary trial (with power to impose a sentence up to one year and fine of up to Rs. 5,000 under the CrPC, now Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023). Time limit for trial: six months (directory). s.145: evidence on affidavit. s.146: the bank’s slip is prima facie evidence of dishonour. s.147: the offence is compoundable ( Damodar S. Prabhu v Sayed Babalal H. , 2010: guidelines on costs for compounding; Meters and Instruments v Kanchan Mehta , 2017). s.143A: Interim compensation (inserted by the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment) Act, 2018 ): the court may direct the drawer to pay interim compensation up to 20% of the cheque amount to the complainant. For a summary trial, on the plea of not guilty; in other cases, upon framing the charge. It is to be paid within 60 days (extendable by 30 days). s.148: in an appeal by the drawer against conviction, the appellate court may order deposit of a minimum of 20% of the fine or compensation awarded by the trial court (2018 amendment; applies to pending appeals: Surinder Singh Deswal v Virender Gandhi , 2019). If the appeal succeeds, the amount is returned with interest. Other leading cases on s.138: NEPC Micon v Magma Leasing (1999): closure of the account amounts to dishonour for insufficiency of funds. Modi Cements v Kuchil Kumar Nandi (1998) and Laxmi Dyechem v State of Gujarat (2012): stop-payment instruction or signature mismatch can attract s.138 if the cheque was issued for a debt. MSR Leathers v S. Palaniappan (2013): a cheque may be presented multiple times within its validity, and a fresh cause of action arises each time (but only one complaint on a given cause). Kusum Ingots & Alloys v Pennar Peterson Securities (2000): the notice is the prerequisite. Indian Bank Association v Union of India (2014): directions for speedy trial; Re: Expeditious Trial of Cases under Section 138 of NI Act (2021): constitution of special courts and procedural reforms. Sampelly Satyanarayana Rao v IREDA (2016): the debt must be legally enforceable. Exam tip: timelines are a favourite: 3 months (presentment), 30 days (notice), 15 days (payment), 1 month (complaint), 20% (interim compensation and appeal deposit), 2 years / twice the amount (punishment).

p: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 · Commercial Law
x: A banker must honour a customer’s cheque if funds are sufficient; wrongful dishonour exposes the bank to damages ( s.31 ). Garnishee orders and countermand (stop-payment) are duties and risk areas; the banker’s lien (s.171 ICA) is a general lien. The Information Technology Act does not apply to negotiable instruments except cheques (First Schedule, post-2002 amendment on cheque truncation ).

p: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 · Commercial Law
x: Basics: in force from 1 March 1882 ; based on English law (Bills of Exchange Act, 1882). The Act applies to promissory notes, bills of exchange and cheques ; usage and custom may recognise other instruments (for example hundis , as saved by s.1).

p: Company Law: Incorporation, Prospectus, Shares and Debentures · Commercial Law
x: s.2(20): a company means a company incorporated under this Act or any previous company law. Characteristics: incorporated association; separate legal personality ; perpetual succession ; limited liability (in most kinds); common seal (optional after the 2015 amendment); transferable shares; capacity to sue and be sued; and separation of ownership from management. Classification: By incorporation: chartered, statutory, and registered companies. By liability: company limited by shares , limited by guarantee (members guarantee a sum on winding up), and unlimited company . By members: private company (s.2(68)), public company (s.2(71)), and One Person Company (OPC) (s.2(62)). By control: holding (s.2(46)) and subsidiary (s.2(87)), associate company (s.2(6): significant influence, holding of 20% or more of total voting power), and government company (s.2(45): at least 51% of paid-up share capital held by the Central or State governments). Others: small company (s.2(85): paid-up capital up to Rs. 4 crore and turnover up to Rs. 40 crore, as revised in 2022; not a holding or subsidiary company, not a s.8 company, and not governed by a special Act); s.8 company (charitable or non-profit objects, licence from the Central Government, no dividend); Nidhi company ; producer company ; foreign company (s.2(42)); listed company ; dormant company (s.455). Private company (s.2(68)): by its articles it (a) restricts the right to transfer its shares, (b) limits the number of members to 200 (excluding employees, and ex-employees who were members while employed), and (c) prohibits any invitation to the public to subscribe to its securities. The 2015 amendment removed the minimum paid-up capital requirement (earlier Rs. 1 lakh for private and Rs. 5 lakh for public). Minimum number of members (s.3): public company 7 ; private company 2 ; OPC 1 (with a nominee). A public company has no maximum . A private company can have a maximum of 200 members. OPC cannot be incorporated by a non-resident (s.3(1)(c), Rule 3: a natural person who is an Indian citizen and resident in India, with the residence defined as 120 days; the Companies (Incorporation) Second Amendment Rules 2021 permitted NRIs to form OPCs). Minimum directors (s.149): public company 3 , private company 2 , OPC 1 . At least one director must be resident in India (stayed at least 182 days in the previous financial year). At least one woman director for prescribed classes of companies (listed companies and public companies with paid-up capital of Rs. 100 crore or more or turnover of Rs. 300 crore or more). Maximum 15 directors (more by special resolution).

t: 8.2 Corporate Personality and Lifting of the Corporate Veil
p: Company Law: Incorporation, Prospectus, Shares and Debentures · Commercial Law
x: Salomon v Salomon & Co. Ltd. (1897): a company is a distinct legal person, separate from its members; the person who held nearly all shares and was a secured creditor was not liable for company debts. Indian recognition: Tata Engineering v State of Bihar (1964) and Bacha F. Guzdar v CIT (1955: a shareholder is not an owner of the company’s assets). Lee v Lee’s Air Farming (1961): a sole shareholder can be an employee. Macaura v Northern Assurance (1925): a shareholder has no insurable interest in the company’s assets. Lifting the veil: Statutory: reduction in membership below the minimum (s.? and continuing liability), misdescription of the company’s name (s.12(3)), fraud (s.7(7) incorporation by fraud, s.34/s.35 misstatement in prospectus, s.447 fraud), fraudulent trading (s.339), investigation (s.216), and holding–subsidiary accounts (consolidated). Judicial grounds: fraud or improper conduct ( Gilford Motor Co. v Horne ; Jones v Lipman ); sham or façade ; agency ( Smith, Stone & Knight v Birmingham Corp. ); enemy character ( Daimler Co. v Continental Tyre ); tax evasion ( Juggilal Kamlapat v CIT , 1969; Re Sir Dinshaw Maneckjee Petit , 1927); welfare of workers and public interest ( State of U.P. v Renusagar Power , 1988); group enterprises ( DHN Food Distributors v Tower Hamlets ). Cases: Delhi Development Authority v Skipper Construction (1996); Subhra Mukherjee v Bharat Coking Coal (2000); Vodafone International Holdings v Union of India (2012: the corporate veil is respected unless there is a sham or tax evasion; look-through is a ‘look at’ analysis); Singer India v Chander Mohan Chadha (2004). Adams v Cape Industries (1990) restricts veil-lifting in English law, and Prest v Petrodel (2013) holds that it applies only for evasion or concealment.

p: Company Law: Incorporation, Prospectus, Shares and Debentures · Commercial Law
x: Promoter (s.2(69)): a person named as such in a prospectus or annual return, or who has control over the company’s affairs directly or indirectly, or in accordance with whose advice the board is accustomed to act (professional advisers are excluded). Position: neither agent nor trustee, but fiduciary ( Erlanger v New Sombrero Phosphate Co. , 1878). Duties: full disclosure of secret profits; the company may rescind or recover the secret profit. Liabilities: for misstatements in the prospectus (s.34, s.35, s.447). Pre-incorporation contracts: the company is not bound (it did not exist) and cannot ratify them ( Kelner v Baxter ; Newborne v Sensolid ). In India, s.15(h) and s.19(e) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 allow a company to enforce them if they are warranted by the terms of incorporation, the contract was entered into by the promoters before the company existed for its purposes, and the company has accepted the contract and communicated it. The promoter remains liable until the company adopts the contract by a fresh contract (novation) .

p: Company Law: Incorporation, Prospectus, Shares and Debentures · Commercial Law
x: Procedure (steps): Name approval through RUN (Reserve Unique Name), or by SPICe+ (the integrated form INC-32). The name must not be identical or too nearly resemble an existing name or trademark (s.4(2)(a)), must not be undesirable, and must end with ‘ Limited ’ (public), ‘ Private Limited ’ (private), or ‘ OPC ’ in brackets for OPC (s.4(5)). Obtaining DIN (Director Identification Number) and digital signature certificates (DSC) for subscribers and directors. Preparation of the memorandum and articles (INC-33 and INC-34 in the integrated filing). Filing (s.7) with the Registrar of Companies: the memorandum and articles; an agreement (if any) to appoint a managing director or whole-time director; a declaration by an advocate, chartered accountant, cost accountant or company secretary engaged in formation that all requirements have been complied with; an affidavit from each subscriber and the first directors that they are not convicted or disqualified; and the address of the registered office . Certificate of incorporation (s.7(2)) , which also has the CIN . It is conclusive evidence that all requirements have been complied with ( s.7(2) ). Under s.7(7), if it is found that the company was incorporated by furnishing false information or suppressing facts, the Tribunal may order regulation of liability, winding up, or removal of the name. Registered office (s.12): within 30 days of incorporation; notice of verification of the registered office within 30 days of incorporation. Commencement of business (s.10A): inserted in 2019 — a company incorporated after 2019 with share capital must file a declaration (Form INC-20A) within 180 days of incorporation that every subscriber has paid the value of the shares agreed. Effect of registration (s.9): the subscribers become a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal , capable of exercising all functions of an incorporated company, with the liability of members limited as stated. Memorandum of Association (s.4): Name clause ; registered office clause (the State in which the registered office is to be situated); objects clause (main objects, and objects incidental or ancillary); liability clause ; capital clause (in a limited-by-shares company: authorised share capital divided into shares of fixed amounts); association (subscription) clause : each subscriber agrees to take at least one share , and the number of shares taken by each subscriber is stated. Forms: Tables A–E in Schedule I (A: limited by shares; B: guarantee, no share capital; C: guarantee with share capital; D: unlimited, no share capital; E: unlimited with share capital). Alteration: name (s.13(2): special resolution and Central Government approval; after 2016 the Registrar approves under Rule; s.16 change of name if identical or resembling, directed within 3 months); registered office (s.13(4): shifting from one State to another requires a special resolution and the approval of the Regional Director ); objects clause (special resolution, s.13(1)); capital clause (s.61); liability clause (s.? special resolution and consent of the members, and increase of liability needs the member’s consent). Doctrine of ultra vires: acts beyond the powers in the memorandum are void and incapable of ratification ( Ashbury Railway Carriage & Iron Co. v Riche , 1875). Indian case: A. Lakshmanaswami Mudaliar v LIC (1963). Remedies: injunction , personal liability of directors, and recovery of company property by tracing. Acts intra vires the company but beyond the directors’ powers can be ratified by members; acts that are irregular may be ratified. Articles of Association (s.5): the regulations for the management of the company’s internal affairs, subordinate to the Memorandum and the Act . A public company may adopt Table F (Schedule I), and companies may adopt provisions. Entrenchment (s.5(3)): specified provisions can be altered only if conditions or procedures stricter than special resolution are met; notice to the Registrar. Binding effect (s.10): the memorandum and articles bind the company and the members to the same extent as if signed by each member. Cases: Hickman v Kent or Romney Marsh Sheepbreeders’ Association (1915: the articles constitute a contract between the company and the members only in their capacity as members); Eley v Positive Government Security Life Assurance Co. (1876: an outsider cannot enforce); Salmon v Quin & Axtens ; Naresh Chandra Sanyal v Calcutta Stock Exchange (1971). Alteration (s.14): by special resolution, filed with the Registrar within 15 days; conversion of a public company into a private company needs the approval of the Tribunal; the alteration must be bona fide for the benefit of the company as a whole ( Allen v Gold Reefs , 1900; Brown v British Abrasive Wheel Co. ) and must not be retrospective to the detriment of a member. Doctrine of constructive notice: every person dealing with a company is deemed to have read the registered documents (memorandum and articles) ( Ernest v Nicholls ). Doctrine of indoor management (Turquand’s rule): an outsider dealing in good faith may assume that the internal procedures have been regularly complied with ( Royal British Bank v Turquand , 1856; Mahony v East Holyford Mining Co. ). Exceptions to the Turquand rule: (a) knowledge of irregularity ( Howard v Patent Ivory Manufacturing Co. ); (b) suspicion that should have prompted inquiry ( Anand Bihari Lal v Dinshaw & Co. , 1946); (c) forgery ( Ruben v Great Fingall Consolidated ); (d) documents or acts not within the apparent authority or outside the memorandum (ultra vires); (e) no reliance on the articles and no actual dealing with the company ( Rama Corporation v Proved Tin & General Investment Co. ). Also, the Indian Companies Act s.? (Turquand’s rule) is not codified .

p: Company Law: Incorporation, Prospectus, Shares and Debentures · Commercial Law
x: Definition (s.2(70)): any document described or issued as a prospectus, including a red herring prospectus (s.32) or shelf prospectus (s.31), or any notice, circular, advertisement or other document inviting offers from the public for the subscription or purchase of any securities of a body corporate. Modes of raising securities (s.23): a public company may issue securities (a) to the public through a prospectus (public offer), (b) through private placement , or (c) through a rights issue or bonus issue . A private company may issue securities by private placement, rights issue or bonus issue (not to the public). s.24: SEBI regulates the issue and transfer of securities by listed companies (and those that intend to list), through the SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, 2018 . Types: Red herring prospectus (s.32): does not include complete particulars of the price of the securities offered or the quantum of securities. It must be filed with the Registrar at least three days before the opening of the subscription list. Used in book-building . Shelf prospectus (s.31): for companies (such as public financial institutions and banks) that issue securities in one or more issues over a period without a separate prospectus each time. The validity period is up to one year (as stated in the prospectus). An information memorandum is filed before each subsequent offer. Abridged prospectus (s.33): a memorandum containing the salient features of the prospectus, issued with every application form. Deemed prospectus (s.25): where a company allots, or agrees to allot, securities to an issue house or any other person with a view to their offer for sale to the public , any document by which the offer is made is deemed to be a prospectus. Contents and registration (s.26): the prospectus must be dated , and signed by every person named as a director or proposed director, and must be filed with the Registrar for registration (on or before the date of publication). Required content (Schedule II, ICDR): objects of the issue, the details of capital structure, risk factors, the reports of the auditors and experts , financial information, promoters’ contribution , litigation , the management, and the terms. Experts’ consent is required, in writing, before the issue of the prospectus (s.26(5)). Dating and effect: the date on the prospectus is the date of publication (s.26(?)). A prospectus issued more than 90 days after registration is invalid (the old 90-day rule). The minimum subscription and application money are regulated by SEBI (ICDR); the allotment must be made within the time prescribed, and money must be refunded in case of failure (s.39(3): within 15 days of the closing of the issue; interest at 15% beyond that period). Misstatements in the prospectus: s.34: criminal liability. Where a prospectus includes an untrue or misleading statement, every person who authorised the issue is liable under s.447 (fraud), unless he proves that the statement was immaterial or that he had reasonable grounds to believe it true. s.35: civil liability. Every person who is a director at the time of the issue , who authorised the issue, who agreed to become a director, the promoter , and the expert (for the part contained in his report), is liable to pay compensation to every person who subscribed for securities on the faith of the prospectus for any loss or damage sustained by reason of any untrue or misleading statement or omission . Defences (s.35(2)) : withdrew consent before issue; issued without his knowledge; reasonable belief; the statement was an expert’s (and he believed in the expert’s competence). s.36: punishment for fraudulently inducing persons to invest money (under s.447). s.37: class actions — compensation to depositors. s.38: punishment for personation to acquire securities (liable under s.447). Remedies of the investor: rescission of the contract (for misrepresentation or non-disclosure, within a reasonable time and before winding up), damages for fraud ( Derry v Peek ), and statutory compensation (s.35). Case law: Derry v Peek (1889: fraud needs knowledge or recklessness); Rex v Kylsant (1932: a half-truth may mislead); New Brunswick & Canada Railway v Muggeridge (1860: the duty to disclose all material facts); Central Railway Co. of Venezuela v Kisch (1867: promoters’ duty); Re Pilot . Also, a material misstatement includes statements of opinion where the opinion is not honestly held.

p: Company Law: Incorporation, Prospectus, Shares and Debentures · Commercial Law
x: s.2(84): a share is a share in the share capital of a company, and includes stock . A share is movable property (s.44) transferable as per the articles, and has a nominal value . Types (s.43): Equity share capital : with voting rights , or with differential rights as to dividend, voting or otherwise (subject to the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014). Preference share capital : (a) a preferential right for the payment of dividend (a fixed amount or at a fixed rate) and (b) a preferential right to return of capital on winding up. s.55: a company limited by shares cannot issue irredeemable preference shares ; they must be redeemed within 20 years ( 30 years for infrastructure projects, subject to conditions). Redemption is only out of profits available for dividend or from the proceeds of a fresh issue , and fully paid. A Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR) must be created where redeemed out of profits. Kinds of preference shares: cumulative and non-cumulative; participating and non-participating; convertible and non-convertible; redeemable. Share capital terms: authorised (nominal/registered), issued , subscribed , called-up , paid-up , uncalled and reserve capital (only on winding up, s.? and Act). Issue of shares: s.23 and s.39: allotment. Allotment must be made within the time prescribed after minimum subscription. A return of allotment ( Form PAS-3 ) must be filed within 30 days . An irregular allotment is voidable at the instance of the applicant within a reasonable time, and the Act prohibits allotment unless the application money is received. s.52: securities premium account : the premium on shares must be credited to this account, and can be used only for (a) issuing fully paid bonus shares , (b) writing off preliminary expenses, (c) writing off expenses of or commission paid or discount allowed on the issue of securities or debentures, (d) providing for the premium on redemption of preference shares or debentures, and (e) purchase of its own securities (buy-back). s.53: no issue at a discount (any such issue is void ), except sweat equity shares (s.54). s.54: sweat equity shares may be issued to employees or directors at a discount or for consideration other than cash (know-how, IPR, value additions), after one year from commencement (startups: ten years), by special resolution . s.62: further issue of share capital: (a) rights issue : offer to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings, with a notice of not less than 15 days and not more than 30 days (the MCA has at times allowed shorter periods) giving them the right to renounce in favour of another; (b) employee stock option (ESOP) : special resolution; (c) preferential allotment : special resolution and compliance with the Rules. s.63: bonus shares: from free reserves , the securities premium account or the capital redemption reserve account only ( not from revaluation reserves), authorised by articles; may be issued in lieu of dividend not. Once declared, a bonus issue cannot be withdrawn. s.64 and s.65: notice of alteration of share capital to the Registrar within 30 days. s.46: share certificate within two months of allotment (or one month from the date of lodging an instrument of transfer; 15 days from a request for a duplicate). A share certificate is prima facie evidence of title (s.46(1)) and creates estoppel against the company as regards the matters stated ( Re Bahia & San Francisco Railway ; **Sri Mahadeo? **). s.29: a public company must issue and transfer securities in dematerialised form (and unlisted public companies from October 2018). Depositories Act, 1996 . Calls, forfeiture and lien: the articles ( Table F ) govern calls on shares (at least 14 days’ notice ; no call may exceed 25% of the face value, and an interval of at least one month between calls, under the old rules), forfeiture for non-payment of calls (only for non-payment; the power must be exercised in good faith and for the purpose of the call), and surrender . The company’s lien (Table F) is a first and paramount lien on partly paid shares (not on fully paid shares in a public company). Transfer s.56: an instrument of transfer ( Form SH-4 ) duly stamped and delivered; the company shall deliver certificates within one month . s.58: a private company may restrict the transfer in its articles, whereas the shares of a public company are freely transferable ; if a private company refuses to register, an appeal lies to the Tribunal within 30 days ; s.58(4) the transferee may appeal. Transmission (s.56(2)) by operation of law (death, insolvency). Distinguish transfer (voluntary act) and transmission (by operation of law). s.59: rectification of the register by the Tribunal. s.59(4) the Tribunal may order rectification, and s.88 is the register of members. Alteration and reduction of capital (ss.61–66): s.61: a company limited by shares, if authorised by the articles, may by ordinary resolution : increase its authorised capital; consolidate and divide shares into larger amounts; convert fully paid shares into stock and vice versa ; sub-divide ; and cancel unissued shares . s.66: reduction of share capital: by special resolution (if authorised by articles) and confirmation by the Tribunal (NCLT), after notice to the Central Government, SEBI and the creditors. A reduction affecting the creditors requires their consent or discharge. The Tribunal may order publication of reasons. s.67: a company may not purchase its own shares or give financial assistance for the purchase of its shares except by buy-back (s.68) and permitted exceptions (for example by a private company with employee-held shares and a scheme for employees). s.68 (buy-back): from free reserves , the securities premium account , or the proceeds of an issue of other shares or specified securities (not from the proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind); the buy-back must not exceed 25% of the total paid-up capital and free reserves ; a board resolution is enough if up to 10% of the paid-up capital and free reserves, and a special resolution beyond that; the debt-equity ratio after the buy-back must not exceed 2:1 ; only fully paid-up shares; the buy-back must be completed within one year of the resolution; a declaration of solvency is required; the bought-back securities must be extinguished and physically destroyed within seven days ; a company cannot make another buy-back offer for a period of one year after the closure of the previous one; and a company cannot buy back if it has defaulted on repayment of deposits, interest, redemption of debentures, preference shares or payment of dividend until the default is remedied. s.70: prohibition on buy-back through subsidiaries and investment companies, and through any fraudulent device. Dividends (ss.123–127): dividend is payable only out of profits of the current or previous years (after providing for depreciation), or out of free reserves; interim dividend may be declared by the board; it must be deposited in a separate bank account within five days of declaration and paid within 30 days (s.127: failure to distribute within 30 days is an offence); unpaid or unclaimed dividend is transferred to the Unpaid Dividend Account within seven days (s.124), and then, after seven years , to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF) (s.125); the shares to which dividends have not been paid for seven consecutive years are also transferred to the IEPF (s.124(6)). Members: a member (s.2(55)) is a subscriber to the memorandum or a person who agrees in writing to be a member and whose name is entered in the register of members , or a beneficial owner whose name is in the register of a depository. Distinction between member and shareholder (a shareholder may be a bearer of a share warrant). s.88: registers of members and debenture holders. s.90: registers of significant beneficial owners ( SBO : an individual who holds at least 10% of shares, voting rights, or the right to receive or participate in dividends, or exercises significant influence or control).

p: Company Law: Incorporation, Prospectus, Shares and Debentures · Commercial Law
x: Definition (s.2(30)): a debenture includes debenture stock, bonds or any other instrument of a company evidencing a debt , whether constituting a charge on the assets of the company or not. A debenture is a document acknowledging a debt ; the holder is a creditor, not a member . Differences between shares and debentures: Basis Share Debenture Status of holder Owner (member) Creditor Return Dividend (from profits) Fixed interest (payable irrespective of profits, charged on revenue) Voting right Yes (equity) No (s.71(1): no company shall issue debentures carrying voting rights) Issue at a discount Not allowed (s.53), except sweat equity Allowed Security Not secured May be secured by a charge Repayment On winding up only (equity), after creditors Repayable at maturity or on winding up, with priority over shareholders Conversion Not applicable May be convertible (s.71(1) requires a special resolution ) Kinds: secured (mortgage) and unsecured (naked); redeemable and irredeemable ; registered and bearer ; convertible (fully or partly) and non-convertible ; fixed charge and floating charge debentures . Debenture stock: a borrowing of one aggregate sum, divided into units. Provisions of s.71: s.71(1): a company may issue debentures with an option to convert into shares, wholly or partly, only with the approval of a special resolution . No voting rights in debentures. s.71(2): secured debentures may be issued subject to prescribed terms; the security must be a charge on the company’s assets, registered under s.77. s.71(5): debenture trustee is appointed before the issue of the prospectus or letter of offer , to protect the interests of the debenture holders; the trust deed is executed within 60 days of the closure of the issue (reduced in 2019 from three months). The trustee is regulated by the SEBI (Debenture Trustees) Regulations, 1993 . s.71(4): Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR): the 2019 amendment (Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Amendment Rules, 2019) exempted listed companies from creating DRR for public issues or private placement; unlisted companies (other than NBFCs and HFCs regulated by RBI/NHB) must create DRR of 10% of the value of outstanding debentures maturing within a year. Companies must also invest or deposit at least 15% of the amount of debentures maturing during the year ending on 31 March of the next year, before 30 April , in specified instruments. s.71(10)–(13): the debenture holders’ remedies: the Tribunal may, on application by a debenture holder or trustee, order the company to redeem the debentures forthwith on payment of principal and interest if the company fails to redeem or pay interest; the debenture certificate must be delivered within two months of allotment. s.72: nomination facility for debenture holders.

p: Company Law: Incorporation, Prospectus, Shares and Debentures · Commercial Law
x: Fixed charge: on specific, ascertained assets (such as land and buildings); the company cannot dispose of them without the consent of the charge holder. Floating charge: on a class of assets present and future , which in the ordinary course of business changes from time to time; the company may deal with the assets until the charge crystallises (on default, on the appointment of a receiver, or on winding up). Features of a floating charge are in Re Yorkshire Woolcombers Association (1903: (a) a charge on a class of assets, present and future; (b) the class is one which, in the ordinary course of business, would be changing from time to time; (c) the company may carry on business until some step is taken by the chargeholders). Related cases: Illingworth v Houldsworth ; Holroyd v Marshall . Priority: a fixed charge usually has priority over a floating charge, and a floating charge is postponed to preferential creditors (workmen’s dues, and secured creditors, under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, s.53 ). Registration (s.77): every charge created by a company must be registered with the Registrar within 30 days of its creation, in the prescribed form (CHG-1 / CHG-9). The Registrar may allow registration within a further period of 300 days on payment of additional fees ( Companies (Amendment) Act, 2019 ); beyond that, the matter goes to the Central Government (Regional Director) under s.87. Unregistered charges are void against the liquidator and any creditor (but the debt remains a valid simple contract debt, and the money becomes immediately payable). s.82: the satisfaction of the charge must be filed within 30 days . s.85: the company must keep a register of charges at the registered office. s.86: offence.

t: Overview: Company Law: Incorporation, Prospectus, Shares and Debentures
p: Company Law: Incorporation, Prospectus, Shares and Debentures · Commercial Law
x: Statute: the Companies Act, 2013 (assent 29 August 2013; notified in phases from 12 September 2013 and mostly from 1 April 2014). It has 470 sections and 7 Schedules (check the latest count in your bare Act), and replaced the Companies Act, 1956. Major amendments: 2015, 2017, 2019, 2020 (decriminalisation), 2022 , and the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 , which rationalised penalties across many statutes including the Companies Act. Before the exam, check the latest MCA notifications , because thresholds and rules are revised often.

p: Company Law: Directors and Meetings · Commercial Law
x: Director (s.2(34)): a director appointed to the Board of a company. Directors are agents of the company in their contracts, trustees of its property and funds in their custody, and fiduciaries in their dealings. A director is not an employee unless he is a whole-time director under a contract of service. Types: executive and non-executive; managing director (s.2(54)) (substantial powers of management, subject to the Board’s superintendence), whole-time director (s.2(94)) , manager (s.2(53)) , independent director , nominee director , additional , alternate and woman director . Key Managerial Personnel (s.2(51)) : the CEO, MD or manager; the company secretary; the whole-time director; the CFO; and other prescribed officers. Composition (s.149): Minimum directors: public 3 ; private 2 ; OPC 1 . Maximum: 15 , which can be increased by a special resolution . One resident director (at least 182 days in India in the previous year). Woman director: at least one for every listed company and every other public company with paid-up share capital of Rs. 100 crore or more, or turnover of Rs. 300 crore or more . Independent directors (IDs): one-third of the total number of directors in a listed public company ; and every public company with paid-up capital of Rs. 10 crore or more , or turnover of Rs. 100 crore or more , or aggregate outstanding loans, debentures and deposits exceeding Rs. 50 crore must have at least two independent directors. Independent director (s.149(6)): a person of integrity, expertise and experience, who is not a promoter or related to the promoter or a director of the company; has no pecuniary relationship with the company (other than remuneration as ID) in the previous two financial years; none of his relatives has a pecuniary relationship exceeding 2% or more of the gross turnover or total income , or Rs. 50 lakh whichever is lower; and has not been an employee, auditor, or professional in the company in the preceding three years . Tenure (s.149(10)–(11)): up to five consecutive years ; may be re-appointed for one more term of five consecutive years by special resolution ; a cooling period of three years before being appointed in any other capacity; no stock options ; not liable to retire by rotation . Schedule IV contains the Code for Independent Directors; s.150 provides for a data bank ; s.149(12) limits an ID’s liability to acts of omission or commission which occurred with his knowledge, attributable through board processes, and with his consent or connivance or where he had not acted diligently. Appointment (ss.152–161): DIN (s.153–155): every director must obtain a Director Identification Number (an 8-digit number); a person cannot hold more than one DIN. Consent to act (Form DIR-2) is needed before appointment. First directors are named in the articles; if none, the subscribers are deemed to be the first directors until directors are appointed. Appointment in general meetings by ordinary resolution (each director by a separate resolution, s.162, unless unanimously approved otherwise). Retirement by rotation (s.152(6)): two-thirds of the total number of directors of a public company must be liable to retire by rotation ( independent directors are excluded ); one-third of those retire at each AGM. s.161: the Board may appoint additional directors (up to the articles’ maximum), who hold office until the next AGM; an alternate director (for a director absent from India for not less than three months ); and fill a casual vacancy (until the term of the vacated director would have expired). Nominee director by an institution or the Government. s.165: a person may hold directorships in at most 20 companies , of which not more than 10 can be public companies (a private company that is a subsidiary of a public company counts as public). SEBI’s LODR limits the number of listed company directorships to seven . s.196–197 and Schedule V: the managing director, whole-time director or manager must be aged between 21 and 70 years (70 or above by special resolution); the term shall not exceed five years at a time. Disqualification (s.164): a person cannot be appointed as a director if he: (a) is of unsound mind declared by a court; (b) is an undischarged insolvent ; (c) has applied to be adjudicated insolvent and the application is pending; (d) has been convicted by a court of any offence involving moral turpitude and sentenced to imprisonment for not less than six months , and a period of five years has not elapsed since the sentence ended; (e) has been disqualified by a court or Tribunal order; (f) has not paid any call on shares held for six months from the last day fixed for payment; (g) has been convicted of an offence dealing with related party transactions (s.188) at any time in the preceding five years ; and (h) has not complied with s.152(3) (no DIN). s.164(2): a director of a company that has not filed financial statements or annual returns for any continuous period of three financial years , or that has failed to repay deposits, redeem debentures on due date or pay interest/dividend and the failure continues for one year or more , is disqualified for five years from being re-appointed in that company and appointed in other companies ( Mukul? v? – see *Union of India v Rajeev Kumar? * for upheld striking-off cases; check recent judgments). Vacation of office (s.167): the office of a director becomes vacant on: disqualification under s.164; absence from all board meetings held in twelve months (with or without leave); acceptance of an office of profit in contravention of s.188; being disqualified by a court; resignation (s.168) , which takes effect from the date of receipt of the notice or the date stated in the notice, whichever is later; and removal (s.169) . Removal (s.169): by ordinary resolution passed after special notice (s.115: 14 days) , in a general meeting. The director has a right to be heard and to have a written representation circulated. Not applicable to directors appointed by the Tribunal under s.242 or by the principle of proportional representation (s.163) . A vacancy so created can be filled by the meeting at which the director is removed.

p: Company Law: Directors and Meetings · Commercial Law
x: Duties of directors (s.166): (1) act in accordance with the articles ; (2) act in good faith to promote the objects of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole, and in the best interests of the company, its employees, shareholders, the community and the protection of the environment; (3) exercise due and reasonable care, skill and diligence and independent judgment ; (4) avoid conflict of interest ; (5) not achieve or attempt to achieve any undue gain or advantage , and if found guilty, pay an amount equal to the gain to the company; and (6) not assign the office (assignment is void). Penalty (s.166(7)): fine of not less than Rs. 1 lakh, which may extend to Rs. 5 lakh . Powers of the Board (s.179): the Board may exercise all powers of the company except those required to be exercised in a general meeting. s.179(3): the Board can exercise by resolutions passed at meetings certain powers: to make calls; to buy back shares; to issue securities (including debentures); to borrow money ; to invest the funds of the company; to grant loans or give guarantee ; to approve financial statements and the Board’s report; to diversify the business ; to approve amalgamation, merger or reconstruction ; to take over a company; and other prescribed matters. s.180: powers requiring a special resolution: to sell, lease or otherwise dispose of the whole or substantially the whole of the undertaking ; to invest compensation received on compulsory acquisition; to borrow money in excess of the aggregate of the paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium ; and to remit or give time for repayment of any debt due from a director. Restrictions and related-party rules: s.184: Disclosure of interest: every director must disclose his concern or interest in any contract or arrangement at the first meeting of the Board in which he participates as a director (and annually, in the first meeting of each financial year, Form MBP-1 ). An interested director must not take part in the discussion or vote (s.184(2)). Contravention is punishable with imprisonment up to one year or a fine of Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 1 lakh, or both. s.185: Loans to directors and persons in whom they are interested are generally prohibited, except as allowed after the 2017 amendment (for example, loans to a wholly owned subsidiary, and guarantees for loans to a subsidiary company, with a special resolution , for principal business activities). s.186: Loans and investments: limited to 60% of the paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium , or 100% of free reserves and securities premium , whichever is more ; beyond this requires a special resolution . Loans to be charged at interest not lower than the prevailing yield of the one-year, three-year, five-year or ten-year Government security closest to the tenor. s.188: Related-party transactions: approval by the Board (with the interested director not voting) and, beyond the prescribed thresholds, by ordinary resolution of the shareholders (related parties do not vote). The company’s transactions at arm’s length and in the ordinary course of business are exempt from board approval (but not from shareholder approval for listed entities under the SEBI LODR). s.189: register of contracts. Liabilities: a director may be liable for breach of fiduciary duty , negligence , ultra vires acts , misfeasance , misstatement in prospectus, fraud (s.447) , and as an ‘officer who is in default’ (s.2(60)) . s.447: punishment for fraud: imprisonment of six months to ten years , and a fine of not less than the amount involved in the fraud, which may extend to three times that amount ; where the fraud involves public interest , imprisonment is not less than three years . Case law: Re City Equitable Fire Insurance Co. (1925): the standard of care expected is that of a reasonable person with the director’s own knowledge and experience; a director need not give continuous attention. Regal (Hastings) Ltd. v Gulliver (1942): a fiduciary must account for secret profits made by use of his position, even if the company could not have taken the opportunity. Cook v Deeks (1916): directors cannot take a corporate opportunity for themselves. Foss v Harbottle (1843): the rule of majority ; the company (not the shareholder) is the proper plaintiff for wrongs done to it. Exceptions: ultra vires acts, fraud on the minority, acts requiring a special majority, infringement of personal rights, and oppression. Oppression and mismanagement (ss.241–244): a member may apply to the Tribunal (NCLT) ; eligibility (s.244) : in a company with a share capital, not less than 100 members or one-tenth of the total number of members, whichever is less , or members holding not less than one-tenth of the issued share capital ; the Tribunal may waive these requirements. Cases: Shanti Prasad Jain v Kalinga Tubes (1965); Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd. (1981); Tata Consultancy Services v Cyrus Investments (2021: the Supreme Court restored Mr. Cyrus Mistry’s removal as chairman and rejected the oppression claims; the Court held that the removal of a director or chairman for loss of confidence is within the Board’s powers, and no oppression was found). Class action (s.245) and derivative suits by members or depositors.

p: Company Law: Directors and Meetings · Commercial Law
x: Kinds of meetings: general meetings (annual and extraordinary), Board meetings , class meetings , creditors’ meetings (schemes of arrangement, s.230), meetings of committees . The statutory meeting (s.165 of the 1956 Act) was abolished by the 2013 Act. Annual General Meeting (s.96): Every company other than an OPC must hold an AGM in each year, and not more than fifteen months may elapse between two AGMs. The first AGM must be held within nine months from the closing of the first financial year; subsequent AGMs within six months of the close of the financial year. The Registrar may extend the time ( by up to three months ) for AGMs other than the first. The AGM must be held during business hours (9 a.m. to 6 p.m.) on a day that is not a national holiday , at the registered office or any place within the city, town or village where the registered office is located. Under MCA circulars, virtual AGMs have been permitted, a measure first introduced during Covid-19 and extended. Default (s.99): fine up to Rs. 1 lakh and a further fine up to Rs. 5,000 per day for continuing default. s.97: the Tribunal can call an AGM on the application of any member if default occurs. Ordinary business at AGM: consideration of financial statements and reports of the Board and auditors; declaration of dividend ; appointment of directors in place of those retiring ; and appointment and fixing of remuneration of auditors . Everything else is special business , which requires an explanatory statement (s.102) . Extraordinary General Meeting (s.100): called by the Board on its own, or on a requisition by members holding not less than one-tenth of the paid-up share capital carrying voting rights (or, if no share capital, one-tenth of the total voting power). The Board must proceed to call a meeting within 21 days from the date of receipt of the requisition, to be held within 45 days of the receipt. If it fails, the requisitionists may call the meeting themselves, within three months from the date of the requisition, and the company must reimburse their expenses. Notice (s.101): at least 21 clear days (in writing or electronic mode), to every member, director, auditor, and others entitled. A meeting may be called on shorter notice if consented to by not less than 95% of the members entitled to vote (in the case of an AGM, in number; in other meetings, 95% of the paid-up share capital carrying a right to vote or of the total voting power). Contents: day, date, hour, place, and a statement of the business (with explanatory statement for special business). Omission to give notice to any member invalidates proceedings, but accidental omission does not (s.101(3)). Special notice (s.115) is required for resolutions to remove a director (s.169) or appoint an auditor other than the retiring auditor (s.140): 14 days before the meeting. Quorum (s.103): (a) public company: five members personally present if the number of members is not more than 1,000 ; 15 if between 1,000 and 5,000; 30 if more than 5,000; (b) private company: two members personally present. If a quorum is not present within half an hour , the meeting is adjourned to the same day in the next week at the same time and place (or such other date as the Board determines); at the adjourned meeting, the members present are a quorum (s.103(2)). A meeting called on a requisition by members is dissolved if quorum is absent. Proxies (s.105): any member entitled to attend and vote may appoint another person ( need not be a member ) as proxy; a member of a company without share capital cannot appoint proxy except as allowed; the proxy has no right to speak and cannot vote on a show of hands but may demand or join in demanding a poll ; the instrument ( Form MGT-11 ) must be deposited at least 48 hours before the meeting ; a person can act as proxy for not more than 50 members , and for members holding not more than 10% of the total voting share capital ; proxy is revocable until the commencement of the meeting. Voting (ss.107–109) and resolutions (s.114): Show of hands (s.107): each member has one vote. Poll (s.109): may be demanded by members having not less than 10% of the total voting power or holding shares on which an aggregate sum of not less than Rs. 5 lakh has been paid up; votes are in proportion to the share capital held. E-voting (s.108) is mandatory for listed companies and companies with 1,000 or more shareholders (Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014, Rule 20). Postal ballot (s.110). Ordinary resolution: simple majority (votes cast in favour exceed votes cast against). Special resolution: the votes cast in favour must be not less than three times the votes cast against ( 75% of the votes cast), and the intention to propose it as a special resolution must be specified in the notice. Resolutions must be filed with the Registrar within 30 days (s.117, Form MGT-14) for special resolutions and certain others. Resolution by circulation (s.175): Board resolutions may be passed by circulation, and must be approved by a majority of directors (unless the directors demand a meeting); noted at the next Board meeting. Board meetings (ss.173–175): First Board meeting within 30 days of incorporation. A minimum of four meetings per year , with a gap of not more than 120 days between two consecutive meetings. OPC, small companies and dormant companies must hold at least one meeting in each half of the calendar year , with a gap of not less than 90 days . Notice: at least seven days in writing to every director; a meeting may be convened at shorter notice if at least one independent director (if the company has any) is present (if absent, decisions are final only on ratification by at least one independent director). Quorum (s.174): one-third of the total strength or two directors , whichever is higher . Participation through video conferencing counts toward the quorum. Certain matters cannot be dealt with via video conference : approval of the annual financial statements, the Board’s report, the prospectus, the audit committee matters, and the approval of takeover, merger or amalgamation (Rule 4 of Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014, until relaxed by MCA circulars; check the present position). Interested director must not vote (s.184); decisions are by majority, and the chairman has the casting vote if the articles provide. Minutes (s.118) and Secretarial Standards: minutes of all general and Board meetings must be recorded within 30 days of the conclusion of the meeting, in minute books, with each page signed and the last page signed and dated by the chairman (or the next chairman). Minutes are conclusive evidence of the proceedings, unless contradicted (s.118(7)). The ICSI issued Secretarial Standards SS-1 (Board Meetings) and SS-2 (General Meetings) under s.118(10), which are mandatory . Committees of the Board: Audit Committee (s.177) (every listed company and public companies with paid-up capital of Rs. 10 crore or more, turnover of Rs. 100 crore or more, or aggregate outstanding loans, debentures and deposits above Rs. 50 crore ): minimum three directors , with independent directors forming a majority ; Nomination and Remuneration Committee (s.178) ; Stakeholders Relationship Committee ; CSR Committee (s.135) ; Risk Management Committee (SEBI LODR). Other officers: Company Secretary (s.203) : mandatory for listed companies and public companies with paid-up capital of Rs. 10 crore or more; KMP .

p: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) · Commercial Law
x: Meaning: CSR is the obligation of a business to act in ways that benefit society and the environment beyond its profit motive and legal minimum. India is widely described as the first country to legislate a mandatory CSR spending requirement (Companies Act, 2013, s.135 , effective 1 April 2014 ). Key theories and models (frequent concept questions): Milton Friedman (shareholder theory): the only social responsibility of business is to increase its profits within the rules of the game. Stakeholder theory (R. Edward Freeman, 1984): a firm owes duties to all stakeholders (employees, customers, suppliers, community, environment), not only to shareholders. Carroll’s pyramid of CSR (1991): four layers: economic (base), legal , ethical , philanthropic (top). Triple bottom line (John Elkington, 1994): People, Planet, Profit . Gandhian trusteeship (the Indian roots of CSR): wealth is held in trust for society. Early Indian business philanthropy: the Tata and Birla groups. Soft-law and international frameworks: the UN Global Compact (2000; ten principles on human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption); UN Sustainable Development Goals (2015); the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (2011); ISO 26000 (guidance, not a certifiable standard); OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises . Indian evolution: MCA Voluntary Guidelines on CSR, 2009 ; DPE guidelines for public sector enterprises (2010); the National Voluntary Guidelines (NVG) on Social, Environmental and Economic Responsibilities of Business, 2011 (nine principles); SEBI’s Business Responsibility Report (BRR) , replaced by the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) , which is mandatory for the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalisation (from FY 2022–23); the Companies Act, 2013 (s.135, Schedule VII, and the CSR Rules).

t: 10.2 Statutory Framework: Section 135, Schedule VII and the CSR Rules
p: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) · Commercial Law
x: Sources: s.135 of the Companies Act, 2013; Schedule VII ; the Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014 , substantially amended by the Companies (CSR Policy) Amendment Rules, 2021 (effective 22 January 2021 ); and the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2019 (unspent CSR provisions) and 2020 . Applicability (s.135(1)): every company, including its holding or subsidiary , and a foreign company having its branch or project office in India, which in the immediately preceding financial year has: (a) net worth of Rs. 500 crore or more , or (b) turnover of Rs. 1,000 crore or more , or (c) net profit of Rs. 5 crore or more . Satisfying any one of the conditions suffices. The obligation continues until the company ceases to meet these thresholds for three consecutive financial years . CSR Committee: The Board of a company to which s.135 applies must constitute a CSR Committee of the Board with three or more directors, at least one of whom is an independent director . An unlisted public company or a private company that is not required to appoint an independent director need have only two directors . A foreign company must have at least two persons, one resident in India and another nominated by the foreign company. Where the company’s CSR obligation does not exceed Rs. 50 lakh , the CSR Committee is not required , and the functions are discharged by the Board (2021 amendment). Functions (s.135(3)): formulate and recommend a CSR Policy indicating the activities to be undertaken (as per Schedule VII); recommend the amount of expenditure ; and monitor the CSR Policy from time to time. The Committee also formulates and recommends an annual action plan to the Board. Board’s responsibilities (s.135(4)–(5)): approve the CSR Policy after considering the Committee’s recommendations; disclose the contents of the policy in its report and on the company’s website ; ensure that the activities are undertaken as per the policy; and ensure that the company spends, in every financial year, at least 2% of the average net profits of the company made during the three immediately preceding financial years , in pursuance of its CSR Policy. A company should give preference to the local area and areas around which it operates. If a company is newly incorporated and has not completed three financial years, the average is of the profits for the immediately preceding financial years since incorporation. Net profit is calculated as per s.198 and excludes profits arising from branches outside India and dividends received from other Indian companies that are covered under and complying with s.135.

p: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) · Commercial Law
x: Eradicating hunger, poverty and malnutrition , promoting health care including preventive health care , sanitation (including contribution to the Swachh Bharat Kosh ) and making available safe drinking water . Promoting education , including special education and employment-enhancing vocation skills , especially among children, women, elderly and the differently abled, and livelihood enhancement projects . Promoting gender equality , empowering women, setting up homes and hostels for women and orphans, old age homes , day care centres and such other facilities for senior citizens, and measures for reducing inequalities faced by socially and economically backward groups. Ensuring environmental sustainability , ecological balance, protection of flora and fauna , animal welfare, agroforestry , conservation of natural resources and maintaining the quality of soil, air and water (including contribution to the Clean Ganga Fund ). Protection of national heritage, art and culture including restoration of buildings and sites of historical importance and works of art; setting up public libraries; promotion and development of traditional art and handicrafts . Measures for the benefit of armed forces veterans, war widows and their dependents , including Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF) and Central Para Military Forces (CPMF) veterans and their dependents. Training to promote rural sports, nationally recognised sports, Paralympic sports and Olympic sports. Contribution to the Prime Minister’s National Relief Fund , or PM CARES Fund , or any other fund set up by the Central Government for socio-economic development and relief and welfare of the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, other backward classes, minorities and women . (a) Contribution to incubators or research and development projects in the field of science, technology, engineering and medicine, funded by the Central Government or State Government or Public Sector Undertaking or any agency of the Central Government or State Government; and (b) contributions to public-funded Universities; IITs; National Laboratories and autonomous bodies established under bodies such as the DAE, DBT, DST, MeitY, ICAR, ICMR and CSIR , engaged in research in science, technology, engineering and medicine aimed at promoting the SDGs. Rural development projects. Slum area development (the explanation defines ‘slum area’ as one notified by the Central or State Government). Disaster management , including relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction activities. Memory aid for the Schedule: H unger/Health, E ducation, G ender, E nvironment, H eritage, V eterans, S ports, P M funds, R &D, R ural, S lums, D isaster. Items (viii) (PM funds) and (ix) (R&D) are favourites for ‘which is included’ questions. Local area preference and ‘employment-enhancing vocational skills’ are also frequent.

t: 10.4 What Does NOT Count as CSR (Rule 2(1)(d) and Rule 4)
p: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) · Commercial Law
x: Activities undertaken in the normal course of business . Any contribution to a political party (s.182) or any political activity . Projects or programmes or activities that benefit only the employees of the company and their families. One-off events such as marathons, awards, charitable contributions, advertisements, sponsorships of TV programmes or movies (except as permitted). Activities outside India (except for training of Indian sports personnel representing any State or Union Territory at national or international level). Expenses incurred for fulfilment of any other statutory obligation under any law in force in India. Sponsorship activities for deriving marketing benefits for products or services.

p: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) · Commercial Law
x: Modes of implementation (Rule 4): directly, or through a Section 8 company, registered public trust or registered society established by the company (alone or with others) or by the Central or State Government, or any entity established under an Act of Parliament or State legislature, or any other Section 8 company, registered trust or society with an established track record of three years in similar activities. Registration (Form CSR-1) with the Registrar of Companies is mandatory for implementing agencies from 1 April 2021 , each receiving a unique CSR registration number . Implementing agencies must also hold 12A and 80G registrations under the Income-tax Act, 1961. Annual action plan (Rule 5(2)): to include the list of CSR projects, the manner of execution, the modalities of utilisation of funds, monitoring and reporting, and the details of the need and impact assessment, if any. Ongoing project (Rule 2(1)(i)): a multi-year project, not exceeding three years excluding the year of commencement , with timelines approved by the Board on the CSR Committee’s recommendation. Unspent CSR (s.135(5)–(6)) and Rule 7: Ongoing projects: the unspent amount must be transferred to a special bank account (the Unspent CSR Account) within 30 days from the end of the financial year , to be spent within three financial years from the date of transfer. If it is not spent in that period, it must be transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within 30 days of the end of the three financial years. Non-ongoing projects: the unspent amount must be transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within six months from the end of the financial year. Set-off (Rule 7(3)): where a company spends in excess of its 2% obligation, the excess may be set off against the CSR requirement of the succeeding three financial years , as per the Board’s resolution. Surplus arising out of CSR activities is not part of business profit and must be ploughed back or transferred. Administrative overheads: shall not exceed 5% of the total CSR expenditure of the company for the financial year. Impact assessment (Rule 8(3)): companies with an average CSR obligation of Rs. 10 crore or more in the three immediately preceding financial years must undertake an impact assessment through an independent agency for projects with an outlay of Rs. 1 crore or more that have been completed not less than one year before the assessment. The expenditure on impact assessment may be counted up to 5% of the total CSR expenditure for the year, or Rs. 50 lakh, whichever is higher . Capital assets created or acquired through CSR funds must be held by the beneficiaries , a registered public trust or society or Section 8 company (not by the company itself). Reporting: a brief outline of the CSR Policy and the composition of the CSR Committee in the Board’s report ( Annexure ); Form CSR-2 filed with the Registrar (as an addendum to AOC-4 ) from FY 2020–21; and web display of the CSR Committee composition, policy and approved projects. Penalty (s.135(7), as amended 2019/2020): if a company fails to transfer the unspent amount as required, the company is liable to a penalty of twice the amount required to be transferred, or Rs. 1 crore, whichever is less , and every officer in default is liable to a penalty of one-tenth of the amount required to be transferred, or Rs. 2 lakh, whichever is less . The older ‘comply or explain’ regime (non-spending with reasons) was replaced by this mandatory regime. The 2020 amendment decriminalised the offence (it earlier carried imprisonment).

t: 10.6 CSR: Analysis Points and Recent Trends for MCQs
p: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) · Commercial Law
x: Criticism: CSR as a statutory 2% ‘tax’ versus a voluntary ethic; spending concentrated in a few states and sectors (education and health dominate; the North-east and aspirational districts get less); ‘box-ticking’; the capacity of implementing agencies ; the local-area preference versus national needs. Trend: rising share of CSR funds towards health care, education and rural development ; during the Covid-19 pandemic, contributions to PM CARES were counted as CSR, and MCA FAQs clarified that Covid-19 related expenses are eligible under the health care and disaster management items. Linkage with the directors’ duties: s.166(2) requires directors to act in the best interests of the company, its employees, shareholders, the community and the protection of the environment. Link with sustainability disclosures: BRSR, ESG and the SDGs. Likely traps: (i) the three alternative thresholds (500 / 1,000 / 5 crore: net worth / turnover / net profit ); (ii) 2% of the average net profit of three preceding years , not of the current year’s profit; (iii) CSR Committee not needed if the obligation is up to Rs. 50 lakh ; (iv) 30 days / 3 years / 6 months for unspent amounts; (v) political contributions and employee-only benefits are excluded; (vi) overheads 5% ; (vii) Form CSR-1 and CSR-2 ; (viii) penalty twice the unspent amount or Rs. 1 crore, whichever is less .
