p: Master Revision: Question Patterns, Cheat Sheet and Common Mistakes · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: Confusing formal (Fuller, Raz, Hayek) with substantive (Dworkin, Allan, Bingham) rule of law. Writing that the UK is a federal state or has a written constitution. Saying India has dual citizenship or dual judiciary . Assuming that US courts give advisory opinions (they do not; India's Article 143 does). Believing that the Swiss Court has full constitutional review of federal laws (it does not; Article 190). Forgetting that the French Council reviews laws before promulgation (and since 2010 also by QPC). Mixing the numbers: Golaknath (11 judges, 1967), Kesavananda (13 judges, 1973).

p: Master Revision: Question Patterns, Cheat Sheet and Common Mistakes · Comparative Public Law and Systems of Governance
x: First pass: read each topic once; underline names, numbers and cases. Second pass: write comparison tables from memory (India vs USA vs UK vs France). Third pass: revise the "Exam Traps" and cheat sheet daily in the last two weeks. Practice: attempt previous-year UGC NET Law questions on this unit to learn the patterns; note which scholars and cases keep repeating. Update check: Indian legal developments (new constitutional amendments, major Supreme Court rulings, the status of the DPDP Act amendment to the RTI Act) should be verified from current sources before the exam.

p: Preamble · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: The Preamble is the introductory statement of the Constitution setting out its guiding purposes, principles, and philosophy. It is NOT a source of legislative or executive power, but IS an interpretive tool to understand constitutional intent. Adopted November 26, 1949; Constitution came into force January 26, 1950.

p: Preamble · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens: JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation; IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.

p: Preamble · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Sovereign — India is not subject to any external authority. No foreign power can dictate governance. India can acquire or cede territory. Tested in Berubari Union Case (1960). Socialist — Added by 42nd Amendment, 1976. Mixed economy, not pure communism. State must minimise inequalities of income and status. In Excel Wear v. Union of India (1978), SC clarified 'socialist' does not mean State can nationalise everything. Secular — Added by 42nd Amendment, 1976. India follows POSITIVE secularism — State has no religion of its own but treats all religions equally (Sarva Dharma Sambhava). Distinctly different from Western negative secularism which rigidly excludes religion from public life. Democratic — Sovereignty rests with the people, exercised through elected representatives. Includes adult suffrage (Article 326), free and fair elections, parliamentary form of government. Republic — Head of State (President) is elected, not hereditary. President is indirectly elected through electoral college. Justice — Three dimensions: Social (no discrimination), Economic (equitable distribution), Political (equal political rights). Inspired by Russian Revolution ideals. Liberty — Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship — linked to Article 19. Not absolute; subject to reasonable restrictions. Equality — Equality of status and opportunity — linked to Articles 14, 15, 16. Includes formal equality (before law) and substantive equality (actual equal treatment). Permits reasonable classification and protective discrimination. Fraternity — Brotherhood among citizens assuring dignity of the individual and unity and integrity of the Nation. The ONLY value in the Preamble without a corresponding justiciable Fundamental Right — it is a moral and social value permeating the whole Constitution.

t: 1.4 Is the Preamble Part of the Constitution?
p: Preamble · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Berubari Union Case (1960): Preamble is NOT part of the Constitution. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): OVERRULED Berubari — Preamble IS part of the Constitution; can be amended under Article 368 but basic features cannot be destroyed. LIC v. Consumer Education Research Centre (1995): Reaffirmed Preamble is part of the Constitution.

p: Preamble · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Yes — 42nd Amendment (1976) added 'Socialist', 'Secular', 'Integrity'. However, basic structure features (sovereignty, democracy, republic, secularism) cannot be destroyed even by amendment (Kesavananda Bharati Basic Structure Doctrine).

p: Preamble · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: SSSDR : Sovereign → Socialist → Secular → Democratic → Republic JLEF : Justice → Liberty → Equality → Fraternity Socialist + Secular + Integrity — all three added together by 42nd Amendment, 1976

p: Fundamental Rights (Articles 12–35) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Part III (Articles 12–35) contains Fundamental Rights — justiciable rights enforceable by courts against the State. Dr. Ambedkar called Article 32 the "heart and soul" of the Constitution. These rights are available against the State as defined in Article 12. Two exceptions apply against private individuals also: Article 17 (untouchability) and Article 23 (forced labour/trafficking).

p: Fundamental Rights (Articles 12–35) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: For Part III purposes, 'State' includes: Government and Parliament of India; Government and Legislature of each State; all local or other authorities within India; all local or other authorities under the control of Government of India. Key expansion through cases: R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority (1979): Body that is an instrumentality or agency of Government is 'State' under Article 12. Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. IICB (2002): 7-judge bench — 'functional test': pervasive governmental control + financial dependence + public importance of functions. Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib (1981): Societies substantially financed and controlled by Government are 'State'.

p: Fundamental Rights (Articles 12–35) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Article 13(1): Pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with FRs are void to the extent of inconsistency — Doctrine of Eclipse applies (law is dormant, revives if FR amended to remove inconsistency — Bhikhaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP, 1955). Article 13(2): State shall NOT make any law abridging FRs — void ab initio. Doctrine of Severability applies — only offending provision severed, rest valid if separable (R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala v. Union of India, 1957). Article 13(3): 'Law' includes ordinances, regulations, bye-laws, rules, notifications, customs, usages. Constitutional amendments are NOT 'law' under Article 13 — subject to Basic Structure doctrine. Doctrine of Eclipse: Pre-constitutional law inconsistent with FR becomes dormant (eclipsed) but not dead. If the FR is subsequently amended to remove the inconsistency, the law automatically revives. Does NOT apply to post-constitutional laws — those are void ab initio. Doctrine of Severability: Only the unconstitutional part of a law is struck down; the rest remains valid if the valid and invalid portions are separable. Test: Would Parliament have enacted the law even without the invalid portion? Doctrine of Waiver: Fundamental Rights cannot be waived — they are given as a matter of public policy and cannot be contracted away (Behram Khurshid Pesikaka v. State of Bombay, 1955).

p: Fundamental Rights (Articles 12–35) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Article 14 — Equality Before Law and Equal Protection of Laws Two distinct guarantees: (1) Equality before law — negative concept, no special privileges (from English Rule of Law — Dicey); (2) Equal protection of laws — positive concept, equals to be treated equally (from US 14th Amendment). Twin tests of reasonable classification: The classification must be based on intelligible differentia (clear and understandable basis) The differentia must have rational nexus to the object sought to be achieved Evolution of Article 14 through case law: State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952): Twin tests laid down E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974): Arbitrariness violates Article 14 — equality is antithetic to arbitrariness Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978): Article 14 read with Articles 19 and 21 — 'golden triangle' Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017): Triple talaq struck down as manifestly arbitrary under Article 14 Article 15 — Prohibition of Discrimination Article 15(1): State shall not discriminate on grounds ONLY of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. Language and domicile are NOT included. Article 15(2): No citizen shall face disabilities in access to public places on these grounds alone. Article 15(3): State may make special provisions for women and children — exception to 15(1). Article 15(4): State may make special provisions for socially/educationally backward classes or SC/ST — inserted by 1st Amendment (1951) after Champakam Dorairajan case. Article 15(5): Reservation for backward classes/SC/ST in private educational institutions — 93rd Amendment (2005), upheld in Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. Union of India (2008). Article 15(6): 10% EWS reservation — 103rd Amendment (2019), upheld in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022) by 3:2 majority. Article 16 — Equality of Opportunity in Public Employment Article 16(4): Reservations for backward classes not adequately represented in State services. 50% ceiling laid down in Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) — the Mandal Case. Creamy layer to be excluded. Article 16(4-A): Reservation in promotion for SC/ST — 77th Amendment (1995). Article 16(4-B): Unfilled SC/ST vacancies carried forward — not subject to 50% cap — 81st Amendment (2000). Article 16(6): 10% EWS reservation in public employment — 103rd Amendment (2019). Article 17 — Abolition of Untouchability Practice forbidden in any form; offence punishable by law. Applies against private individuals too. Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 enforces this. Article 18 — Abolition of Titles No title (except military/academic) shall be conferred by the State. Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are NOT 'titles' under Article 18 — Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996).

p: Fundamental Rights (Articles 12–35) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: SIX freedoms guaranteed to CITIZENS only: (a) Speech and expression: Includes freedom of press, right to know, commercial speech, right to silence. Restrictions (Art. 19(2)): sovereignty, integrity, security, friendly relations, public order, decency, morality, contempt, defamation, incitement. (b) Peaceful assembly without arms: Restrictions (Art. 19(3)): sovereignty, integrity, public order. (c) Form associations/unions: Includes trade unions, political parties. Restrictions (Art. 19(4)): sovereignty, integrity, public order, morality. (d) Move freely throughout India: Restrictions (Art. 19(5)): general public interest, protection of Scheduled Tribes. (e) Reside and settle anywhere: Restrictions (Art. 19(5)): same as above. (g) Practise any profession/occupation/trade/business: Restrictions (Art. 19(6)): professional qualifications, State monopoly. Note: Article 19(1)(f) (right to property) was deleted by 44th Amendment, 1978. Now only 6 freedoms. All restrictions must be: (i) imposed by law, (ii) reasonable, (iii) in relation to specified grounds only.

t: 2.6 Right to Life and Personal Liberty (Articles 20–22)
p: Fundamental Rights (Articles 12–35) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Article 20 — Triple Protection (non-suspendable even during Emergency): No ex post facto criminal law No double jeopardy (Nemo bis punitur pro eodem delicto) No compelled self-incrimination Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010): Narco-analysis, brain mapping, polygraph without consent violate Article 20(3). Article 21 — Right to Life and Personal Liberty (most expansive FR): Narrow start: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) — any procedure prescribed by law suffices. Landmark expansion: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) — procedure must be just, fair, and reasonable. Substantive due process imported. Post-Maneka judicially expanded rights under Article 21: Right to livelihood (Olga Tellis v. BMC, 1985) Right to speedy trial (Hussainara Khatoon, 1979) Right to legal aid (M.H. Hoskot v. State of Maharashtra, 1978) Right to education — now Article 21-A (Unnikrishnan JP v. State of AP, 1993) Right to clean environment (M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, 1987) Right to privacy (K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, 2017 — 9-judge bench) Right to die with dignity — passive euthanasia (Common Cause v. Union of India, 2018) Right to health and medical care (Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity, 1996) Right to shelter (Chameli Singh v. State of UP, 1996) Article 21-A — Right to Education: Inserted by 86th Amendment (2002). Free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14. Implemented by Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009. Article 22 — Protection Against Arrest: Two parts: (1) Rights of arrested person — inform grounds, right to legal counsel, produce before magistrate within 24 hours; (2) Preventive detention — Advisory Board required for detention beyond 3 months.

p: Fundamental Rights (Articles 12–35) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Article 23: Prohibits trafficking, begar, and forced labour. Applies against State AND private individuals. Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984): SC ordered identification, release, and rehabilitation of bonded labourers. Article 24: No child below 14 years in factories, mines, or other hazardous employment. Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2016 expanded the prohibition.

p: Fundamental Rights (Articles 12–35) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Article 25: Right to freely profess, practise, and propagate religion — subject to public order, morality, health. State can regulate secular activities associated with religion. Article 26: Religious denomination's right to establish institutions, manage religious affairs, own property. Article 27: No compulsion to pay taxes for promotion of any particular religion. Distinction between 'tax' (compulsory — Art. 27 applies) and 'fee' (for services — Art. 27 does not apply). Article 28: No religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained out of State funds.

p: Fundamental Rights (Articles 12–35) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Article 29: Right of any section of citizens with distinct language/script/culture to conserve the same. No denial of admission to State-maintained/aided institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste, or language. Article 30: All religious and linguistic minorities have right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. State can regulate to ensure academic standards. T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002) — 11-judge bench laid down the law.

p: Fundamental Rights (Articles 12–35) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: 'Heart and soul' of the Constitution (Dr. Ambedkar). Five writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto. Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right — cannot be suspended except under Article 359 during National Emergency (and even then Arts. 20 and 21 remain enforceable).

p: Fundamental Duties (Article 51-A) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Not in original Constitution. Inserted by 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 (Swaran Singh Committee recommendation) — borrowed from USSR Constitution. 86th Amendment (2002) added the 11th duty.

p: Fundamental Duties (Article 51-A) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals, institutions, National Flag, National Anthem Cherish noble ideals of national freedom struggle Uphold and protect sovereignty, unity, integrity of India Defend the country and render national service when called upon Promote harmony and common brotherhood; renounce practices derogatory to women's dignity Value and preserve rich heritage of composite culture Protect and improve natural environment; compassion for living creatures Develop scientific temper, humanism, spirit of inquiry and reform Safeguard public property; abjure violence Strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity Provide opportunities for education to child/ward between 6–14 years (86th Amendment, 2002)

p: Fundamental Duties (Article 51-A) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: NON-JUSTICIABLE — no court can directly enforce or punish breach Apply to CITIZENS only (not non-citizens) Parliament CAN pass laws to enforce duties indirectly — protected from Article 19 challenges (AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS, 2001) Courts use them to balance rights against responsibilities and interpret ambiguous laws Verma Committee (J.S. Verma, 1999) noted duties have legal dimensions in appropriate contexts Ranganatha Misra Commission (2009) recommended making some duties justiciable — not yet implemented

p: Directive Principles of State Policy (Articles 36–51) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Part IV (Articles 36–51) contains DPSPs. Non-justiciable (Article 37 — "shall not be enforceable by any court") but fundamental in the governance of the country. Borrowed from the Irish Constitution (1937). Dr. Ambedkar described them as a 'novel feature.' Aim: to establish a welfare state.

p: Directive Principles of State Policy (Articles 36–51) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Socialistic Directives: Article 38: State to secure social order for welfare of people Article 39: Equal right to livelihood (a); equal pay for equal work (d); protection of children from exploitation (f) Article 39-A: Equal justice and free legal aid — 42nd Amendment, 1976 Article 41: Right to work, education, public assistance in unemployment/sickness Article 42: Just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief Article 43: Living wage for workers Article 43-A: Workers' participation in management — 42nd Amendment, 1976 Article 47: Raise standard of living; prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs Gandhian Directives: Article 40: Organise village panchayats Article 43: Promote cottage industries Article 43-B: Promotion of co-operative societies — 97th Amendment, 2011 Article 46: Promote educational and economic interests of SC, ST, weaker sections Article 48: Organise agriculture and animal husbandry; prohibit slaughter of cattle Liberal Intellectualist Directives: Article 44: Uniform Civil Code Article 45: Early childhood care (amended by 86th Amendment) Article 48-A: Protection and improvement of environment — 42nd Amendment, 1976 Article 49: Protection of monuments Article 50: Separation of judiciary from executive Article 51: Promotion of international peace

t: 4.3 FRs vs. DPSPs: The Constitutional Journey
p: Directive Principles of State Policy (Articles 36–51) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: This is the single most analytically important topic in this Unit. Champakam Dorairajan (1951): FRs prevail over DPSPs → prompted 1st Amendment (Art. 15(4)) Golak Nath (1967): Parliament cannot amend FRs → DPSPs forever subordinate Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Parliament can amend FRs but not destroy basic structure → balance restored Minerva Mills (1980): 42nd Amendment's absolute primacy to DPSPs struck down — harmony between Parts III and IV IS itself a basic feature. Neither can completely override the other. Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981): Laws giving effect to DPSPs can go in Ninth Schedule — subject to I.R. Coelho (2007) limitation (laws after April 24, 1973 can be challenged if they violate basic structure)

t: 4.4 Key DPSPs That Led to Legislation
p: Directive Principles of State Policy (Articles 36–51) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Article 39(b)/(c) → Nationalisation of industries, land reform laws Article 40 → 73rd and 74th Amendments (Panchayati Raj and Municipal Bodies) Article 44 → Debate on Uniform Civil Code (Shah Bano, Sarla Mudgal; Uttarakhand UCC 2024) Article 48-A → Environment Protection Act, 1986 Article 50 → Gradual separation of judiciary from executive through various Acts

p: Union Executive · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Constitutional Position: Executive power of the Union vested in President under Article 53. The President is the constitutional head — acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74). Not a rubber stamp but has limited real discretionary powers. Qualifications (Article 58): Citizen of India; at least 35 years; qualified as Lok Sabha member; must not hold office of profit. Election (Article 54): Indirect election through electoral college — elected members of both Houses of Parliament AND elected members of State Legislative Assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry). Nominated members and members of State Legislative Councils excluded. Single transferable vote system with proportional representation to ensure parity between States. Term: 5 years (Article 56). Eligible for re-election. Only President elected twice: Rajendra Prasad. Removal (Article 61): Impeachment for violation of Constitution. Each House passes a resolution by special majority (2/3 of total membership). The other House investigates and if it resolves by 2/3 majority that charge is sustained, President is removed. Powers of the President: Executive: All executive actions expressed in President's name (Article 77). Appoints PM, Cabinet, Governors, CAG, CEC, CJI and SC/HC judges, Attorney General, Ambassadors. Legislative: Summons, prorogues, dissolves Parliament. Addresses Parliament. Nominates 12 Rajya Sabha members. Gives assent to Bills — cannot withhold after reconsideration (Article 111). Promulgates Ordinances when Parliament not in session (Article 123) — Ordinance ceases within 6 weeks of Parliament's reassembly. Judicial: Pardoning power under Article 72 — pardon, reprieve, respite, remission, commutation. Covers: death sentences, court martial offences, Union law offences. D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987): Re-promulgation of Ordinances without bringing them before legislature is fraud on the Constitution. Emergency: Proclaims National Emergency (Art. 352), President's Rule (Art. 356), Financial Emergency (Art. 360). Discretionary Powers: Limited real discretion: (a) Can refer Cabinet advice back once for reconsideration — must act on reconsidered advice (Article 74(1) proviso — 44th Amendment); (b) Appointment of PM when no clear majority; (c) Dissolution of Lok Sabha if PM's advice appears improper. Pardoning Power Comparison: President (Article 72): Death sentences ✓ | Court martial ✓ | Union law offences ✓ | State law offences ✗ Governor (Article 161): Death sentences ✗ | Court martial ✗ | Union law offences ✗ | State law offences ✓

p: Union Executive · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha (Article 64). Elected by members of both Houses of Parliament — both elected AND nominated members (unlike President's electoral college). Term: 5 years. Removed by Rajya Sabha resolution (simple majority) agreed to by Lok Sabha (Article 67). Acts as President when vacancy arises (Article 65).

t: 5.3 Prime Minister and Council of Ministers
p: Union Executive · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Article 75: PM appointed by President. Other Ministers appointed by President on PM's advice. Council of Ministers collectively responsible to Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)). A Minister not a member of either House for 6 consecutive months ceases to be Minister. Cabinet vs. Council of Ministers: Cabinet (Cabinet Ministers only) is the inner circle — the real executive. Council of Ministers is the wider body. Collective responsibility means the entire Cabinet must resign if it loses Lok Sabha confidence.

p: State Executive and the Governor · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Governor is constitutional head of State executive. Article 153: Governor for each State. One person can be Governor of two or more States. Executive power vested in Governor (Article 154) but exercised on aid and advice of Council of Ministers headed by CM.

p: State Executive and the Governor · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Appointed by President under Article 155 Qualifications (Article 157): Citizen of India; at least 35 years Conditions (Article 158): Not a member of any legislature; not hold office of profit Term (Article 156): 5 years OR during the pleasure of the President — whichever is earlier

p: State Executive and the Governor · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Holds office during pleasure of President (Article 156(1)). B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010): Power to remove Governor is not absolute — cannot be exercised arbitrarily, capriciously, or for political reasons.

p: State Executive and the Governor · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Executive: Appoints CM when no clear majority (genuine discretion). Appoints other ministers on CM's advice. Seeks information from CM on administration (Article 167). Legislative — Assent to Bills (Article 200): Four options: (i) give assent; (ii) withhold assent; (iii) return non-Money Bill for reconsideration; (iv) reserve for President's consideration. CRITICAL: If Bill is re-passed by State Legislature, Governor MUST give assent — cannot withhold a second time. Presidential consideration (Article 201): President has WIDER discretion than Governor — not bound to assent even after Bill is re-passed by State Legislature. Ordinance-making (Article 213): When Legislature not in session AND immediate action necessary. Ceases to operate if: (1) not approved within 6 weeks of reassembly; (2) resolution disapproving it passed; (3) Governor revokes it. Pardoning Power (Article 161): State law offences ONLY. CANNOT pardon death sentences (President's exclusive power under Article 72). Discretionary Powers (Article 163): Appointment of CM when no clear majority Dismissal of Council of Ministers that has lost majority but refuses to resign Dissolution of State Assembly (limited by S.R. Bommai) Reservation of Bills for President's consideration Seeking information from CM (Article 167) Recommending President's Rule (Article 356) Immunity (Article 361): Complete immunity from court proceedings during tenure. No criminal proceedings whatsoever. Civil proceedings for personal acts: 2 months' notice required.

p: State Executive and the Governor · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974): Governor is constitutional head; acts on CoM advice except in matters of express constitutional discretion S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994): Governor's report under Art. 356 is justiciable; floor of House is sole test of majority; Assembly in suspended animation until Parliament approves Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006): Dissolution of Bihar Assembly by Governor struck down as mala fide B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010): Removal of Governor cannot be arbitrary or for political reasons Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker, Arunachal Pradesh (2016): Governor cannot advance session contrary to CoM advice

p: Parliament · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Rajya Sabha (Article 80): Maximum 250 (238 elected + 12 nominated by President). Permanent body — cannot be dissolved. 1/3 members retire every 2 years. Chaired by Vice President. Lok Sabha (Article 81): Maximum 543 elected members (after 104th Amendment, 2020 — abolished Anglo-Indian nominated seats). Direct election on basis of adult suffrage. Normal term: 5 years. Chaired by Speaker.

p: Parliament · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Deals ONLY with matters in Article 110(1)(a) to (g): taxes, borrowing, Consolidated Fund, appropriation, supplementary expenditure, audit of accounts. Must be introduced ONLY in Lok Sabha. Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations within 14 days. Speaker's certification is final (Article 110(3)).

p: Parliament · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Freedom of speech in Parliament — no liability for anything said or vote cast No arrest in civil cases during session + 40 days before/after Courts cannot question Parliamentary proceedings Publication of Parliamentary reports protected Key evolution: P.V. Narasimha Rao v. State (1998) — bribery for vote protected by Art. 105. Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024): 7-judge bench OVERRULED P.V. Narasimha Rao — bribery NOT protected by Article 105(2).

p: Parliament · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Disqualification if: (1) voluntarily gives up party membership; (2) votes/abstains contrary to party direction without permission and party does not condone within 15 days. 91st Amendment (2003): 'split' exception abolished; only merger of 2/3 members recognised. Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992): Tenth Schedule upheld; Speaker's decision subject to judicial review.

p: Parliament · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Simple majority: Creation of new States, changing State names Special majority (2/3 of present and voting + majority of total): Most provisions Special majority + Ratification by half of State Legislatures: Federal provisions (Arts. 54, 55, 73, 162, Seventh Schedule, etc.)

p: Union–State Legislative Relations · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Union List (List I): Parliament only — Defence, Foreign Affairs, Currency, Banking, Railways, etc. Residuary powers also vest in Parliament (Article 248). State List (List II): State Legislature only — Public Order, Police, Agriculture, Land, Local Government, Public Health, etc. Concurrent List (List III): Both Parliament and State — Education, Criminal Law, Marriage, Contracts, Labour. In repugnancy, Union law prevails (Article 254). Exception: State law with Presidential assent prevails in that State — but Parliament can override.

p: Union–State Legislative Relations · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Pith and Substance: Courts look at the true nature and character of legislation. If it falls substantially within the legislature's competence, it is valid even if it incidentally trenches on another legislature's field. Case: State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951). Colorable Legislation: The legislature cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly. If the substance encroaches on another legislature's domain, it is colorable. Case: K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953). Occupied Field: When Parliament intends to legislate exhaustively on a Concurrent List subject, States cannot legislate on the same subject. Article 254 — Repugnancy: Union law on Concurrent List prevails over State law. Exception: State law with Presidential assent prevails in that State — but Parliament can supersede by subsequent legislation.

t: 8.3 When Parliament Legislates on State List
p: Union–State Legislative Relations · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Article 249: Rajya Sabha resolution by 2/3 majority — national interest Article 250: During National Emergency Article 252: Parliament legislates for two or more States by consent Article 253: To implement international treaties — even State List subjects Article 356: During President's Rule — Parliament legislates for the State

p: Judiciary · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Composition: CJI + maximum 33 other judges (Parliament can increase). Retirement: 65 years. Salaries charged to Consolidated Fund of India — not subject to vote. Appointment (Collegium System): Three Judges Cases established the collegium (CJI + 4 senior-most SC judges). The NJAC (99th Amendment, 2014) was struck down in 2015 as violating judicial independence — a basic structure element. Removal (Article 124(4)): By address of each House by special majority on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. Jurisdiction: Original (Article 131): Inter-State disputes — exclusive Appellate (Articles 132–134): Constitutional, civil, criminal matters SLP (Article 136): Discretionary — widest appellate power; from any court or tribunal Writ (Article 32): For enforcement of Fundamental Rights Advisory (Article 143): President's reference — opinion advisory, not binding Court of Record (Article 129): Binding precedents; contempt power Article 141: Law declared by SC is binding on ALL courts in India. SC not bound by its own decisions. Article 142: SC can make any order to do complete justice — extraordinary power used for structural injunctions and unique remedies.

p: Judiciary · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Composition: Chief Justice + other judges. Retirement: 62 years. Appointment (Article 217): By President in consultation with CJI, Governor, Chief Justice of HC. Writ jurisdiction (Article 226): WIDER than Article 32 — any legal right, not just FRs Superintendence (Article 227): Over all subordinate courts and tribunals Transfer of constitutional questions (Article 228): Can withdraw cases involving constitutional questions

p: Judiciary · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: First Judges Case (S.P. Gupta, 1981): Executive primacy in appointments Second Judges Case (1993): Collegium — CJI's opinion gets primacy; CJI + 2 senior judges Third Judges Case (1998): Collegium expanded — CJI + 4 senior-most SC judges NJAC Case (2015): 99th Amendment struck down — judicial independence is basic structure

p: Judiciary · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Evolved by SC (Justice P.N. Bhagwati and Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer) in late 1970s–1980s. Liberalised locus standi — any public-spirited person can approach courts on behalf of those unable to access justice. Letters to court treated as writ petitions. Key cases: Hussainara Khatoon (1979), Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984), M.C. Mehta (1987), Vishaka (1997), Common Cause (2018).

p: Emergency Provisions · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Grounds: War, external aggression, or armed rebellion. 'Armed rebellion' replaced 'internal disturbance' by 44th Amendment, 1978 — to prevent misuse like the 1975 Emergency. Proclamation: Written advice of Cabinet (not PM alone — 44th Amendment). Approved by Parliament by special majority within one month. Renewed every 6 months by special majority. NO maximum period — continues indefinitely while renewed. Revocation: President can revoke on own. Lok Sabha alone can pass simple majority resolution to disapprove (Article 352(8)) — the ONLY instance where Lok Sabha can constitutionally act alone. Effects during National Emergency: Parliament legislates on State List (Article 250) Revenue distribution modified (Article 354) Article 19 freedoms automatically suspended (Article 358) — for laws made DURING Emergency only (not pre-existing laws) Other FRs can be suspended by Presidential Order (Article 359) — BUT NOT Articles 20 and 21 Fundamental duty to defend country becomes enforceable Historical use: 1962 (Chinese aggression), 1965 (Indo-Pak war), 1971 (Bangladesh war), 1975–1977 (internal disturbance — the most controversial, last Emergency)

p: Emergency Provisions · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Article 358: Suspends Article 19 rights | AUTOMATICALLY | Only war/external aggression | Only for laws made during Emergency | Does not affect pre-existing laws Article 359: Suspends other specified FRs | Requires Presidential Order | All types of National Emergency | Cannot suspend Articles 20 and 21 | Covers laws and executive action during Emergency

p: Emergency Provisions · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Grounds: Constitutional machinery of State has failed. Also: failure to comply with Union directions (Article 365). Duration: 2 months (initial, pending Parliament approval) → 6 months (after approval) → renewed every 6 months → maximum 3 years. Extension beyond 1 year requires: (a) National Emergency in operation; OR (b) Election Commission certifies elections cannot be held. Effects: President assumes State executive functions; Parliament legislates on State List; Governor becomes Centre's agent; Assembly is dissolved or kept in suspended animation. S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) — 9-judge bench — KEY PRINCIPLES: Art. 356 proclamation is subject to judicial review Until Parliament approves, Assembly is in 'suspended animation' — NOT dissolved Secularism is a basic feature — anti-secular State government can be dismissed Floor of the House is the SOLE test of majority — Governor cannot assess majority elsewhere Courts can examine whether material before President was relevant and germane

p: Emergency Provisions · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Grounds: Financial stability or credit of India or any part is threatened. Key features: Has NEVER been proclaimed in India's history No maximum period — continues until revoked by President President can direct reduction of salaries of ALL government servants including SC and HC judges (Article 360(4)(b)) — a unique constitutional provision Centre can give directions to States on financial matters during Financial Emergency

p: Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions (Part XXI) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Part XXI (Articles 369–392) contains provisions that were transitional at the time of adoption, and special provisions for specific States reflecting their unique historical, cultural, or political circumstances.

p: Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions (Part XXI) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Granted J&K special autonomous status — most provisions of the Constitution applied to J&K only with Presidential concurrence/consent. Abrogated in August 2019 by Presidential Order CO 272. J&K reorganised into two Union Territories: J&K (with Legislature) and Ladakh (without Legislature). SC upheld the abrogation in Dr. Farooq Abdullah v. Union of India (2023) by 5-judge bench.

p: Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions (Part XXI) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Article 371: Maharashtra and Gujarat — Governor has special responsibility for certain regions Article 371-A: Nagaland — customary law and practices protected; Acts of Parliament on Naga customary law require State Legislature's request Article 371-B: Assam — committee of tribal area members in Legislature Article 371-C: Manipur — similar committee Article 371-D and E: Andhra Pradesh/Telangana — equitable opportunities in public services Article 371-F: Sikkim — protection of rights and existing laws Article 371-G: Mizoram — similar to Nagaland Article 371-H: Arunachal Pradesh — Governor's special responsibility for law and order Article 371-I: Goa — minimum size of Legislative Assembly Article 371-J: Hyderabad-Karnataka region — reservation of seats

p: Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions (Part XXI) · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Administered by President through Administrator/Lieutenant Governor (Articles 239–241). Article 239-A: Parliament can create a legislature for certain UTs. Delhi's unique status: Government of NCT of Delhi Act, 1991 created Delhi Legislative Assembly. Delhi LG vs. Delhi Government dispute repeatedly litigated — Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018): Constitutional bench held LG is bound by Cabinet's aid and advice on most matters; Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2023): SC held Delhi government has control over services (later overridden by constitutional amendment).

p: Election Commission of India · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Article 324: Superintendence, direction, and control of preparation of electoral rolls and conduct of all elections to Parliament and State Legislatures vested in Election Commission of India.

p: Election Commission of India · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: CEC + such number of other ECs as President may fix (Article 324(2)). Appointed by President. The Chief Election Commissioner Act, 2023 changed the appointment process — selection committee (PM + Leader of Opposition + Cabinet Minister). This change (removing CJI from selection) is under judicial challenge.

p: Election Commission of India · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Term: 6 years or 65 years — whichever is earlier. The CEC can be removed ONLY in the same manner as a SC judge — by impeachment process (Article 324(5)). Other ECs can be removed by President on recommendation of CEC. T.N. Seshan v. Union of India (1995): CEC and other ECs have equal powers; CEC has no veto.

p: Election Commission of India · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Preparation and revision of electoral rolls Recognition of political parties; allotment of election symbols Model Code of Conduct enforcement (not statutory — based on Art. 324 plenary power) Setting election schedules; monitoring of elections Disqualification of candidates for corrupt practices (on reference from President/Governor) Advice on disqualification of MPs/MLAs under Articles 103 and 192

p: Election Commission of India · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: T.N. Seshan v. Union of India (1995): Equal powers of CEC and ECs; CEC has no veto Mohinder Singh Gill v. CEC (1978): Election Commission's superintendence powers are plenary Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (2002): Candidates must disclose criminal antecedents, assets, educational qualifications — right to information is part of Art. 19(1)(a) Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013): Convicted MPs/MLAs disqualified from date of conviction — Section 8(4) RPA struck down

p: Administrative Law: Nature and Scope · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Administrative law is that branch of public law which deals with the organisation, powers, and procedures of administrative authorities, and the legal remedies available to persons adversely affected by public administration. It governs the relationship between individuals and the State in the exercise of governmental power. Key definitions: H.W.R. Wade: "The law relating to the control of governmental power" Garner: "That branch of public law concerned with the composition, powers and duties of administrative authorities" Ivor Jennings: "The law relating to the administration — determines the organisation, powers and duties of administrative authorities" K.C. Davis (USA): "Deals with powers and procedures of administrative agencies, including especially judicial review of administrative action"

t: 13.2 Reasons for Growth of Administrative Law
p: Administrative Law: Nature and Scope · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: The growth of administrative law is directly linked to the transition from a laissez-faire (minimal government) state to a welfare state. Key reasons: Welfare State concept: State regulates health, education, housing, environment, labour Complexity of modern society: Parliament cannot foresee every situation; delegated legislation fills the gap Need for technical expertise: Regulatory bodies (SEBI, TRAI, RBI) require specialist knowledge courts lack Speed and flexibility: Administrative adjudication is faster than courts Parliamentary time constraints: Parliament cannot deal with all regulatory minutiae

p: Administrative Law: Nature and Scope · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: A.V. Dicey opposed administrative law because he believed it violated the Rule of Law — it created a separate system of law for government officials. Dicey saw the French Droit Administratif system (Conseil d'État) as contrary to English principles of equality before law. Dicey's three meanings of Rule of Law: Supremacy of law — no man punished except for breach of established ordinary law Equality before the law — every man, including officials, subject to ordinary courts Constitution as consequence of rights declared by ordinary courts Dicey was later criticised by Ivor Jennings, W.A. Robson, and H.W.R. Wade who showed that French Droit Administratif actually provides MORE protection to citizens against the State than Dicey acknowledged, and that the English common law too has developed substantial administrative law.

p: Administrative Law: Nature and Scope · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Rule of Law is a basic feature of the Indian Constitution (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973; Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain, 1975). Constitutional pillars of Rule of Law in India: Article 13: No law can violate Fundamental Rights Article 14: Equal protection of laws Article 21: Procedure must be just, fair, and reasonable (Maneka Gandhi, 1978) Articles 32 and 226: Judicial review enforces Rule of Law Independence of judiciary (basic structure)

p: Administrative Law: Nature and Scope · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: India does not have strict Montesquieu-style separation but a functional separation with checks and balances. Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955): Indian Constitution does not adopt strict separation of powers but contemplates a system of checks and balances. The judiciary is the watchdog — reviews legislative and executive action.

p: Administrative Law: Nature and Scope · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Legislation made by executive or administrative bodies under authority delegated by Parliament. Justified by: technical nature of subjects, parliamentary time constraints, need for flexibility, local expertise. Types: Rules, Regulations, Bye-laws, Notifications, Schemes. Controls: Parliamentary control: Laying procedure (affirmative or negative resolution); Committee on Subordinate Legislation in both Houses Judicial control: Courts strike down if ultra vires, violates FRs, procedurally defective, or unreasonable Procedural controls: Mandatory consultation, public notice, publication in Official Gazette Limits on Delegation — Delhi Laws Act Case (1951): Parliament cannot delegate the 'essential legislative function' — must lay down policy. Details of implementation only can be delegated. Excessive delegation (abdication of legislative function) is unconstitutional. Sub-delegation requires express or implied permission (delegatus non potest delegare). D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987): Repeated repromulgation of Ordinances without bringing them before the Legislature is a fraud on the Constitution — misuse of delegated legislative power.

p: Administrative Law: Nature and Scope · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Ombudsman concept originated in Sweden (1809) — an independent official appointed by Parliament to investigate complaints against government officials. India's equivalent: Lokpal (Union level) and Lokayukta (State level). Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013: Jurisdiction: PM (with restrictions), Ministers, MPs, Group A/B/C/D government servants, and certain NGOs Chairperson: Former CJI or SC judge or eminent person with 25+ years' experience First Lokpal: Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose (appointed 2019) Complaints against PM excluded if related to external affairs, security, public order

p: Principles of Natural Justice · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Natural justice consists of procedural requirements that must be observed by courts, tribunals, and administrative bodies before making decisions that adversely affect persons. Rooted in natural law theory — principles so fundamental to justice that they are universally self-evident. Not merely technical procedural rules — a fundamental guarantee of fairness rooted in human dignity.

p: Principles of Natural Justice · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Rule 1 — Nemo debet esse judex in propria sua causa (Rule Against Bias): No person shall be a judge in his own cause. The decision-maker must not have any interest — personal, financial, or otherwise — in the outcome. Ensures both actual fairness AND appearance of fairness. Types of Bias: Pecuniary bias: ANY financial interest in the outcome — AUTOMATIC disqualification — no need to prove actual influence. Dimes v. Grand Junction Canal (1852): Lord Chancellor held shares; decree set aside. Personal bias: Friendship, hostility, or other personal relationship with a party. Subject matter bias: Pre-judgment — the adjudicator has already formed a view before hearing. Departmental/Institutional bias: The entire department has a pre-determined stance. Gullapalli Nageswara Rao v. A.P. SRTC (1959): Investigator cannot be adjudicator — officer who heard objections cannot sanction the same scheme. Policy bias: Adjudicator under pressure to follow a government policy predetermining the outcome. Test for bias in India (A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India, 1970): 'Real danger' or 'Reasonable suspicion' of bias. R v. Sussex Justices (1924): 'Justice must not only be done but must also be seen to be done.' Rule 2 — Audi alteram partem (Right to Fair Hearing): Hear the other side before deciding against a person. No one should be condemned unheard. Core components: Notice: Adequate notice of proceedings and the charge/allegation Opportunity to be heard: In writing or orally (oral hearing not always required) Right to know the case against: Access to material relied upon by decision-maker Opportunity to present evidence and cross-examine: NOT always required — depends on context (Russell v. Duke of Norfolk, 1949) Right to legal representation: NOT automatic — depends on statutory provision and nature of proceedings Speaking/Reasoned order: Duty to give reasons (Bhagat Raja v. Union of India, 1967) Key case history: Cooper v. Wandsworth Board of Works (1863): House demolished without notice — violated NJ even though no statute required a hearing Ridge v. Baldwin (1964) [HL]: LANDMARK — NJ applies to decisions affecting rights, not just strictly judicial functions; revived the scope of NJ A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India (1970): Boundary between administrative and quasi-judicial is not rigid — NJ applies to administrative functions affecting rights Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978): Impounding passport without prior hearing — procedure must be fair; post-decisional hearing is generally inadequate Swadeshi Cotton Mills v. Union of India (1981): NJ content is flexible — depends on statutory framework, nature of power, consequences, public interest Rule 3 — Speaking Orders (Duty to Give Reasons): The decision-maker must record reasons so the aggrieved party can challenge the decision effectively. Applies to quasi-judicial orders. Bhagat Raja v. Union of India (1967): This requirement is an element of natural justice for quasi-judicial orders.

t: 14.3 When Natural Justice Can Be Excluded
p: Principles of Natural Justice · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Statutory exclusion — express statutory provision (but cannot violate Articles 14/21 — Maneka Gandhi principle) Emergency — urgency makes prior hearing impossible (must give post-decisional remedy) Impracticability — mass action where individual hearing is impractical Confidentiality/National security — disclosure would prejudice State security Purely administrative action — policy-making with no individual rights affected Waiver — the affected party can voluntarily and knowingly waive the right

p: Principles of Natural Justice · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: A person has a 'legitimate expectation' when a public authority has, by its conduct, promise, or consistent practice, led a person to reasonably expect that a certain procedure will be followed or a benefit will not be withdrawn without an opportunity to be heard. Council of Civil Service Unions v. Minister for Civil Service (GCHQ Case, 1985) [HL]: PM banned union membership at GCHQ without consulting unions — breach of legitimate expectation of consultation Navjyoti Coop. Group Housing Society v. Union of India (1992): First clear Indian recognition — change of policy without notice to affected parties was invalid Food Corporation of India v. Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries (1993): LE gives right to be heard before adverse action, not necessarily the substantive benefit expected Union of India v. Hindustan Development Corporation (1993): LE gives only procedural right — NOT a substantive right to the expected benefit Promissory Estoppel vs. Legitimate Expectation: Promissory Estoppel (Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of UP, 1979): Government cannot retract a clear representation on which a party has acted to its detriment — equitable doctrine. Legitimate Expectation is broader — based on reasonable expectation from conduct/practice, not necessarily a specific promise — public law doctrine.

p: Judicial Review of Administrative Action: Grounds · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Judicial review is the power of the judiciary to examine the lawfulness of administrative action. In India, it flows from Articles 32 and 226 (writ jurisdiction) and is a basic feature of the Constitution. It is a constitutional power, not merely a statutory one (L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, 1997).

t: 15.2 Lord Diplock's Three Grounds: GCHQ Case (1985)
p: Judicial Review of Administrative Action: Grounds · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: In Council of Civil Service Unions v. Minister for Civil Service (GCHQ Case, 1985), Lord Diplock classified grounds of judicial review into three authoritative categories: 1. Illegality: The decision-maker must understand the law regulating the decision-making power and give effect to it. Sub-categories: No jurisdiction (acting without authority) Excess of jurisdiction Failure to exercise jurisdiction Error of law (post-Anisminic, 1969 — ANY error of law goes to jurisdiction) Mala fide/Improper purpose — exercising power for an unauthorised purpose Irrelevant considerations — taking into account matters not authorised by statute Failure to consider relevant matters 2. Irrationality (Wednesbury Unreasonableness): From Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd. v. Wednesbury Corporation [1948]. Lord Greene MR: A decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could ever have come to it. HIGH threshold — courts do not substitute their own judgment for that of the authority. The court asks: was the decision within the range of reasonable responses? 3. Procedural Impropriety: Failure to observe procedural rules prescribed by statute (procedural ultra vires) OR failure to observe rules of natural justice — breach of audi alteram partem and rule against bias.

t: 15.3 The Indian Grounds of Judicial Review
p: Judicial Review of Administrative Action: Grounds · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Indian courts have developed a comprehensive jurisprudence: Lack of jurisdiction (no jurisdiction): Administrative authority has no power in the matter at all Excess of jurisdiction: Authority has power but has exceeded it Abuse of discretion: Exercise of discretion for improper purpose (colourable exercise) Taking irrelevant considerations into account Ignoring relevant considerations Acting mala fide Arbitrary or unreasonable decision Error of law: Following Anisminic (1969) — any error of law, not just 'jurisdictional' error in the narrow sense Error of fact going to jurisdiction Violation of natural justice: Breach of audi alteram partem or rule against bias Legitimate expectation: Failure to honour a legitimate expectation Proportionality: Means used must be proportionate to ends sought

p: Judicial Review of Administrative Action: Grounds · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Stricter standard than Wednesbury unreasonableness. Structured inquiry: Is the objective legitimate? Are the means suitable for achieving the objective? Are the means necessary — could less restrictive means achieve the same goal? Is there a fair balance between individual rights and public interest? Om Kumar v. Union of India (2001): SC adopted proportionality as a ground of review for punishments imposed on government servants. Modern Dental College v. State of MP (2016) and K.S. Puttaswamy (2017): Proportionality test applied to restrictions on Fundamental Rights.

p: Judicial Review of Administrative Action: Grounds · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Habeas Corpus ('you have the body'): Compels production of detained person before court to examine legality of detention. Most important writ for personal liberty. Wide scope — lies against State AND private individuals. Available even during Emergency (subject to Art. 359 orders — but Arts. 20/21 cannot be suspended). Mandamus ('we command'): Issued to public authority commanding performance of a public duty which has been refused or neglected. Enforces statutory duties, constitutional duties. Does NOT lie against: private contractual obligations; purely discretionary decisions (only compels exercise of discretion, not a particular outcome); judicial authority in purely judicial matters; private individuals. Certiorari ('to be certified'): Issued to inferior tribunal to bring record before superior court for examination and quash if defective. CURATIVE — issued AFTER decision. Grounds: excess of jurisdiction, lack of jurisdiction, violation of NJ, error apparent on the face of record (Syed Yakoob v. K.S. Radhakrishnan, 1964). Prohibition: Issued to inferior tribunal to STOP it proceeding in excess of jurisdiction. PREVENTIVE — issued BEFORE decision is made. If decision already made, certiorari is the appropriate remedy. Quo Warranto ('by what authority'): Issued against a person who has usurped or holds a public office without legal authority. Only lies for public offices of a substantive character created by statute or Constitution. A discretionary writ — not a writ of right (University of Mysore v. C.D. Govinda Rao, 1964).

p: Judicial Review of Administrative Action: Grounds · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Article 323-A (42nd Amendment, 1976) provides for Administrative Tribunals for service disputes. Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 established the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT). Article 323-B: Tribunals for other matters (taxation, elections, industrial disputes). L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997): Power of High Courts under Articles 226 and 227 is part of the basic structure of the Constitution and CANNOT be excluded. CAT decisions are subject to HC Division Bench review. SC can entertain SLPs from HC decisions on CAT matters.

p: Key Doctrines: Constitutional and Administrative Law · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Basic Structure Doctrine Origin: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973). Parliament can amend the Constitution under Art. 368 but cannot destroy its basic structure. Recognised elements: supremacy of Constitution, republican and democratic form, secular character, separation of powers, federal character, judicial review, free and fair elections, dignity of individual, unity and integrity of nation, parliamentary system, rule of law, equality, social justice, and independence of judiciary. Doctrine of Eclipse Origin: Bhikhaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP (1955). Pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are not void but dormant — eclipsed. They automatically revive if the constitutional bar (FR) is amended to remove the inconsistency. Does NOT apply to post-constitutional laws (those are void ab initio under Art. 13(2)). Doctrine of Severability Origin: R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala v. Union of India (1957). Only the unconstitutional part of a law is struck down; the rest remains valid if separable and independently workable. Test: Would Parliament have enacted the law even without the invalid portion? Doctrine of Colourable Legislation Origin: K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953). Even where a legislature appears to act within its powers, if in substance it is encroaching upon another legislature's domain, the legislation is 'coloured' or 'disguised' — and is invalid. The label does not matter; the substance does. Pith and Substance Doctrine Origin: Profulla Kumar Mukherjee v. Bank of Khulna (1947, PC); State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951). If a law incidentally trenches on another legislature's field, courts look at its true nature and character. If it falls substantially within the legislature's competence, it is valid despite incidental encroachment. Doctrine of Occupied Field When Parliament legislates exhaustively on a Concurrent List subject, it occupies the entire field — States cannot legislate on the same subject. Related to Art. 254 repugnancy. Doctrine of Pleasure (Article 310) Government servants hold office during the pleasure of the President/Governor. Subject to Art. 311 procedural safeguards. Does NOT apply to SC/HC judges (who hold during good behaviour) or Constitutional authorities with specific security of tenure. Doctrine of Implied Powers Powers not expressly conferred but necessarily implied from express provisions. Applied to fill lacunae in the Constitution. Doctrine of Prospective Overruling Origin in India: Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967) — Subba Rao CJ. When the SC overrules a previous decision, it can declare that the overruling shall operate only prospectively — not affecting past transactions. Prevents injustice from retroactive application of a new legal rule. Doctrine of Double Jeopardy (Article 20(2)) No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. Narrower than the common law autrefois acquit/convict — applies only to prosecution AND punishment, not to mere prosecution. Disciplinary proceedings + criminal proceedings on the same facts do NOT violate Art. 20(2). Doctrine of Sovereign Immunity The State is not liable for acts done in the exercise of sovereign functions. In P. & O. Steam Navigation Co. v. Secretary of State for India (1861), a distinction was drawn between sovereign and non-sovereign functions. Post-Constitution, the SC in Kasturi Lal Ralia Ram Jain v. State of UP (1965) upheld the distinction. Later cases (N. Nagendra Rao & Co. v. State of AP, 1994) significantly eroded it — State cannot claim immunity for tortious acts of its servants. Doctrine of Res Judicata in Constitutional Matters In Devilal Modi v. STO (1964), the SC held that res judicata applies to writ petitions also. A petition dismissed on merits creates res judicata — but a petition dismissed on grounds of alternative remedy does not bar a fresh petition.

p: Key Doctrines: Constitutional and Administrative Law · Constitutional and Administrative Law
x: Doctrine of Ultra Vires An act beyond the powers conferred by the enabling statute is ultra vires and void. Two types: Substantive ultra vires (acting beyond scope) and Procedural ultra vires (not following prescribed procedure). In delegated legislation: mandatory procedural requirements must be followed; directory requirements — their breach may not invalidate the legislation. Doctrine of Legitimate Expectation A person has a legitimate expectation if a public authority has, by conduct, promise, or consistent practice, led them to reasonably expect a certain procedure will be followed or benefit will not be withdrawn without a hearing. Gives procedural right only — not substantive right to the expected benefit (Union of India v. Hindustan Development Corp., 1993). The authority can always override LE for larger public interest, provided it gives an opportunity to be heard. Doctrine of Proportionality The means used by the State to achieve a legitimate aim must be proportionate — not more restrictive of rights than necessary. Four-stage test: (1) legitimate aim; (2) rational connection; (3) necessity (minimum impairment); (4) proportionality stricto sensu (fair balance). Adopted in Om Kumar (2001) for service matters; expanded to FR restrictions in Modern Dental College (2016) and Puttaswamy (2017). Doctrine of Wednesbury Unreasonableness From Associated Provincial Picture Houses v. Wednesbury Corporation (1948). A decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could ever have come to it. High threshold — courts do not evaluate the merits of the decision; only ask whether it was within the range of reasonable responses. Slowly being replaced in rights-based cases by proportionality. Doctrine of Fairness (Duty to Act Fairly) Wider than natural justice. Even in cases where formal natural justice rules may not apply, a public authority must act fairly. Maneka Gandhi (1978) expanded the duty of fairness to all State action affecting persons. Doctrine of Promissory Estoppel The government is estopped from going back on a promise or representation on which a citizen has acted to his detriment. Confirmed in Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills (1979). Exceptions: (1) Public interest requires the change; (2) The original promise was made without authority. Differs from legitimate expectation (LE is wider — no specific promise needed). Delegatus Non Potest Delegare A delegate cannot further delegate the power delegated to it unless expressly or impliedly permitted by the parent Act. Prevents uncontrolled sub-delegation of legislative power. Doctrine of Excessive Delegation Parliament cannot abdicate its essential legislative function. It must lay down the policy and the standards — delegation of powers to fill in details is permissible, but delegation of the entire legislative field is unconstitutional. In re Delhi Laws Act (1951): SC held that the essential legislative functions cannot be delegated.

p: Exam Pattern, Trends and Priority Map · Environment and Human Rights
x: Paper 2 (Law) has 100 objective questions of 2 marks each (200 marks); Paper 1 has 50 questions (100 marks). Both are taken in a single 3-hour sitting. The official notices state that there is no negative marking. The paper is divided into 10 units, so Unit VIII typically contributes roughly 8 to 12 questions. The split is not fixed, but it is always a mix of environment law and human rights law. Question formats seen in recent cycles: (a) direct one-line factual questions; (b) Statement I / Statement II (true-false pairs); (c) Match List I with List II (case with principle, convention with year, Article with subject, commission with statute); (d) "which of the following is/are correct" multi-statement questions; (e) chronological ordering of conferences or instruments; (f) occasional Assertion-Reason. Public question banks for this unit show that questions on the UN Human Rights Council, the UN Decade for Human Rights Education (1995–2004) and the body that constitutes the NHRC have been asked. Expect the same style of fact-recall again.

p: Exam Pattern, Trends and Priority Map · Environment and Human Rights
x: The human rights half is steadier and more factual (UDHR, ICCPR, ICESCR, Optional Protocols, Vienna Declaration 1993, the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 and its amendments of 2006 and 2019). Questions on NHRC composition, appointment and removal recur almost every cycle. The environment half rewards case law and dates. Vellore Citizens, M.C. Mehta (several), Rural Litigation, Subhash Kumar, Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action, A.P. Pollution Control Board v. Nayudu, T.N. Godavarman and the Kamal Nath public trust case are the usual match-the-following material. The NGT is the single most examined environmental topic because it is compact: Act of 2010, Sections 14 to 22, composition, jurisdiction, limitation, appeal to the Supreme Court within 90 days, the seven scheduled Acts. International conferences are a perennial chronological question: Stockholm 1972, Nairobi 1982, Brundtland 1987, Rio 1992, Kyoto 1997, Johannesburg 2002, Rio+20 2012, Paris 2015, Glasgow 2021. Group rights questions are statute-driven : Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016, Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007, Juvenile Justice Act 2015, POCSO 2012, Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005, POSH Act 2013, the minorities commission statute of 1992, and Articles 338, 338A and 338B for the SC, ST and backward classes commissions. Recent developments are a small but real slice. Examples covered below: the Jan Vishwas amendments to the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 (penalty regime from 1 April 2024), the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, India's 2026–28 UN Human Rights Council term, and the Supreme Court's 2025 Vanashakti judgment and its recall.

These notes cover every listed topic and sub-topic in detail.

p: Meaning and Concept of Environment and Environmental Pollution · Environment and Human Rights
x: Components. Abiotic (air, water, soil, sunlight, minerals, climate) and biotic (plants, animals, microorganisms, humans). The two interact through food chains, nutrient cycles and energy flow. Natural and man-made environment. Natural: forests, rivers, atmosphere. Man-made (built): cities, industries, roads, dams. Some writers add the social and cultural environment. Segments (spheres). Atmosphere (air), hydrosphere (water), lithosphere (land and soil), biosphere (life). Ecology and ecosystem. Ecology (term by Ernst Haeckel, 1866) studies relationships between organisms and surroundings. An ecosystem is a functional unit of living things and their physical environment. Statutory definition: Environment (Protection) Act 1986, s.2(a). “Environment” includes water, air and land and the inter-relationship which exists among and between water, air and land, and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organisms and property. Note the three physical elements plus the inter-relationship , and the inclusion of property. This is the most-asked definition in the unit.

p: Meaning and Concept of Environment and Environmental Pollution · Environment and Human Rights
x: Pollution is the introduction into the environment of substances or energy in such quantity or concentration that they harm living things, ecosystems, property or the quality of the environment. Term Statute and section Core idea Environmental pollutant EP Act 1986, s.2(b) Any solid, liquid or gaseous substance present in such concentration as may be, or tend to be, injurious to the environment Environmental pollution EP Act 1986, s.2(c) The presence in the environment of any environmental pollutant Handling EP Act s.2(d) Manufacture, processing, treatment, package, storage, transportation, use, collection, destruction, conversion, offering for sale, transfer or the like Hazardous substance EP Act s.2(e) Any substance or preparation which, by reason of its chemical or physico-chemical properties or handling, is liable to cause harm to human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organisms, property or the environment Occupier EP Act s.2(f) A person who has control over the affairs of the factory or premises, including in relation to any substance, the person in possession of it Water pollution Water Act 1974, s.2(e) Contamination of water or alteration of its physical, chemical or biological properties, or discharge of sewage, trade effluent or other liquid, gaseous or solid substance which may create a nuisance or render water harmful to public health or safety, to domestic, commercial, industrial, agricultural or other legitimate uses, or to aquatic organisms, livestock, wild animals and plants Air pollutant Air Act 1981, s.2(a) Any solid, liquid or gaseous substance (including noise) present in the atmosphere in such concentration as may be or tend to be injurious to human beings, other living creatures, plants, property or environment Air pollution Air Act s.2(b) The presence in the atmosphere of any air pollutant Exam angle. Noise was brought into the definition of “air pollutant” by the 1987 amendment to the Air Act. The Water Act’s definition of pollution is wider than the EP Act’s, because it speaks of a “nuisance” and of harm to uses of water. Do not confuse “environmental pollutant” (s.2(b)) with “hazardous substance” (s.2(e)).

p: Meaning and Concept of Environment and Environmental Pollution · Environment and Human Rights
x: Air pollution: vehicles, industry, burning of fuels and biomass, construction dust. Key pollutants: particulate matter (PM10, PM2.5), sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, ozone, lead. Water pollution: untreated sewage, industrial effluents, agricultural runoff (fertilisers, pesticides), oil spills, thermal discharge. Soil and land pollution: solid and hazardous waste, mining, agro-chemicals. Noise pollution: governed in India by the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000 under the EP Act; Article 21 and the case of Church of God (Full Gospel) in India v. K.K.R. Majestic Colony Welfare Association (2000) hold that loudspeaker noise cannot be justified by religious freedom. Marine, radioactive, plastic, electronic waste and light pollution are further categories. Point-source versus non-point source pollution is a common conceptual distinction: a factory pipe versus agricultural runoff.

t: 1.4 Principles that explain what the law is protecting
p: Meaning and Concept of Environment and Environmental Pollution · Environment and Human Rights
x: Sustainable development: development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs (Brundtland Report, Our Common Future , 1987). Indian courts treat it as a part of the law of the land ( Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum , 1996). Precautionary principle: where there are threats of serious or irreversible damage, lack of full scientific certainty must not be used as a reason to postpone measures to prevent degradation. Rio Declaration Principle 15. In India, the burden of proof lies on the person proposing the activity ( A.P. Pollution Control Board v. M.V. Nayudu , 1999). Polluter pays principle: the polluter bears the cost of remedying the damage and restoring the environment ( Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India , 1996; Vellore ). Rio Principle 16. Public trust doctrine: the State holds natural resources as trustee for the public ( M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath , 1997). Intergenerational equity: present generations hold the planet in trust for the future. Absolute liability: hazardous industries are strictly and absolutely liable for harm, with no exceptions ( M.C. Mehta v. Union of India , the Oleum Gas Leak case, 1986/87), extending beyond Rylands v. Fletcher . Doctrine of eco-centrism versus anthropocentrism: anthropocentrism values nature for human use; eco-centrism (deep ecology, Arne Næss) gives nature intrinsic value. The Supreme Court has leaned towards eco-centric language in Animal Welfare Board v. A. Nagaraja (2014) and in cases on rivers and glaciers’ legal personhood debates; the Uttarakhand High Court’s 2017 orders granting legal personhood to the Ganga and Yamuna were stayed by the Supreme Court. Right to a clean environment is a facet of the right to life under Article 21 ( Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar , 1991; Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P. , 1985, the Doon Valley case, the first case in which the Supreme Court ordered the closure of limestone quarries on ecological grounds). Climate rights: in M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court recognised a right against the adverse effects of climate change as part of Articles 14 and 21.

t: Overview: Meaning and Concept of Environment and Environmental Pollution
p: Meaning and Concept of Environment and Environmental Pollution · Environment and Human Rights
x: The word “environment” comes from the French environner , to encircle or surround. In law, it means everything that surrounds a living being and influences its life: air, water, land, climate, flora and fauna, and the interactions between them and human society. Modern environmental law moved from a narrow, resource-by-resource approach (protect a river, control a factory) to a holistic, ecosystem approach in which protection of the environment is tied to human dignity, development and the rights of future generations. This shift is why the unit begins with definitions: almost every later topic (statutes, tribunals, conferences, cases) depends on how “environment” and “pollution” are defined.

p: International Environmental Law and UN Conferences · Environment and Human Rights
x: Treaties and conventions (hard law): e.g. UNFCCC, CBD, Montreal Protocol. Customary international law: the duty to prevent transboundary harm, the duty to cooperate, the duty to notify and consult, and (increasingly) the duty to conduct environmental impact assessment. General principles of law and judicial decisions (Article 38, ICJ Statute). Soft law: declarations, action plans and guidelines such as the Stockholm Declaration, Rio Declaration, Agenda 21 and the Forest Principles. They are not binding but shape treaties and domestic law, and Indian courts use them to interpret statutes.

p: International Environmental Law and UN Conferences · Environment and Human Rights
x: Attended by 113 States. Indira Gandhi’s speech (“poverty is the greatest polluter”) set out the developing-country position that environment and development cannot be separated. Principle 1: Man has the fundamental right to freedom, equality and adequate conditions of life, in an environment of a quality that permits a life of dignity and well-being, and bears a solemn responsibility to protect and improve the environment for present and future generations. Principle 21: States have, in accordance with the UN Charter and principles of international law, the sovereign right to exploit their own resources pursuant to their own environmental policies, and the responsibility to ensure that activities within their jurisdiction or control do not cause damage to the environment of other States or of areas beyond national jurisdiction. This is the classic statement of the no-harm rule. Principle 22: States shall cooperate to develop international law on liability and compensation for victims of pollution. Impact on India: the 42nd Amendment 1976 inserted Article 48A (Directive Principle) and Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty). The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974 was enacted by Parliament under Article 252 on resolutions from States, expressly to implement decisions taken at Stockholm. The Environment (Protection) Act 1986 was enacted under Article 253 and its preamble refers to Stockholm.

x: Rio Declaration key principles: P1 humans are at the centre of concerns for sustainable development; P3 right to development must be fulfilled so as to equitably meet developmental and environmental needs of present and future generations; P4 environmental protection is an integral part of development; P7 common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR); P10 public participation and access to information and justice; P15 precautionary approach; P16 internalisation of environmental costs and the polluter pays principle; P17 environmental impact assessment as a national instrument; P22 role of indigenous people. Forest Principles: a non-legally binding authoritative statement of principles for a global consensus on forests. UNFCCC (entered into force 1994) and CBD (entered into force 1993) were opened for signature at Rio.
