p: International Environmental Law and UN Conferences · Environment and Human Rights
x: India’s negotiating stance is built on CBDR and equity, “right to development”, and climate finance and technology transfer by developed countries. India ratified the Kyoto Protocol (2002) and the Paris Agreement (2 October 2016), and is a party to the Montreal Protocol, Basel, CBD and CITES. It ratified the Kigali Amendment in 2021. Domestic implementation: the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 (Article 253), the Biological Diversity Act 2002 (CBD), the Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972 (CITES), the Ozone Depleting Substances (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000 (Montreal Protocol), and the Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules 2016 (Basel). Constitutional hooks: Article 51(c) (respect for international law and treaty obligations) and Article 253 (Parliament may legislate to implement international agreements). In Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum (1996) the Supreme Court said that the precautionary and polluter pays principles are part of the environmental law of the country, and that customary international law not contrary to domestic law is part of it. India’s Paris-era commitments (as updated in 2022): reduce emissions intensity of GDP by 45% from 2005 levels by 2030; about 50% of installed electric power capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030; net zero by 2070. Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment) was launched in 2022.

t: Overview: International Environmental Law and UN Conferences
p: International Environmental Law and UN Conferences · Environment and Human Rights
x: International environmental law (IEL) is the body of treaties, customary rules, general principles and soft-law instruments that regulate how States use and protect the shared environment. It grew out of transboundary harm disputes (a river, a smelter, a fishery) and expanded into global concerns (ozone, climate, biodiversity) after the first great UN conference at Stockholm in 1972. For the exam, this topic is chronological: learn the conferences in order, the key documents each produced, and the principle each one is known for.

p: Constitutional and Legal Framework for Environment Protection in India · Environment and Human Rights
x: Background. Enacted after the Bhopal Gas Tragedy (the night of 2–3 December 1984, leak of methyl isocyanate from the Union Carbide plant). It is an umbrella Act passed under Article 253 to implement the decisions of the Stockholm Conference. It extends to the whole of India, came into force on 19 November 1986 , has 26 sections in four chapters , and fills gaps left by the Water and Air Acts. Chapter Sections Content I Preliminary 1–2 Short title, definitions II General powers of the Central Government 3–6 s.3 power to take all measures for protecting and improving the environment, including setting up authorities (s.3(3)); s.4 appointment of officers; s.5 power to issue directions including closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry and stoppage or regulation of electricity or water supply; s.6 rules to regulate environmental pollution III Prevention, control and abatement 7–17 s.7 no person to emit or discharge pollutants beyond standards; s.8 handling of hazardous substances only with procedural safeguards; s.9 duty to give information about accidents or discharges; s.10 entry and inspection; s.11 sampling; s.12 environmental laboratories; s.13 government analysts; s.15 penalty; s.16 offences by companies; s.17 offences by Government departments IV Miscellaneous 18–26 s.19 cognizance of offences (on complaint by the Government or authorised officer, or by any person after giving 60 days’ notice); s.22 bar on civil court jurisdiction; s.24 the EPA prevails over inconsistent provisions; s.25 rule-making power Penalty regime. Before the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act 2023, s.15 provided imprisonment up to five years, or fine up to Rs 1 lakh, or both, with additional fine for continuing offences and up to seven years of imprisonment if the contravention continued beyond one year after conviction. After the Jan Vishwas Act (in force from 1 April 2024), contravention attracts a monetary penalty of Rs 10,000 to Rs 15 lakh decided by an adjudicating officer (not below the rank of Joint Secretary to the Government of India) rather than criminal prosecution, with appeal to the NGT; an Environment Protection Fund collects penalties. Some commentaries add that imprisonment (up to three years) can follow non-payment. Verify the exact text of the amended sections in the bare Act. Rules for utilisation of the Environment (Protection) Fund were notified in January 2026. Delegated legislation under the EPA (frequently listed in match-type questions): Environment (Protection) Rules 1986; Manufacture, Storage and Import of Hazardous Chemicals Rules 1989; Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules 2016; Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules 2016; Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 (replaced or revised by newer rules in 2026, check); Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 (single-use plastic ban from 1 July 2022); E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022; Battery Waste Management Rules 2022; Construction and Demolition Waste Management Rules 2016; Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000; Ozone Depleting Substances (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000; Coastal Regulation Zone Notification 2019; Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules 2017; EIA Notification 2006.

t: 3.3 The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974
p: Constitutional and Legal Framework for Environment Protection in India · Environment and Human Rights
x: First environmental statute after Stockholm. Enacted under Article 252 after resolutions from the State legislatures; later extended to all States. Machinery: Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB, constituted in September 1974) and State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs). Powers and functions: CPCB (s.16), State Boards (s.17). The Boards advise on standards, plan programmes, inspect, collect samples (s.21) and test. Consent mechanism: s.25 (no new industry, outlet or discharge without prior consent of the State Board); s.24 (prohibition on using a stream or well for disposing of poisonous, noxious or polluting matter); s.32 (emergency measures); s.33A (power to give directions, added in 1988); s.49 (cognizance of offences; a complaint can follow 60 days’ notice by a citizen). Amendments: 1988 (stronger penalties and citizen complaint); the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Amendment Act 2024 removed imprisonment for many offences in favour of penalties decided by an adjudicating officer, gave the Central Government a say in prescribing how the Chair of a State Board is nominated, and allowed exemption of certain industrial categories from consent. Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act 1977: levy and collection of a cess on water consumed by industries and local authorities to augment Board resources.

t: 3.4 The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1981
p: Constitutional and Legal Framework for Environment Protection in India · Environment and Human Rights
x: Enacted under Article 253 to implement the Stockholm decisions on preserving air quality. Extends to the whole of India. Machinery: CPCB and SPCBs administer it. State Governments, in consultation with the State Board, may declare air pollution control areas (s.19). Consent for establishing or operating an industrial plant in such an area is needed (s.21). Emission standards: s.17 and s.22. Power to approach a court to restrain emissions: s.22A. Directions: s.31A (1987 amendment). Noise was included in the definition of air pollutant by the 1987 amendment. Penalties: s.37 (failure to comply with consent provisions: imprisonment from one and a half years to six years and fine, with extended terms for continuing offences) as strengthened in 1987; moved to a penalty-based approach, along with the EPA and the Public Liability Insurance Act, by the Jan Vishwas Act 2023 (check the amended text). Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Act 2021: created CAQM, a statutory body that replaced the EPCA (Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority, set up in 1998 on the Supreme Court’s direction in M.C. Mehta litigation).

t: Overview: Constitutional and Legal Framework for Environment Protection in India
p: Constitutional and Legal Framework for Environment Protection in India · Environment and Human Rights
x: India’s environmental protection rests on three layers. The first is constitutional: Articles 21, 48A and 51A(g), supported by the writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and High Courts. The second is statutory: a body of central Acts and rules that begins with the Water Act 1974 and reaches its umbrella form in the Environment (Protection) Act 1986. The third is judicial: the courts, through public interest litigation, have made environmental law more than the statute book by reading ecological rights into Article 21 and developing doctrines such as absolute liability, the precautionary principle and the public trust. Until the 1970s the Constitution did not mention the environment at all; the Stockholm Conference and the 42nd Amendment (1976) changed that.

p: Environmental Impact Assessment and Control of Hazardous Waste in India · Environment and Human Rights
x: Definition. A systematic process to identify, predict, evaluate and mitigate the biophysical, social and other relevant effects of proposed projects before major decisions are taken and commitments made. Origin. The U.S. National Environmental Policy Act 1969 was the first law to require EIA. Rio Declaration Principle 17 asks States to undertake EIA for proposed activities likely to have a significant adverse impact. The ICJ in Pulp Mills (2010) treated EIA as a requirement of general international law for activities with significant transboundary effects. India. Environmental appraisal began in 1976–77 with river valley projects. The EIA Notification of 27 January 1994 under s.3 EPA and Rule 5(3)(d) of the Environment (Protection) Rules 1986 made prior environmental clearance (EC) mandatory for listed projects. It was replaced by the EIA Notification 2006 (S.O. 1533(E), 14 September 2006) , which is the operative regime, as amended many times. A draft EIA Notification 2020 was widely criticised and has not replaced the 2006 Notification. Objectives: prevention, informed decision-making, public participation, sustainable development, and a record of project commitments (conditions).

p: Environmental Impact Assessment and Control of Hazardous Waste in India · Environment and Human Rights
x: Projects. The Schedule lists projects (39 items in eight broad groups, for example mining, power, primary processing, manufacturing, services, physical infrastructure, building and construction) that need prior EC. Each item has thresholds by size or capacity. Categories. Category Appraised by EC granted by A (large impacts) Expert Appraisal Committee (EAC) at the Centre MoEFCC (Central Government) B (smaller) State Expert Appraisal Committee (SEAC) State Environment Impact Assessment Authority (SEIAA) B1 (within B) Needs a full EIA report and public consultation B2 (within B) No EIA report or public hearing required Category B projects are classified as B1 or B2 at the screening stage, and a project located in a critically polluted area or an ecologically sensitive zone may be treated differently under the general conditions of the Notification. The four stages of the EC process. Screening (only for Category B projects): decides whether an EIA is needed (B1) or not (B2). Scoping: the EAC/SEAC determines comprehensive Terms of Reference (ToR) for the EIA study, on the basis of Form 1 and a pre-feasibility report. Public consultation: a public hearing near the site (organised by the State Pollution Control Board) and written responses from people likely to be affected. Certain categories are exempt, such as the modernisation of irrigation projects and expansion of highways under specified limits, and projects in industrial estates (see the Notification). Appraisal and decision: the EAC/SEAC examines the EIA report and public consultation record and recommends grant or rejection; the regulatory authority decides, normally by accepting the recommendation. The prescribed timeline is about 105 days in total (60 days for appraisal, 45 days for the decision). After clearance: the project proponent must submit compliance reports on conditions (half-yearly), and the authority can monitor and revoke. EC validity differs by project type, with longer periods for mining and river valley projects, and has been extended in later amendments; check the current text. Contents of an EIA report: project description, baseline environmental data, prediction and evaluation of impacts, analysis of alternatives, Environmental Management Plan (EMP), environmental monitoring plan, risk assessment, disaster management plan, cost-benefit analysis, and summary.

p: Environmental Impact Assessment and Control of Hazardous Waste in India · Environment and Human Rights
x: Strategic Environmental Assessment (policies, plans and programmes) versus project EIA; Cumulative impact assessment ; Social Impact Assessment under the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013; Environmental audit ; Carrying capacity studies . Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification 2019 (under the EPA) regulates activity along coastlines (CRZ-I to IV) and requires clearance for permitted projects. Eco-Sensitive Zones around protected areas are notified under the EPA; critically polluted areas and the Comprehensive Environmental Pollution Index are used to restrict new industries. Forest clearance (under the Van Adhiniyam 1980) and wildlife clearance run alongside EC; the EC is an additional, not a substitute, requirement.

p: Environmental Impact Assessment and Control of Hazardous Waste in India · Environment and Human Rights
x: Lafarge Umiam Mining v. Union of India (2011): environmental clearances must be given on the basis of sustainable development, precaution and intergenerational equity; courts accept a role for expert bodies and for independent regulators. Utkarsh Mandal v. Union of India (2009, Delhi High Court) on the public-notice requirement for amendments to the Notification. Hanuman Laxman Aroskar v. Union of India (2019): EIA is not a formality; the Court held that the committee must examine cumulative impact and quashed a clearance for the Mopa airport (Goa) for want of proper appraisal and sent it back. Common Cause v. Union of India (2017) and Alembic Pharmaceuticals v. Rohit Prajapati (2020): ex post facto (retrospective) clearance is incompatible with the precautionary principle, save in exceptional cases. Vanashakti v. Union of India (May 2025) struck down the 2017 notification and 2021 office memorandum on ex post facto clearances; a three-judge bench recalled the judgment on 18 November 2025 by a 2:1 majority (Justice Bhuyan dissenting) and asked that the matter be heard afresh. The position remains under consideration. Recent changes: a January 2025 notification exempted industrial sheds, educational institutions and hostels from EC up to a built-up area of 1,50,000 square metres (examined by the Supreme Court in 2025); late 2025 proposals sought to exempt common effluent treatment plants and common municipal solid-waste facilities; the Jan Vishwas reforms changed penalties for non-compliance. Treat all of these as developing law.

p: Environmental Impact Assessment and Control of Hazardous Waste in India · Environment and Human Rights
x: Hazardous waste (Rule 3 of the 2016 Rules): any waste which, by reason of its physical, chemical, reactive, toxic, flammable, explosive or corrosive characteristics, causes danger or is likely to cause danger to health or environment, whether alone or in contact with other wastes or substances. It includes wastes from processes listed in Schedule I , wastes containing constituents in Schedule II above prescribed concentration limits, and wastes in Schedule III (Parts A and B, relating to Basel Convention lists). Schedule IV lists “other wastes” such as waste tyres, paper waste, metal scrap and used electronic items. Legal chain: Hazardous Wastes (Management and Handling) Rules 1989 → 2003 amendment → Hazardous Wastes (Management, Handling and Transboundary Movement) Rules 2008 → Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016 (HOWM Rules, in force 4 April 2016, replaced the 2008 Rules). Key features of the 2016 Rules: emphasis on waste minimisation, reuse, recycling and recovery before disposal; the occupier (generator) is responsible for safe storage, packaging, labelling and disposal; authorisation from the SPCB is required for generating, handling and disposing of waste; the manifest system tracks waste from generation to disposal; storage limited to a period not exceeding 90 days (reflected in the 2024 amendment); import of hazardous waste for disposal is prohibited ; import for recycling or reuse requires permission from the Ministry; Prior Informed Consent applies to transboundary movement, in line with the Basel Convention; the CPCB and SPCBs maintain inventories and develop guidelines; treatment, storage and disposal facilities (TSDFs) must meet standards; Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) applies to waste tyres and used oil. Recent amendments: the 2024 Amendment Rules revised EPR deadlines for waste tyres and used oil, set price limits for EPR certificates and permitted import of certain pre-consumer polyethylene waste subject to conditions; the 2025 Amendment Rules (in force 1 April 2026) added a new Chapter VIII on EPR for scrap of non-ferrous metals (aluminium, copper, zinc and alloys), with recycling targets rising from 10% in 2026–27 towards 75% by 2032–33, EPR certificates, a CPCB portal and environmental compensation for non-compliance.

t: Overview: Environmental Impact Assessment and Control of Hazardous Waste in India
p: Environmental Impact Assessment and Control of Hazardous Waste in India · Environment and Human Rights
x: Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) is the preventive tool of environmental law: it asks, before a project starts, what it will do to air, water, land, ecology and people, and whether the harm can be avoided or reduced. Hazardous waste control is the corrective and regulatory side: it governs how dangerous wastes are generated, stored, moved, treated and disposed of, from “cradle to grave”. Both are made under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986, so they are delegated legislation (a notification and a set of rules), not Acts of Parliament.

t: Memory Capsule: Environmental Impact Assessment and Control of Hazardous Waste in India
p: Environmental Impact Assessment and Control of Hazardous Waste in India · Environment and Human Rights
x: EIA Notification 1994 → 2006 ; Category A = Centre (EAC, MoEFCC), Category B = State (SEAC, SEIAA). Four steps: Screening, Scoping, Public consultation, Appraisal. Hazardous waste rules: 1989 → 2008 → 2016 ; 90-day storage limit; no import of hazardous waste for disposal.

p: National Green Tribunal (NGT) · Environment and Human Rights
x: Environmental litigation was clogging the High Courts and the Supreme Court, which were deciding technical questions without scientific expertise. In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1986), Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India (1996) and A.P. Pollution Control Board v. M.V. Nayudu (1999) the Supreme Court recommended specialised environmental courts with judicial and technical members. The Law Commission of India (186th Report, 2003) made the same proposal. Earlier statutes had failed: the National Environment Tribunal Act 1995 (strict liability tribunal) was never brought into operation, and the National Environment Appellate Authority Act 1997 set up the NEAA, which handled appeals against environmental clearances. The NGT Act 2010 repealed both. Constitutional anchor: Article 21 (right to a healthy environment), supported by Articles 48A and 51A(g). The Act says in its preamble that it is for effective and expeditious disposal of environmental cases and for giving effect to the Stockholm Declaration 1972 and the Rio Declaration 1992 (to which India is committed).

p: National Green Tribunal (NGT) · Environment and Human Rights
x: Establishment (s.3): by notification of the Central Government. Principal Bench at New Delhi ; regional (zonal) benches at Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata and Chennai ; circuit benches sit at other places (for example Shimla, Shillong, Jodhpur and Kochi). Composition (s.4): a full-time Chairperson plus full-time Judicial Members and Expert Members , numbering not less than ten and not more than twenty of each kind, as notified (the combined figure of 10 to 20 members is how the section is commonly summarised; check the bare Act for the wording and later changes). A bench comprises at least one judicial member and one expert member. Qualifications: the Chairperson is a sitting or retired Judge of the Supreme Court or Chief Justice of a High Court. A Judicial Member is a sitting or former Judge of a High Court. An Expert Member has a qualifying degree (science, engineering or technology or equivalent) and substantial experience (about fifteen years, with a part in environmental or forest matters), or administrative experience in the field. Appointment: by the Central Government on the recommendation of a Selection Committee. Term: originally five years, not eligible for reappointment; later tribunal-reform legislation standardised service conditions and age limits (70 for the Chairperson and 67 for members); check the current provision. Specialised members: the principle behind the NGT is that expert members sit with judicial members so that science and law are brought together.

p: National Green Tribunal (NGT) · Environment and Human Rights
x: Section Content s.14 Original jurisdiction: all civil cases where a substantial question relating to environment (including enforcement of any legal right relating to the environment) is involved, and the question arises out of the implementation of the enactments specified in Schedule I . Limitation: six months from the date on which the cause of action first arose, extendable by up to 60 days if sufficient cause is shown s.15 Relief, compensation and restitution: (a) relief and compensation to victims of pollution and other environmental damage, including accidents with hazardous substances; (b) restitution of property damaged; (c) restitution of the environment for the affected area. Limitation: five years from the date of the cause of action s.16 Appellate jurisdiction: appeals against orders under the Water Act (ss.28, 29, 30), the Water Cess Act, the Air Act (s.13), directions under the EPA (s.5) and orders granting or refusing environmental clearance (EIA Notification), and orders under the Biological Diversity Act. Limitation: 30 days from the date of communication of the order, extendable by up to 60 days The seven Acts in Schedule I Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974 Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act 1977 Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 (now the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam 1980) Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1981 Environment (Protection) Act 1986 Public Liability Insurance Act 1991 Biological Diversity Act 2002 Not in Schedule I: the Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972, the Indian Forest Act 1927, and State laws on the preservation of trees. This omission is often tested, and the Supreme Court has said that where a case needs to be heard on such laws, the High Court or the Supreme Court may entertain it (and the NGT can still deal with the questions that arise under a Schedule I Act). The NGT may also not entertain questions that have no “substantial question relating to environment”. “Substantial question relating to environment” (explained in s.2(m)) is involved where (a) there is a direct violation of a specific statutory environmental obligation by which the community at large (other than an individual or group of individuals) is affected or likely to be affected, or the gravity of damage to environment or property is substantial, or the damage to public health is broadly measurable; and (b) the environmental consequences relate to a specific activity or a point source of pollution.

p: National Green Tribunal (NGT) · Environment and Human Rights
x: s.17 Liability: the Tribunal awards relief and compensation where death, injury or damage to property results from an accident or adverse impact of an activity under the Schedule I enactments; it applies the principle of no fault . The scale of compensation follows the framework of the Public Liability Insurance Act. s.18 Procedure: applications for relief may be made by the person injured, the owner of the damaged property, their legal representatives, any person aggrieved including a representative body or organisation, the Central or State Government or a local authority. The Tribunal must endeavour to dispose of an application or appeal within six months of filing (s.18(3)). The Supreme Court has held that the NGT can act suo motu ( Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha , 2021). s.19 Powers: the Tribunal is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 or the Indian Evidence Act 1872 but is guided by principles of natural justice . It has the powers of a civil court for discovery, summoning, receiving evidence on affidavit, issuing commissions, reviewing its own decisions, and dismissing or setting aside ex parte decisions. It regulates its own procedure. s.20 Principles to apply: the Tribunal must apply the principles of sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle . s.21 Execution: an order is executable as a decree of a civil court. s.22 Appeal: to the Supreme Court within 90 days from the date of communication of the award, decision or order of the Tribunal. s.26 Penalty for non-compliance: imprisonment up to three years or fine up to Rs 10 crore, or both; for a company, fine up to Rs 25 crore; a continuing contravention attracts an additional fine of up to Rs 25,000 per day. s.29 Bar of civil courts: no civil court can entertain matters that the Tribunal can decide. Rules: National Green Tribunal (Practice and Procedure) Rules 2011.

p: National Green Tribunal (NGT) · Environment and Human Rights
x: Not bound by the Evidence Act and CPC (s.19), so it can take up cases quickly and use experts. Expert and judicial members together ; the experts are not mere advisers but members of the bench. Quick disposal target of six months (s.18(3)). Polluter pays and no-fault liability embedded in the Act (ss.17 and 20). Relief to victims and restitution of the environment (s.15), so the NGT is a remedial forum as well as an enforcement forum. Environmental compensation: the NGT has awarded compensation on the basis of the polluter pays principle in many cases, for example the 2016 order imposing Rs 5 crore on the Art of Living Foundation for damage to the Yamuna floodplain. Supreme Court decisions on the NGT: the NGT Act was upheld; the Court said that environmental matters should be heard by the NGT in the first instance ( Bhopal Gas Peedith Mahila Udyog Sangathan v. Union of India , 2012); the Court set aside the NGT’s order permitting reopening of the Sterlite copper smelter (Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board v. Sterlite, 2019); Ankita Sinha confirmed suo motu power.

p: National Green Tribunal (NGT) · Environment and Human Rights
x: The National Green Tribunal is a specialised statutory forum for the speedy and effective disposal of cases relating to environmental protection, conservation of forests and other natural resources, enforcement of legal rights relating to the environment, and relief and compensation for damage to persons and property. It was created by the National Green Tribunal Act 2010 (Act 19 of 2010) and began functioning on 18 October 2010 . India became the third country in the world, after Australia and New Zealand, to set up a specialised environmental tribunal, and the first developing country to do so. Because the statute is short and has numbered sections, this is the most examinable topic in the environmental half of the unit.

p: National Green Tribunal (NGT) · Environment and Human Rights
x: 2010, Act 19; 18 October 2010; Delhi + Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai. 6 months (original claim, and the disposal target); 5 years (compensation); 30 days (appeal to NGT) plus 60; 90 days (appeal to the Supreme Court). s.14, s.15, s.16, s.17, s.18, s.19, s.20, s.22 form a five-minute checklist: jurisdiction, relief, appeals, liability, procedure, powers, principles, Supreme Court. The NGT applies three principles : sustainable development, precaution, polluter pays.

p: Concept and Development of Human Rights · Environment and Human Rights
x: Statutory definition (Protection of Human Rights Act 1993, s.2(1)(d)): “human rights” means the rights relating to life, liberty, equality and dignity of the individual guaranteed by the Constitution or embodied in the International Covenants and enforceable by courts in India . Under s.2(1)(f), “International Covenants” means the ICCPR and the ICESCR , adopted by the UN General Assembly on 16 December 1966. Note that the Indian definition does not list the UDHR. Characteristics: inherent (not granted by the State), inalienable, universal, equal and non-discriminatory, indivisible, interdependent and interrelated (Vienna Declaration 1993), and (for many rights) enforceable against the State. Human rights versus fundamental rights: human rights are moral and international in origin and universal; fundamental rights are those the Constitution (Part III) guarantees and courts enforce under Articles 32 and 226. Some fundamental rights are available only to citizens (Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, 30), while human rights belong to everyone. Derogable and non-derogable rights: ICCPR Article 4(2) lists rights that cannot be suspended even in a public emergency: right to life (Art. 6), freedom from torture (Art. 7), freedom from slavery (Art. 8(1) and (2)), freedom from imprisonment for inability to fulfil a contractual obligation (Art. 11), no retrospective penalties (Art. 15), recognition as a person before the law (Art. 16), and freedom of thought, conscience and religion (Art. 18). Jus cogens and erga omnes: prohibition of genocide, slavery, torture and racial discrimination are peremptory norms; obligations erga omnes are owed to the international community as a whole ( Barcelona Traction case, ICJ 1970).

p: Concept and Development of Human Rights · Environment and Human Rights
x: Theory Idea Associated thinkers Natural rights (natural law) Rights flow from human nature or divine/natural law, before and above the State Aquinas, Grotius, John Locke (life, liberty and property), Rousseau, Thomas Paine ( Rights of Man ) Legal positivist Rights exist only if recognised by law; there are no pre-legal rights Jeremy Bentham (“natural rights are simple nonsense, natural and imprescriptible rights, rhetorical nonsense, nonsense upon stilts”), John Austin Utilitarian Rights are justified by general welfare Bentham, J.S. t: 6.5 The UN Charter and human rights
p: Concept and Development of Human Rights · Environment and Human Rights
x: Preamble: faith in fundamental human rights, in the dignity and worth of the human person, in the equal rights of men and women. Article 1(3): one purpose of the UN is promoting and encouraging respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms for all without distinction as to race, sex, language or religion. Article 13(1)(b): General Assembly shall make recommendations for assisting in the realisation of human rights. Articles 55 and 56: UN shall promote universal respect for human rights; all members pledge themselves to take joint and separate action in cooperation with the UN. Article 62(2) and 68: ECOSOC may make recommendations on human rights and shall set up commissions for the promotion of human rights. Article 2(7) (domestic jurisdiction) is the usual counterargument to international scrutiny.

p: Concept and Development of Human Rights · Environment and Human Rights
x: UN Human Rights Council (UNHRC): created in 2006 by General Assembly Resolution 60/251 to replace the Commission on Human Rights; seats in Geneva; 47 members elected by the General Assembly for three-year terms on the basis of regional distribution; periodic review of all UN member States through the Universal Periodic Review (UPR); special procedures (special rapporteurs and working groups); complaint procedure. India was elected for the 2026–28 term, its seventh term on the Council. Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR): post created in 1993 (after the Vienna conference); seat in Geneva. Treaty bodies: Human Rights Committee (ICCPR; 18 members), Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, CERD, CEDAW, Committee against Torture, Committee on the Rights of the Child, Committee on Migrant Workers, Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, Committee on Enforced Disappearances. Others: General Assembly (Third Committee), ECOSOC, Security Council (human rights as a threat to peace), ICJ, International Criminal Court, UNHCR, UNICEF, ILO, UN Women. Regional systems: Europe (European Court of Human Rights, Strasbourg); the Americas (Inter-American Commission in Washington and Court at San Jose, Costa Rica); Africa (African Commission, Banjul, and the African Court); the Arab Charter (2004). Asia has no region-wide court.

p: Concept and Development of Human Rights · Environment and Human Rights
x: Pre-constitutional: the Constitution of India Bill 1895; Nehru Report 1928; the Karachi Resolution 1931 on fundamental rights and economic programme. Constitution: Part III (Articles 12–35) and Part IV (Articles 36–51); the Preamble secures justice, liberty, equality and fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual. India voted for the UDHR in 1948 (Hansa Mehta and Lakshmi Menon took part in the debates). International treaties: India ratified CERD (1968), the ICCPR and ICESCR (10 April 1979), CEDAW (1993), CRC (1992) and CRPD (2007). It has signed but not ratified the Convention against Torture (signed 1997); it is not a party to the Optional Protocols to the ICCPR and has not ratified the Refugee Convention. Domestic implementation: Article 51(c); Article 253; the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 (see section 10). In Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) the Court used CEDAW to fill a legislative gap; in Jolly George Varghese (1980) the Court read the ICCPR in aid of the Constitution; in Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993), compensation was awarded as a public-law remedy for custodial death. Judicial landmarks: A.K. Gopalan (1950) to Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), which read due process into Article 21 and made the doctrine of the right to life expansive; Hussainara Khatoon (1979, speedy trial), Sunil Batra (1978/80, prisoners), Francis Coralie Mullin (1981, dignity), D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997, arrest guidelines), Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017, privacy as a fundamental right), Navtej Singh Johar (2018).

t: Overview: Concept and Development of Human Rights
p: Concept and Development of Human Rights · Environment and Human Rights
x: Human rights are the basic rights and freedoms to which every person is entitled simply by being human, regardless of nationality, sex, race, religion, language or status. The idea moved from religious and philosophical thought (natural law), through the great constitutional documents of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, to its modern international form in the UN Charter (1945) and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948). For the exam, you need three things: the definitions (particularly the statutory definition in India), the theories and generations of rights, and the historical timeline with its dates.

p: Universalism and Cultural Relativism · Environment and Human Rights
x: Core claim: human rights belong to every human being simply as a human being, everywhere and at all times, because of shared human dignity. They are not created by States or cultures, so no culture or government can legitimately deny them. Foundations: natural law and natural rights (Locke, Kant on dignity), the idea of a common humanity, the moral minimum necessary for a decent life. Textual support: the UDHR (1948) claims to be “a common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations”; the Vienna Declaration and Programme of Action 1993 (Part I, paragraph 1) says the universal nature of human rights is beyond question, and paragraph 5 says all human rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent and interrelated , that national and regional particularities and different historical, cultural and religious backgrounds must be borne in mind, but that it is the duty of States, whatever their political, economic and cultural systems, to promote and protect all human rights and fundamental freedoms. Evidence of universality: near-universal ratification of the Convention on the Rights of the Child; wide acceptance of the ICCPR and ICESCR; the status of some norms as customary law or jus cogens (prohibition of genocide, torture, slavery); the Universal Periodic Review of every State. Arguments for universalism: (a) cultures are not monolithic and have internal dissenters (women, minorities, dissidents) whose rights relativism would silence; (b) relativism is often invoked by ruling elites rather than by the people; (c) practices such as female genital mutilation, honour killings, child marriage and slavery cannot be justified by tradition; (d) every major culture contains ideas of dignity and justice, so rights are not purely “Western”; (e) a rejection of universality leads to moral relativism with no basis to condemn atrocities.

p: Universalism and Cultural Relativism · Environment and Human Rights
x: Core claim: moral values and rights are products of particular cultures, so there is no culture-independent standard by which one culture may judge another; the universal claim of rights is a form of cultural imperialism or ethnocentrism. Origins: the American Anthropological Association submitted a statement to the UN Commission on Human Rights in 1947 (drafted by Melville Herskovits) warning that a declaration reflecting only one culture’s values would not command respect; the same logic underlies the abstentions at the UDHR vote (Soviet bloc States, South Africa, Saudi Arabia). Types: radical (strong) relativism holds culture is the sole source of validity of a moral right or rule. Moderate (weak) relativism accepts a core of universal rights but allows cultural variation in interpretation and implementation. Arguments for relativism: (a) the UDHR was drafted mostly by Western States and reflects individualism; many societies stress community, family and duties; (b) colonial history and selective use of human rights to pursue political interests (“double standards”); (c) priority of economic development and collective rights in the developing world (Declaration on the Right to Development 1986); (d) respect for the right of peoples to cultural self-determination. Instruments associated with relativist positions: Bangkok Declaration 1993 (Asian States, before Vienna): human rights are universal, but must be considered in the context of a dynamic and evolving process of norm-setting, bearing in mind national and regional particularities and different historical, cultural and religious backgrounds; stresses the right to development and non-interference. Cairo Declaration on Human Rights in Islam 1990 (Organisation of the Islamic Conference): rights are subject to the Islamic Shari’ah (Articles 24 and 25). African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights 1981 (Banjul Charter): recognises peoples’ rights and imposes duties on individuals towards family, society and the State. Arab Charter on Human Rights 2004; ASEAN Human Rights Declaration 2012. “Asian values” (Lee Kuan Yew of Singapore, Mahathir Mohamad of Malaysia): emphasis on community, order, family, and economic development ahead of civil and political liberties. Reservations to human rights treaties (for example to Articles 2 and 16 of CEDAW) based on religious or cultural law; reservations incompatible with the object and purpose of the treaty are invalid under Article 19 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties and General Comment 24 of the Human Rights Committee (1994).

p: Universalism and Cultural Relativism · Environment and Human Rights
x: Ethnocentrism (judging other cultures by one’s own), cultural imperialism , moral relativism , cultural pluralism , cultural rights (Article 27 UDHR; Article 15 ICESCR; UNESCO Universal Declaration on Cultural Diversity 2001; UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples 2007). Indivisibility (Western States prioritised civil-political rights, socialist and developing States prioritised socio-economic rights; the two Covenants in 1966 were the compromise). Cultural defence in criminal law (courts accept cultural background as relevant to mitigation, not as a justification).

p: Universalism and Cultural Relativism · Environment and Human Rights
x: India’s official position favours universality along with indivisibility and the right to development, plus respect for cultural diversity; at Vienna (1993) India argued against using human rights conditionally to pressure developing States. Constitutional approach: the Constitution is itself a universalist rights document adapted to a plural society. It protects religious freedom (Articles 25–28) and minority cultural rights (Articles 29–30) but subordinates religious and cultural practices to public order, morality, health and the other fundamental rights. Courts and culture: Commissioner of Hindu Religious Endowments v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt (1954) and the later “essential religious practices” test. Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985): maintenance for a divorced Muslim woman under s.125 CrPC; the legislative response (Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act 1986) shows the cultural-rights tension. Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017): instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) held unconstitutional. Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (2018, Sabarimala): restriction on women of menstruating age held unconstitutional by majority; the dissent argued for judicial restraint in matters of faith. A larger bench reference on the scope of religious freedom was pending after the 2019 review reference. Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018): constitutional morality prevails over social morality. Independent Thought v. Union of India (2017): sexual intercourse with a wife below 18 is rape (children’s rights over cultural acceptance of child marriage). Statutory interventions against customary practices: abolition of untouchability (Article 17 and the Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955), Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act 1987, Child Marriage Restraint Act 1929 replaced by the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006, the Dowry Prohibition Act 1961.

p: Universalism and Cultural Relativism · Environment and Human Rights
x: The central philosophical dispute in international human rights is whether human rights are the same everywhere (universalism) or whether their meaning and validity depend on the culture in which they operate (cultural relativism). The debate is not purely academic. It determines whether a State can defend a practice (a punishment, a dress code, a family law rule, a restriction on speech) as “our culture” against international criticism, and it explains reservations to human rights treaties, regional charters, and the Asian values and Islamic human rights declarations. For the exam, know the definitions, the main arguments on each side, the instruments (Vienna Declaration 1993, Bangkok Declaration 1993, Cairo Declaration 1990), the thinkers, and the compromise positions.

p: International Bill of Rights · Environment and Human Rights
x: Adoption and drafting Adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948 (Resolution 217 A (III)) at the Palais de Chaillot, Paris, by 48 votes in favour, none against and 8 abstentions (the Soviet Union, Byelorussian SSR, Ukrainian SSR, Czechoslovakia, Poland, Yugoslavia, Saudi Arabia and South Africa). Two members were absent (Honduras and Yemen). 10 December is celebrated as Human Rights Day . Drafted by the Commission on Human Rights (chair: Eleanor Roosevelt ). The eight-member drafting committee included Roosevelt, René Cassin (France), Charles Malik (Lebanon), P.C. Chang (China) and John Humphrey (Canada, Director of the UN Division of Human Rights, whose first draft was the working text), Hernán Santa Cruz (Chile), Alexandre Bogomolov (USSR) and Charles Dukes (UK). India’s Hansa Mehta is credited with changing “all men are born free and equal” to “all human beings are born free and equal”. Structure: a Preamble and 30 Articles . Legal status: a declaration, not a treaty, so not binding in itself. It has acquired strong legal significance: the 1968 Proclamation of Teheran stated that it states a common understanding of the peoples of the world and constitutes an obligation for the members of the international community; many of its provisions are regarded as customary international law; it has been incorporated into national constitutions and cited by courts (including the Indian Supreme Court). Content by group of Articles Articles Group Key rights 1–2 Foundations Born free and equal in dignity and rights (Art. 1); non-discrimination (Art. 2) 3–11 Individual civil rights Life, liberty and security (3); no slavery (4); no torture (5); recognition before the law (6); equality before the law (7); effective remedy (8); no arbitrary arrest (9); fair and public hearing (10); presumption of innocence and no retroactive penalty (11) 12–17 Relations to civil society Privacy (12); movement (13); asylum (14); nationality (15); marriage and family (16); property (17) 18–21 Spiritual, public and political rights Thought, conscience and religion (18); opinion and expression (19); peaceful assembly and association (20); participation in government and genuine periodic elections (21) 22–27 Economic, social and cultural rights Social security (22); work, equal pay, trade unions (23); rest and leisure (24); adequate standard of living, including food, clothing, housing and medical care (25); education (26); cultural life and protection of authors’ interests (27) 28–30 Duties and limits Entitlement to a social and international order in which rights can be realised (28); duties to the community and permissible limits only as determined by law to secure due recognition of others’ rights and the requirements of morality, public order and the general welfare in a democratic society (29); no interpretation to destroy rights (30) Points often asked: the right to property is in the UDHR (Art. 17) but not in either Covenant; the right to asylum is in Art. 14; the right to nationality is in Art. 15; Art. 25 is the basis of the right to an adequate standard of living; Art. 29(1) is the only reference to duties.

t: 8.2 International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, 1966
p: International Bill of Rights · Environment and Human Rights
x: Adopted on 16 December 1966 (GA Resolution 2200A (XXI)); in force 23 March 1976 (three months after the 35th ratification). It has a preamble and 53 Articles in six Parts . Article 1: right of all peoples to self-determination (common to ICCPR and ICESCR); permanent sovereignty over natural wealth and resources. Part II (Arts. 2–5): States undertake to respect and ensure the rights to all individuals within their territory and subject to their jurisdiction (Art. 2(1)); effective remedy (Art. 2(3)); equal rights of men and women (Art. 3); derogation in public emergency (Art. 4), with no derogation from Arts. 6, 7, 8 (paragraphs 1 and 2), 11, 15, 16 and 18. Part III (Arts. 6–27), the substantive rights: Article Right 6 Inherent right to life; death penalty only for the most serious crimes, not for those below 18 or pregnant women 7 Freedom from torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment; no medical or scientific experimentation without free consent 8 Freedom from slavery, servitude and forced labour 9 Liberty and security of person; arrest only on grounds established by law; right to compensation for unlawful arrest (9(5)) 10 Humane treatment of persons deprived of liberty 11 No imprisonment merely for inability to fulfil a contractual obligation 12–13 Liberty of movement; procedural safeguards on expulsion of aliens 14 Fair trial; presumption of innocence; compensation for miscarriage of justice (14(6)); protection from double jeopardy (14(7)) 15 No retrospective criminal penalties 16 Recognition as a person before the law 17 Privacy, family, home and correspondence 18 Freedom of thought, conscience and religion 19 Freedom of opinion and expression 20 Prohibition of propaganda for war and of advocacy of national, racial or religious hatred 21–22 Peaceful assembly; association including trade unions 23 Marriage and family 24 Rights of the child (protection, registration, name and nationality) 25 Participation in public affairs, voting, access to public service 26 Equality before the law and equal protection 27 Rights of ethnic, religious and linguistic minorities Human Rights Committee (Part IV, Arts. 28–45): 18 independent experts, elected for four-year terms, who serve in their personal capacity. Functions: examining periodic reports by States (Art. 40); issuing General Comments ; considering inter-State complaints (Art. 41, optional); and, under the First Optional Protocol, individual communications . First Optional Protocol (1966, in force 1976): individual communications against States Parties for alleged violations of ICCPR rights, after exhaustion of domestic remedies. India is not a party. Second Optional Protocol (1989, in force 1991): aims at the abolition of the death penalty ; the only permitted reservation relates to wartime crimes of a military nature. India: acceded to both the ICCPR and the ICESCR on 10 April 1979 , with declarations (for example that the right to self-determination in Art. 1 applies to peoples under foreign domination and not to sovereign States, and that Arts. 9, 13, 19, 21 and 22 are to be applied consistently with the Constitution; and that the right to compensation for unlawful arrest in Art. 9(5) is not enforceable in India as a legal right in the manner of the Covenant).

t: 8.3 International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, 1966
p: International Bill of Rights · Environment and Human Rights
x: Adopted on 16 December 1966 ; in force 3 January 1976 . It has a preamble and 31 Articles in five Parts . Article 1: self-determination. Article 2(1): each State undertakes to take steps, individually and through international assistance and cooperation, to the maximum of its available resources , with a view to achieving progressively the full realisation of the rights; Art. 2(2): non-discrimination; Art. 3: equal right of men and women; Art. 4: limitations only as determined by law and solely for promoting the general welfare in a democratic society. Article Right 6 Right to work 7 Just and favourable conditions of work, fair wages and equal pay 8 Trade unions, the right to strike 9 Social security 10 Protection of the family, mothers and children 11 Adequate standard of living including food, clothing and housing; freedom from hunger 12 Highest attainable standard of physical and mental health 13–14 Education (primary compulsory and free) 15 Cultural life; benefits of scientific progress; protection of authors’ moral and material interests Monitoring: the Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (18 experts) was established by ECOSOC in 1985 (it is not created by the Covenant itself). It reviews State reports and issues General Comments (for example General Comment 3 on the nature of State obligations, with the concept of a minimum core obligation ). Optional Protocol to ICESCR adopted 10 December 2008 , in force 5 May 2013 : individual communications, inter-State communications, and an inquiry procedure. Interpretation guides: Limburg Principles 1986 , Maastricht Guidelines 1997 , Maastricht Principles 2011 (extraterritorial obligations).

p: International Bill of Rights · Environment and Human Rights
x: The “International Bill of Rights” (more formally the International Bill of Human Rights) is the core of the UN human rights system. It consists of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) 1948 , the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) 1966 with its two Optional Protocols, and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR) 1966 (with its Optional Protocol of 2008). The UN Commission on Human Rights under Eleanor Roosevelt originally planned a single three-part “Bill” (declaration, covenant, measures of implementation). Cold War divisions over civil-political versus socio-economic rights led to two separate covenants. This is one of the highest-yield topics in the unit because every fact in it is a number, a date or an Article.
