punishable with imprisonment up to three years Equal Remuneration Act 1976 Now merged into the Code on Wages 2019 National Commission for Women Act 1990 See section 10 Landmark cases on women’s rights Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997): guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace; CEDAW read into Arts. 14, 15, 19 and 21. Apparel Export Promotion Council v. A.K. Chopra (1999): sexual harassment includes any unwelcome sexually determined behaviour; international conventions used to interpret fundamental rights. Mary Roy v. State of Kerala (1986): Syrian Christian women governed by the Indian Succession Act, not the Travancore Act. Githa Hariharan v. Reserve Bank of India (1999): mother can act as natural guardian of the minor in appropriate cases. Air India v. Nargesh Meerza (1981): rule terminating air hostesses on first pregnancy struck down. Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985); Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001); Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) on Muslim women and maintenance and talaq. Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018): adultery provision of the IPC (s.497) struck down as discriminatory and treating women as property. Laxmi v. Union of India (2014): regulation of sale of acid; compensation to victims. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020): daughters are coparceners by birth irrespective of whether the father was alive on 9 September 2005. Secretary, Ministry of Defence v. Babita Puniya (2020): permanent commission for women officers in the Army. Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014): guidelines against automatic arrest in cruelty and dowry cases. Bodhisattwa Gautam v. Subhra Chakraborty (1996): rape violates Art. 21 and is a crime against basic human rights; Delhi Domestic Working Women’s Forum v. Union of India (1995): compensation and legal assistance to rape victims.

p: Group Rights: Women, Children, Persons with Disabilities, Elderly, Minorities and Weaker Sections · Environment and Human Rights
x: International framework Geneva Declaration of the Rights of the Child 1924; UN Declaration of the Rights of the Child 1959 ; Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) : adopted 20 November 1989 , in force 2 September 1990 , 54 Articles, the most widely ratified human rights treaty. “Child” means every human being below 18 unless majority is attained earlier (Art. 1). Four guiding principles: non-discrimination (Art. 2), best interests of the child (Art. 3), right to life, survival and development (Art. 6), respect for the views of the child (Art. 12) . Monitoring: Committee on the Rights of the Child (18 experts). Optional Protocols (2000): on the involvement of children in armed conflict and on the sale of children, child prostitution and child pornography (India ratified both in 2005); third Protocol on a communications procedure (2011; not ratified by India). India ratified the CRC on 11 December 1992. Other instruments: ILO Convention 138 (minimum age) and 182 (worst forms of child labour), both ratified by India in 2017; Hague Convention on Intercountry Adoption 1993 (India party since 2003); UNICEF (1946). Constitutional provisions: Art. 15(3); Art. 21A (free and compulsory education for children 6 to 14 years, inserted by the 86th Amendment 2002); Art. 24 ; Art. 39(e) and (f) (health and strength of children, opportunities and facilities for healthy development); Art. 45 (early childhood care and education below six); Art. 51A(k) (duty of parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education for children six to fourteen). Statutes Law Key points Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 In force 1 April 2010; s.12(1)(c) requires private unaided schools to reserve 25% of entry-level seats for economically weaker and disadvantaged children; upheld in Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012); not applicable to minority institutions ( Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India , 2014) Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act 2015 Child in conflict with law (below 18); Juvenile Justice Board; Child Welfare Committee; children aged 16 to 18 accused of heinous offences may be tried as adults after preliminary assessment; adoption framework (CARA); the 2021 amendment gave District Magistrates a larger role Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act 2012 (POCSO) Child means below 18; gender-neutral; special courts; child-friendly procedures; mandatory reporting; aggravated offences, with the 2019 amendment increasing punishment up to death for aggravated penetrative sexual assault Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006 Replaced the Child Marriage Restraint Act 1929; minimum age 18 for girls and 21 for boys; child marriages are voidable at the option of the child party Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986 (amended 2016) Prohibits employment of children below 14 in all occupations (with limited exceptions for family enterprises and audio-visual entertainment outside school hours); adolescents (14–18) not to be employed in hazardous occupations Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act 2005 National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR, set up March 2007) and State Commissions Guardians and Wards Act 1890; Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act 1956; Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976; IT Act s.67B Guardianship, bonded labour and child sexual abuse material Landmark cases on children People’s Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (1982, Asiad workers): Art. 24 is enforceable and construction is a hazardous employment. M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu (1996): child labour in the Sivakasi match industry; directions for rehabilitation, with a welfare fund of Rs 20,000 per child employed in hazardous work. Laxmikant Pandey v. Union of India (1984): guidelines for inter-country adoption. Sheela Barse v. Union of India (1986): children in jails; speedy trial and separate facilities. Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992) and Unni Krishnan v. State of A.P. (1993): right to education as part of Art. 21, limited to children up to 14 (and later codified in Art. 21A). Bachpan Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2011): trafficking of children for circuses. Gaurav Jain v. Union of India (1997): children of sex workers; right to be rehabilitated. Independent Thought v. Union of India (2017): exception to rape for a wife aged 15 to 18 read down. Sampurna Behrua v. Union of India (2018): directions for the implementation of child protection laws.

p: Group Rights: Women, Children, Persons with Disabilities, Elderly, Minorities and Weaker Sections · Environment and Human Rights
x: International framework Declaration on the Rights of Disabled Persons 1975; International Year of Disabled Persons 1981; UN Decade of Disabled Persons 1983–92; World Programme of Action 1982; Standard Rules on the Equalization of Opportunities for Persons with Disabilities 1993. The Asia and Pacific decades (1993–2002; 2003–12) led to the Biwako Millennium Framework. Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD): adopted 13 December 2006, opened for signature 30 March 2007, in force 3 May 2008 ; 50 Articles; a human rights treaty with a social development dimension; adopts the social model (disability results from the interaction of impairment with barriers); general principles in Art. 3 (dignity, non-discrimination, full participation, respect for difference, accessibility, equality of opportunity, gender equality, evolving capacities of children). Monitored by the Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (18 experts); the Optional Protocol allows individual communications. India signed on 30 March 2007 and ratified on 1 October 2007 ; India has not ratified the Optional Protocol. International Day of Persons with Disabilities: 3 December . Constitutional provisions: Art. 41 (right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement); Art. 21; Arts. 14, 15 and 16; Seventh Schedule, State List Entry 9 (relief of the disabled and unemployable). Statutes Law Key points Rehabilitation Council of India Act 1992 Regulates rehabilitation professionals and training Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Act 1995 The first comprehensive law: seven categories of disability; 3% reservation in government jobs; repealed by the 2016 Act National Trust for Welfare of Persons with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, Mental Retardation and Multiple Disabilities Act 1999 Establishes the National Trust and legal guardianship mechanism Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 (RPwD Act) In force 19 April 2017; implements CRPD; 21 specified disabilities (including locomotor disability, leprosy cured persons, cerebral palsy, dwarfism, acid attack victims, blindness and low vision, deaf and hard of hearing, speech and language disability, intellectual disability, specific learning disabilities, autism spectrum disorder, mental illness, chronic neurological conditions, haemophilia, thalassaemia, sickle cell disease, multiple disabilities including deaf-blindness); “person with benchmark disability” means a person with not less than 40% of a specified disability; 4% reservation in government posts for benchmark disabilities (horizontal reservation, divided among categories of disabilities); 5% reservation in higher education institutions ; free education for benchmark disabled children from 6 to 18; Chief Commissioner and State Commissioners for Persons with Disabilities; special courts; penalties for discrimination and for atrocities (imprisonment of six months to five years with fine) Mental Healthcare Act 2017 Replaced the Mental Health Act 1987; right to access mental healthcare; advance directives; Mental Health Review Boards; presumption of severe stress in attempted suicide cases (s.115) Schemes Accessible India Campaign (Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan, 2015); Unique Disability ID; assistive-devices scheme Cases Union of India v. National Federation of the Blind (2013): reservation computed on the total number of vacancies in the identified posts. Jeeja Ghosh v. Union of India (2016): a person with a disability was removed from an aircraft; the Court stressed dignity, non-discrimination and accessibility. Rajive Raturi v. Union of India (2017): directions to ensure accessibility of public spaces and transport. Siddaraju v. State of Karnataka (2020): reservation for persons with disabilities in promotions. Vikash Kumar v. UPSC (2021): scribe for a candidate with writer’s cramp; reasonable accommodation as part of the right to equality.

p: Group Rights: Women, Children, Persons with Disabilities, Elderly, Minorities and Weaker Sections · Environment and Human Rights
x: International framework: Vienna International Plan of Action on Ageing 1982 (First World Assembly on Ageing); UN Principles for Older Persons 1991 (GA Resolution 46/91: independence, participation, care, self-fulfilment, dignity); International Year of Older Persons 1999; Madrid International Plan of Action on Ageing 2002 ; International Day of Older Persons on 1 October ; Open-ended Working Group on Ageing (2010); UN Decade of Healthy Ageing 2021–2030; the Inter-American Convention on Protecting the Human Rights of Older Persons 2015 is the first binding regional treaty on the subject. Constitutional provisions: Art. 41 (public assistance in old age); Art. 21; Art. 47; Seventh Schedule, Concurrent List Entry 24 (welfare of labour, social security and social insurance). Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007 (MWPSC Act) Senior citizen: a citizen of India aged 60 years or above . Parent includes a biological, adoptive or step-father or mother, whether or not a senior citizen. Duty of maintenance: children (and relatives who inherit the property of a childless senior citizen) must maintain parents and senior citizens so that they can lead a normal life. A senior citizen may apply to a Maintenance Tribunal (constituted at the sub-division level, usually headed by the Sub-Divisional Officer), with appeal to an Appellate Tribunal (District Magistrate). Tribunals are to decide within 90 days (extendable once by 30 days). Maintenance allowance: the 2007 Act capped the monthly allowance at Rs 10,000; the 2019 Amendment Bill (not enacted) proposed removing the cap and widening the definition of children; check the present position. Protection of property and life: s.23 renders a transfer of property by a senior citizen void if the transferee fails to provide basic amenities and physical needs (applied in Sudesh Chhikara v. Ramti Devi , 2022); s.22 requires State action to protect life and property; s.19 requires State Governments to establish old age homes (at least one in each district); s.24 punishes abandonment of a senior citizen (imprisonment up to three months, or fine up to Rs 5,000, or both). Related laws: s.125 CrPC (now the corresponding BNSS provision) and s.20 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act 1956 (maintenance of parents). S. Vanitha v. Deputy Commissioner, Bengaluru Urban District (2020): the Supreme Court harmonised the remedies under the 2007 Act and the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, and recognised a senior citizen’s right to seek eviction from a shared household in appropriate cases. Policies and schemes: National Policy on Older Persons 1999; Integrated Programme for Older Persons; National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly; Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (National Social Assistance Programme); Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana; Pradhan Mantri Vaya Vandana Yojana; Ayushman Vay Vandana (health cover for persons aged 70 and above).

p: Group Rights: Women, Children, Persons with Disabilities, Elderly, Minorities and Weaker Sections · Environment and Human Rights
x: Concept and definition The Indian Constitution uses the word “minorities” in Arts. 29 and 30 and in the headings of Arts. 350A and 350B but does not define it. The courts have said that minorities are determined State-wise (for linguistic minorities, Re Kerala Education Bill , 1958 and D.A.V. College v. State of Punjab , 1971; for religious minorities, T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka , 2002, by 11 judges). International definitions: Capotorti (1977): a group numerically inferior to the rest of the population, in a non-dominant position, whose members, being nationals of the State, have ethnic, religious or linguistic characteristics different from the rest and show a sense of solidarity directed towards preserving their culture, traditions, religion or language. Deschenes (1985) is a similar definition. International instruments: ICCPR Art. 27 (persons belonging to ethnic, religious or linguistic minorities shall not be denied the right, in community with others, to enjoy their culture, profess and practise their religion, or use their language); UN Declaration on the Rights of Persons Belonging to National or Ethnic, Religious and Linguistic Minorities, 1992 (GA Resolution 47/135, 18 December 1992); the Working Group on Minorities (1995–2007), then the Forum on Minority Issues (2007); the UN Special Rapporteur on minority issues (2005); the Council of Europe’s Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities (1995). India observes 18 December as Minorities Rights Day . Constitutional provisions Article Content 25–28 Freedom of religion (conscience, profession, practice and propagation; management of religious affairs; no taxes for a particular religion; no compulsory religious instruction in State institutions) 29(1) Any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture has the right to conserve it 29(2) No citizen shall be denied admission to an institution maintained by the State or receiving State aid on grounds only of religion, race, caste or language 30(1) All minorities, whether based on religion or language, have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice 30(1A) (44th Amendment 1978) Compensation for compulsory acquisition of the property of a minority educational institution must not restrict or abrogate the right 30(2) No discrimination in State aid against an institution managed by a minority 347, 350A, 350B Recognition of a language spoken by a substantial part of the population; facilities for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage; Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities National machinery: the National Commission for Minorities Act 1992 (see section 10) led to the notification of Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists and Zoroastrians (Parsis) in 1993, and Jains were added in January 2014, making six notified communities. The Ministry of Minority Affairs was created in January 2006. Other bodies and reports: Sachar Committee (2005–06, on the socio-economic status of Muslims), Ranganath Misra Commission (National Commission for Religious and Linguistic Minorities, 2004–07), the Prime Minister’s 15-Point Programme for Minorities (2006), the National Commission for Minority Educational Institutions Act 2004, and the Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities. Cases on minority rights Re Kerala Education Bill (1958): the Art. 30(1) right is subject to reasonable regulation to secure educational standards. S. Azeez Basha v. Union of India (1968): AMU was held not to be established by the Muslim minority; the issue was reopened in Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal (2024), where a seven-judge bench by majority overruled Azeez Basha , holding that an institution does not lose minority status merely because a statute gave it legal form, and left the actual status of AMU for a regular bench. St. Xavier’s College v. State of Gujarat (1974): affiliation is not a matter of choice; the right is not absolute. T.M.A. Pai Foundation (2002): the State is the unit for identifying minorities; no right to maladminister; regulatory measures are allowed; P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005): no reservation can be imposed on private unaided minority institutions. Bal Patil v. Union of India (2005): Jains were not treated as a national minority at that time (and were later notified in 2014). Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India (2014): the RTE Act does not apply to minority schools. Waqf (Amendment) Act 2025 : a recent amendment to the law on Muslim endowments, litigated before the Supreme Court, which passed an interim order in September 2025 on certain provisions. Treat as a current-affairs item and check the latest position. Criminal law: provisions on promoting enmity between groups (IPC s.153A) and deliberate acts to outrage religious feelings (s.295A), with their BNS counterparts; Places of Worship (Special Provisions) Act 1991.

t: 9.6 Weaker sections: Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, backward classes, EWS and others
p: Group Rights: Women, Children, Persons with Disabilities, Elderly, Minorities and Weaker Sections · Environment and Human Rights
x: Meaning. “Weaker sections” is a constitutional and policy expression (Art. 46) covering SC, ST and other socially and educationally backward classes, and by extension women, children, persons with disabilities, bonded labourers, the economically weak and other disadvantaged groups. Art. 366(24) and (25) define SC and ST by reference to Arts. 341 and 342 (President’s lists); Art. 366(26C) defines socially and educationally backward classes (102nd Amendment 2018). Constitutional framework: Arts. 15(4), 15(5), 15(6); 16(4), 16(4A), 16(4B), 16(6); 17; 23; 46; 244 with the Fifth Schedule (administration of Scheduled Areas) and Sixth Schedule (tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram); 330–334; 335; 338, 338A and 338B (national commissions, section 10); 340 (Commission to investigate backward classes); 341, 342, 342A. Statutes Law Key points Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955 Renamed in 1976 from the Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955; penalises practising untouchability Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989 Special offences, Special Courts, Exclusive Special Courts, relief and rehabilitation; amended in 2015 and in 2018 (s.18A: no preliminary inquiry or prior approval needed for arrest and no anticipatory bail, following the Supreme Court’s 2018 judgment in Subhash Kashinath Mahajan ; the amendment was upheld in Prathvi Raj Chauhan v. Union of India , 2020) Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act 2013 Bans manual scavenging and insanitary latrines; rehabilitation Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976 Abolishes bonded labour (Art. 23) Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act 2006; PESA 1996 Forest rights; self-governance in Scheduled Areas Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 NALSA; free legal aid (Art. 39A) for SC/ST, women, children, disabled persons, victims of trafficking, industrial workmen and persons in custody Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 Right to 100 days of wage employment (rural) National Food Security Act 2013 Legal entitlement to subsidised foodgrains for up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population; Antyodaya households Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019 Follows NALSA v. Union of India (2014), which recognised a third gender Reservation jurisprudence Case Holding M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore (1963) Reservation should ordinarily not exceed 50% State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas (1976) Art. 16(4) is not an exception to Art. 16(1); it is a facet of equality Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), nine judges Upheld 27% OBC reservation; creamy layer to be excluded; 50% cap (exceptions in extraordinary situations); no reservation in promotions (later overcome by Art. 16(4A)); backwardness not determined by caste alone M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006) Reservation in promotion allowed if the State shows quantifiable data on backwardness, inadequate representation and efficiency Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. Union of India (2008) OBC reservation in higher education upheld; creamy layer excluded Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018) Creamy layer principle applies to SC/ST for reservation in promotion; quantifiable data on backwardness not required Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. Chief Minister, Maharashtra (2021) Maratha reservation struck down; 50% ceiling reaffirmed; the 102nd Amendment restricted State power to identify SEBCs (restored by the 105th Amendment 2021) Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022) 10% EWS reservation (103rd Amendment) upheld by a 3:2 majority State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024), seven judges Sub-classification within SC/ST is permissible; overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2005) Other leading cases on weaker sections: People’s Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (1982) and Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984) on bonded labour and Art. 23; Samatha v. State of A.P. (1997) protecting tribal land from transfer; Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979) and M.H. Hoskot v. State of Maharashtra (1978) on free legal aid as part of Art. 21; National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014) on transgender persons.

t: Overview: Group Rights: Women, Children, Persons with Disabilities, Elderly, Minorities and Weaker Sections
p: Group Rights: Women, Children, Persons with Disabilities, Elderly, Minorities and Weaker Sections · Environment and Human Rights
x: “Group rights” here means the rights of groups that are historically disadvantaged, numerically small or otherwise vulnerable, and which need special protection beyond the general guarantee of equality. The legal idea is substantive equality : treating unequals equally can itself be discrimination, so the Constitution (Articles 14 to 16, 46) and international law (non-discrimination plus “special measures”) permit and sometimes require protective discrimination. The syllabus covers six groups. For each group, learn four layers: constitutional provisions, international instruments, statutes, and landmark cases.

t: Memory Capsule: Group Rights: Women, Children, Persons with Disabilities, Elderly, Minorities and Weaker Sections
p: Group Rights: Women, Children, Persons with Disabilities, Elderly, Minorities and Weaker Sections · Environment and Human Rights
x: CEDAW 1979/1981 , India 1993; CRC 1989/1990 , India 1992; CRPD 2006/2008 , India 2007; UN Principles for Older Persons 1991 ; Minorities Declaration 1992 . RPwD Act 2016: 21 disabilities, 40% benchmark, 4% jobs, 5% higher education. Senior citizen: 60 years (MWPSC 2007). Child: below 18 (CRC, POCSO, JJ Act); RTE ages 6–14. Six notified minorities (Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis, Jains). Indra Sawhney 1992: 50% and creamy layer; Davinder Singh 2024: sub-classification.

p: Protection and Enforcement of Human Rights in India: NHRC and National Commissions · Environment and Human Rights
x: Article 32 (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called it the “heart and soul” of the Constitution) and Article 226 give the right to move the Supreme Court and High Courts for enforcement of rights through writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto). The Supreme Court can act also on letters and on its own motion. Public interest litigation: the relaxation of locus standi in S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981, the Judges Transfer case), Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979, undertrial prisoners), Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984) and People’s Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (1982). Compensation as a public-law remedy: Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983, first award for illegal detention), Bhim Singh v. State of J&K (1985), Sebastian Hongray v. Union of India (1984), Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993), D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997). Custodial rights and police: D.K. Basu (1997) laid down arrest and detention guidelines; Joginder Kumar v. State of U.P. (1994) on arrest; Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006) on police reforms; People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. State of Maharashtra (2014) on the procedure for investigating police encounters. Armed forces: Naga People’s Movement of Human Rights v. Union of India (1997) upheld the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act 1958; Extra Judicial Execution Victim Families Association v. Union of India (2016) held that there is no absolute immunity for excesses in AFSPA areas. Human Rights Courts (PHRA ss.30–31): the State Government, with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of the High Court, may specify a Court of Session in each district as a Human Rights Court for speedy trial of offences arising from violations of human rights, and appoint a Special Public Prosecutor.

p: Protection and Enforcement of Human Rights in India: NHRC and National Commissions · Environment and Human Rights
x: The Principles relating to the Status of National Institutions (Paris Principles) , endorsed by the UN General Assembly in 1993 (Resolution 48/134, 20 December 1993), require national human rights institutions to have a broad mandate, independence (appointment and tenure), pluralism, adequate resources and investigative powers. Accreditation is carried out by the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI) through its Sub-Committee on Accreditation: A status means full compliance and B status partial compliance. India’s NHRC has held A status, but its re-accreditation was deferred in 2023 and the sub-committee reportedly recommended downgrading in April 2025; check the latest status.

p: Protection and Enforcement of Human Rights in India: NHRC and National Commissions · Environment and Human Rights
x: Origin. The NHRC was constituted on 12 October 1993 under an Ordinance, and the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 received assent on 8 January 1994 (deemed in force from 28 September 1993). The Act has been amended in 2006 (changes to the structure and working of the Commissions) and in 2019 (composition, tenure and eligibility). The first Chairperson was Justice Ranganath Misra . Its seat is in New Delhi. The Chairperson since December 2024 is Justice V. Ramasubramanian (check for later changes). Definition clauses (s.2). “Human rights” (s.2(1)(d)) and “International Covenants” (s.2(1)(f)), as in section 6 above; “armed forces” means the naval, military and air forces and includes any other armed forces of the Union (s.2(1)(a)). Composition (s.3, as amended in 2019) Category Members Chairperson A person who has been the Chief Justice of India or a Judge of the Supreme Court (the pre-2019 text required a former Chief Justice of India) Full-time Members One person who is, or has been, a Judge of the Supreme Court ; one person who is, or has been, a Chief Justice of a High Court ; and three Members , of whom at least one must be a woman , with knowledge of or practical experience in matters relating to human rights (before 2019 there were two such Members) Deemed Members (ex officio) Chairpersons of the National Commission for Minorities, SC, ST, Women, Backward Classes and Protection of Child Rights , and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities (before 2019, only the first four commissions) Officers Secretary-General (Chief Executive Officer, who exercises the powers of the Commission as delegated) Appointment (s.4). The Chairperson and Members are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee consisting of: the Prime Minister (Chairperson) , the Speaker of the Lok Sabha , the Minister in charge of the Ministry of Home Affairs , the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha , the Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha , and the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha . A sitting Judge of the Supreme Court or Chief Justice of a High Court can be appointed only after consultation with the Chief Justice of India. No appointment is invalid merely because of a vacancy in the committee. Term and eligibility (s.6). The Chairperson and Members hold office for three years or until the age of 70, whichever is earlier (before 2019: five years or 70), and are eligible for reappointment . On ceasing to hold office, they are ineligible for further employment under the Central or State Government. Removal (s.5). The President may remove the Chairperson or a Member for proved misbehaviour or incapacity only after the Supreme Court , on a reference by the President, has held an inquiry and reported that the person ought to be removed. The President may also remove by order a person who (a) is adjudged insolvent; (b) engages during his term in paid employment outside the duties of his office; (c) is unfit to continue by reason of infirmity of mind or body; (d) is of unsound mind and so declared by a competent court; or (e) is convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for an offence which, in the President’s opinion, involves moral turpitude. Resignation is by a letter addressed to the President. The model is the same as for removal of a Judge, except that the Supreme Court makes the inquiry on the President’s reference. Functions (s.12). The Commission shall: (a) inquire, suo motu or on a petition by a victim or a person on his behalf, or on a direction or order of any court, into a complaint of violation of human rights or abetment thereof , or negligence in the prevention of such violation by a public servant ; (b) intervene in any proceeding involving an allegation of violation of human rights pending before a court, with the approval of that court; (c) visit jails and other institutions under the control of the State Government where persons are detained or lodged for treatment, reformation or protection, and study the living conditions of inmates (under intimation to the State Government); (d) review the safeguards for the protection of human rights under the Constitution or any law and recommend measures for effective implementation; (e) review the factors, including acts of terrorism, that inhibit the enjoyment of human rights and recommend remedial measures; (f) study treaties and other international instruments on human rights and make recommendations for their effective implementation; (g) undertake and promote research in the field of human rights; (h) spread human rights literacy among various sections of society and promote awareness of the safeguards; (i) encourage the efforts of non-governmental organisations and institutions working in the field of human rights; (j) perform such other functions as it considers necessary for the promotion of human rights. Powers and procedure. Powers of a civil court under the CPC while trying a suit (summoning and examining witnesses, discovery and production of documents, receiving evidence on affidavits, requisitioning public records, issuing commissions) (s.13); the Commission may use the services of any officer or investigating agency of the Central or State Government, with concurrence (s.14); it may regulate its own procedure. It deals with a complaint free of charge and in any language. Limits. Limitation (s.36(2)): the Commission may not inquire into a matter after one year from the date on which the alleged act was committed. Pending matters (s.36(1)): it shall not inquire into a matter pending before a State Commission or any other Commission duly constituted under any law. Armed forces (s.19): for complaints of violation by members of the armed forces, the Commission may only seek a report from the Central Government and make recommendations; it has no power to investigate independently. Recommendatory nature: the Commission’s findings are not binding . Under s.18, it may recommend prosecution or other action, approach the Supreme Court or High Court for directions or writs, recommend interim relief to victims, and publish its report. The concerned Government must forward its comments and the action taken on the recommendation within one month (or such longer time as the Commission allows). The Commission submits an annual report to the Central Government, which is laid before Parliament with a memorandum of action taken (s.20). NHRC Procedure Regulations, 1994 list grounds on which complaints are ordinarily not entertained, such as anonymous or vague complaints, matters that are sub judice, service matters, and matters older than one year. Notable NHRC and court interactions: the Supreme Court referred the case of mass illegal cremations in Punjab to the NHRC ( Paramjit Kaur v. State of Punjab , 1999); the NHRC itself moved the Supreme Court to protect Chakma refugees in Arunachal Pradesh ( NHRC v. State of Arunachal Pradesh , 1996); the NHRC issued guidelines on reporting of encounter deaths (2003, revised in 2010).

x: Statute: National Commission for Women Act 1990; constituted on 31 January 1992 . First Chairperson: Jayanti Patnaik. Composition (s.3): a Chairperson committed to the cause of women; five Members nominated by the Central Government from persons of ability, integrity and standing with experience in law or legislation, trade unionism, management of an industry employing women, women’s voluntary organisations, administration, economic development, health, education or social welfare; at least one Member from SC and one from ST ; a Member-Secretary (an expert in management, organisational structure or sociological movement, or an officer of the civil service). The Chairperson and Members hold office for a term not exceeding three years (s.4). Functions (s.10): investigate and examine the safeguards provided for women under the Constitution and other laws; present annual and special reports to the Central Government; review existing laws and suggest amendments; take up cases of violation of the provisions of the Constitution and other laws relating to women with the appropriate authorities; look into complaints and take suo motu notice of the deprivation of women’s rights or non-implementation of protective laws; participate and advise on the socio-economic development planning process; inspect jails, remand homes and other places of custody; fund litigation involving issues affecting a large body of women; and undertake promotional and educational research. Powers (s.8): civil court powers while investigating matters (summoning, discovery, evidence on affidavits, public records, commissions). Nature: a recommendatory body; it cannot adjudicate or impose penalties. Chairperson since October 2024: Vijaya Rahatkar (check).

p: Protection and Enforcement of Human Rights in India: NHRC and National Commissions · Environment and Human Rights
x: Statute: National Commission for Minorities Act 1992. The Minorities Commission was first set up by a Government resolution on 12 January 1978; it became statutory in 1992 and the NCM began functioning on 17 May 1993 . It is under the Ministry of Minority Affairs. Notified minorities: Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists and Zoroastrians (Parsis) (1993); Jains (2014). Composition (s.3): a Chairperson, a Vice-Chairperson and five Members , nominated by the Central Government from persons of eminence, ability and integrity; five of the seven (including the Chairperson) must be from the minority communities. Term: three years (s.4). Functions (s.9): evaluate the progress of the development of minorities under the Union and the States; monitor the working of the constitutional and legal safeguards; make recommendations for their effective implementation; look into specific complaints regarding deprivation of rights and safeguards and take them up with the authorities; cause studies and research on discrimination; suggest measures; make periodical and special reports to the Central Government.

t: 10.7 National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC) and National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST)
p: Protection and Enforcement of Human Rights in India: NHRC and National Commissions · Environment and Human Rights
x: History: The original Art. 338 provided a Special Officer (Commissioner for SC and ST). The 65th Amendment 1990 replaced it with a multi-member National Commission for SC and ST (from 1992). The 89th Amendment 2003 split it into the NCSC (Art. 338) and the NCST (Art. 338A) , effective from 19 February 2004. The Ministry of Tribal Affairs was created in 1999. Composition: each Commission has a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and three other Members , appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal ; conditions of service and tenure are determined by rules made by the President (three-year terms in practice). Functions (Art. 338(5) and Art. 338A(5)): investigate and monitor all matters relating to the safeguards provided for SC (or ST) under the Constitution or any other law or Government order and evaluate their working; inquire into specific complaints about deprivation of rights; participate and advise on the planning process of socio-economic development of SC (or ST) and evaluate progress; present annual reports to the President (laid before Parliament with a memorandum of action taken, Art. 338(6)); recommend measures for effective implementation of safeguards and for welfare and development; and discharge other functions as the President may specify. NCST also has functions regarding forest rights, minor forest produce, and displacement of tribal communities. Powers (Art. 338(8) and 338A(8)): the Commission has all the powers of a civil court while investigating or inquiring into complaints (summoning, discovery, evidence on affidavits, requisitioning public records, issuing commissions). Consultation (Art. 338(9)): the Union and every State Government must consult the Commission on all major policy matters affecting SC (or ST).

x: History: The First Backward Classes Commission ( Kaka Kalelkar , 1953) and the Second ( B.P. Mandal , 1979; report 1980; 3,743 castes and communities identified; recommended 27% reservation, implemented in 1990 by the V.P. Singh Government) were set under Art. 340 . After Indra Sawhney (1992), the National Commission for Backward Classes Act 1993 created a statutory NCBC, with the task of examining requests for inclusion in and complaints of over-inclusion or under-inclusion in the lists of backward classes. Constitutional status: the 102nd Constitution Amendment Act 2018 inserted Art. 338B (NCBC as a constitutional body, in force from 15 August 2018), Art. 342A (President specifies the socially and educationally backward classes for each State and Union Territory, Parliament may amend the list), and Art. 366(26C) ; the 1993 Act was repealed. The 105th Amendment 2021 restored the power of States and Union Territories to prepare their own lists of SEBCs. Composition: Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and three other Members, appointed by the President by warrant under hand and seal. Functions (Art. 338B(5)): investigate and monitor safeguards for socially and educationally backward classes; inquire into specific complaints; participate and advise on the planning process of their socio-economic development; present annual reports to the President; recommend measures; and discharge other functions. It also has the civil court powers (Art. 338B(8)). The Centre and States must consult the NCBC on major policy matters (this requirement was removed for State lists by the 105th Amendment). Sub-categorisation: the Rohini Commission (appointed under Art. 340 in 2017, chaired by Justice G. Rohini, a former Chief Justice of the Delhi High Court) examined sub-categorisation of OBCs and submitted its report in July 2023.

x: Human rights in India are protected by four overlapping mechanisms: (1) constitutional remedies (writs under Articles 32 and 226 and the creative use of public interest litigation and compensation); (2) the statutory human rights machinery under the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 (PHRA) : the National Human Rights Commission, State Human Rights Commissions and Human Rights Courts; (3) specialised commissions for particular groups (minorities, women, SC, ST, backward classes, children and others); and (4) other legal institutions (legal services authorities, the Right to Information Act, and the Lok Adalats). The syllabus lists six bodies: NHRC, NCM, NCW, NCSC, NCST and NCBC . The recurring exam questions are about composition, appointment, removal, term, limitation and the binding or recommendatory nature of their orders.

p: Exam Pattern, Recent Trends and How to Use These Notes · Family Law
x: Constitutional lens on personal law. Questions ask which Article a judgment used (Shayara Bano: Article 14 ‘manifest arbitrariness’; Hadiya and Nandakumar: Article 21 choice of partner; Supriyo: no fundamental right to marry). Judge-made divorce law. Article 142 divorces for irretrievable breakdown (Shilpa Sailesh, 2023) and the waiver of the 6-month cooling-off period (Amardeep Singh, 2017) are now standard framework questions. New criminal codes. Old IPC/CrPC/Evidence Act numbers are being replaced by BNS/BNSS/BSA numbers: bigamy BNS 82, cruelty BNS 85, dowry death BNS 80, maintenance BNSS 144, presumption of legitimacy BSA 116. Know both numbers. Women’s property and maintenance. Vineeta Sharma (2020), Rajnesh v Neha (2020), Mohd. Abdul Samad (2024) and stridhan rulings recur. State-level codification. Uttarakhand (2024) and Gujarat (2026) UCCs, Goa’s Civil Code, and the ‘can a State enact a UCC?’ debate. Waqf. Waqf (Amendment) Act 2025 and the Supreme Court’s interim order of 15 September 2025 are almost certain current-affairs material.

p: Exam Pattern, Recent Trends and How to Use These Notes · Family Law
x: Hindu marriage is a sacrament in origin; Section 7 requires customary rites, and saptapadi completes it where applicable. Section 5 HMA conditions: monogamy, sound mind, age 21/18, not prohibited degrees, not sapindas (unless custom). Clause (vi) was omitted in 1978. Void: Section 11 (breach of 5(i), (iv), (v)). Voidable: Section 12 (impotence, 5(ii), force/fraud, pre-marital pregnancy by another). Section 16 HMA: children of void and voidable marriages are legitimate; Revanasiddappa (2023) extends property rights to parents’ share. Divorce grounds Section 13(1); wife-only grounds Section 13(2); mutual consent Section 13B (1 year separation + 6–18 month motion window). Amardeep Singh (2017): 6-month period is directory. Shilpa Sailesh (2023): Article 142 can dissolve a marriage for irretrievable breakdown. Saroj Rani (1984) upheld restitution of conjugal rights; T. Sareetha (1983) struck it down. Dastane (1975): cruelty proved on preponderance of probability. Samar Ghosh (2007): mental cruelty illustrations. Bipinchandra (1957): four elements of desertion. Muslim marriage is a civil contract; Shia recognise muta; Sunnis do not. Talaq-e-biddat void: Shayara Bano (2017, 3:2); criminalised by the 2019 Act. Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939: Section 2 lists nine grounds; wife’s conversion does not dissolve the marriage (Section 4). Mahr: debt, not price; wife has lien but no title (Maina Bibi; Kapore Chand). Shah Bano (1985) → Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act 1986 → Danial Latifi (2001) → Mohd. Abdul Samad (2024). Section 125 CrPC / Section 144 BNSS: no monetary ceiling since 2001; secular remedy. HAMA: Section 6 requisites, Section 11 conditions, Section 12 effect, datta homam not essential. Shabnam Hashmi (2014): JJ Act adoption is open to all irrespective of religion; it is an enabling law. HMGA Section 6: father natural guardian ‘after’ whom the mother; Gita Hariharan (1999) reads ‘after’ as ‘in absence of’. Mother ordinarily has custody under 5. HSA Section 6 (2005): daughters coparceners by birth; Vineeta Sharma (2020) says father need not be alive on 9 September 2005. HSA Section 14: female Hindu is full owner; Tulasamma (1977) on widow’s maintenance-in-lieu. Muslim will: up to one-third of net estate without heirs’ consent; no registration, no writing needed. Hiba needs declaration, acceptance and delivery of possession; Section 129 TPA keeps Muslim gifts outside Section 123. Y. Narasimha Rao (1991): test for recognising foreign matrimonial decrees; Section 13 CPC exceptions (a)–(f). Live-in: Velusamy (2010) four conditions; Indra Sarma (2013) guidelines; DV Act Section 2(f) ‘relationship in the nature of marriage’. Article 44: UCC is a Directive Principle; Shah Bano, Sarla Mudgal, John Vallamattom urge it; Goa (Portuguese Civil Code), Uttarakhand (2024) and Gujarat (2026) are the practical examples.

Every question is an MCQ worth 2 marks, there is no negative marking, and Papers 1 and 2 are attempted together in one 3-hour sitting (150 questions, 300 marks). Family Law rewards three things: exact section numbers and time limits, landmark case–principle pairs, and 2023–2026 developments. Recent NET papers lean on ‘current’ law, and your revised syllabus now names live-in relationships and the Uniform Civil Code outright, so both are fair game. These notes follow the ten syllabus topics in order. Each topic has (1) a concept core in plain paragraphs, (2) bullet lists of provisions and conditions, (3) tables for case laws and comparisons, (4) a ‘Recent trend’ box, and (5) ‘MCQ traps’. Items marked (verify) are recent developments taken from news and legal-portal reports (up to October 2026); confirm the exact title or holding on the Supreme Court website or LiveLaw before relying on them for a numerical or ‘who decided’ question.

p: Sources and Schools of Family Law · Family Law
x: Who is a Hindu (Section 2 HMA 1955; same pattern in HSA, HAMA, HMGA). The Acts apply to: (a) Hindus by religion in any form or development, including Virashaivas, Lingayats and followers of the Brahmo, Prarthana or Arya Samaj; (b) Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs; (c) any person domiciled in the territories to which the Act extends who is not a Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew by religion, unless it is proved that he would not have been governed by Hindu law or custom but for the Act. Children of Hindu parents (legitimate or illegitimate) and children of a Hindu parent brought up as Hindu, and converts or reconverts, are covered. Scheduled Tribes are excluded unless the Central Government notifies otherwise (Section 2(2)). Perumal Nadar v Ponnuswami (1970) and Yagnapurushdasji v Muldas (1966) are the usual cases on who counts as a Hindu. Sources of Hindu law Category Content Exam notes Shruti Four Vedas (Rig, Yajur, Sama, Atharva), Upanishads ‘Heard’ revelation; basic source Smriti Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras: Manu, Yajnavalkya, Narada, Brihaspati, Katyayana, Gautama, Vishnu ‘Remembered’; Manu Smriti oldest and most authoritative among metrical codes Commentaries and digests Mitakshara (Vijnaneshwara, on Yajnavalkya), Dayabhaga (Jimutavahana), Dattaka Mimamsa, Dattaka Chandrika, Vyavahara Mayukha, Smriti Chandrika, Viramitrodaya Shape the schools Custom Ancient, certain, reasonable, continuous, not immoral and not opposed to public policy or statute Collector of Madura v Moottoo Ramalinga Sathupathy (PC, 1868): clear proof of usage outweighs written text; Section 3(a) HMA defines ‘custom and usage’ Justice, equity and good conscience Used when no rule exists Fills gaps Precedents Privy Council and Supreme Court Binding under Article 141 Legislation Hindu Code 1955–56: HMA, HSA, HMGA, HAMA; plus Caste Disabilities Removal Act 1850, Hindu Widows’ Remarriage Act 1856, Hindu Women’s Rights to Property Act 1937 Statute overrides text and custom where inconsistent (Section 4 HMA) Section 4 HMA: the Act overrides any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu law, custom or usage, and any other law in force, to the extent it is inconsistent with the Act. Schools (applicable to joint family, partition and some succession matters) Mitakshara (all India except Bengal and Assam): sub-schools Benares (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar parts), Mithila (North Bihar), Maharashtra or Bombay (Vyavahara Mayukha is dominant here), Dravida or Madras (south India). Interest by birth; survivorship; coparcenary of male lineal descendants (daughters added by 2005 amendment to Section 6 HSA); inheritance by proximity of blood (nearest-in-blood rule); son cannot be disinherited of ancestral property by father’s gift. Dayabhaga (Bengal and Assam): founded on the doctrine of religious efficacy or spiritual benefit (pinda offering); right arises only on father’s death, so no birth-right; no survivorship, sons hold as tenants in common; father is absolute owner of ancestral property. Point Mitakshara Dayabhaga Author Vijnaneshwara Jimutavahana Area Everywhere except Bengal and Assam Bengal and Assam Birth-right Yes (son acquires interest by birth) No (arises on father’s death) Mode of devolution Survivorship (and succession for separate property) Succession only Basis of inheritance Propinquity (nearness of blood) Spiritual benefit Share before partition Fluctuating, unascertained Definite and ascertained Alienation by coparcener Not allowed without consent of others (except in limited cases) Allowed (shares defined) Women Daughters are coparceners by birth (Section 6 HSA, 2005 amendment) No birth-right coparcenary; sons and daughters take by succession after the owner’s death State amendments: Andhra Pradesh (1986), Tamil Nadu (1989), Karnataka (1994) and Maharashtra (1994) gave daughters coparcenary rights earlier than the 2005 central amendment; Kerala abolished the joint family system in 1975 (Kerala Joint Hindu Family System (Abolition) Act).

p: Sources and Schools of Family Law · Family Law
x: Primary sources: (1) the Quran (word of God; revealed through Prophet Muhammad; only a small fraction of verses are strictly legal); (2) Sunnah or Ahadis (traditions of the Prophet: Sunnat-ul-fail (acts), Sunnat-ul-qawl (sayings), Sunnat-ul-taqrir (tacit approval); Hadis may be mutawatir (continuous), mashhur (well known) or ahad (isolated)); (3) Ijma (consensus of jurists; Ijma of companions, of jurists, of the community); (4) Qiyas (analogical deduction). Secondary sources: custom (urf) not opposed to the Quran; judicial precedents (Privy Council and Indian courts); legislation; equity or istihsan (juristic preference, used by Hanafis) and istislah (public interest, Malikis). Schools Branch School Founder and facts Region or followers Sunni Hanafi Abu Hanifa (Kufa); uses Qiyas and istihsan; most liberal; his disciples Abu Yusuf and Imam Muhammad Majority of Indian Sunnis Sunni Maliki Imam Malik (Medina); Al-Muwatta; relies on practice of Medina North and West Africa Sunni Shafi’i Imam Shafi’i; Al-Risala; systematised usul al-fiqh Kerala (Mappillas), Egypt, East Africa Sunni Hanbali Ahmad ibn Hanbal; strictest reliance on hadith Saudi Arabia Shia Ithna Ashari (Twelvers) Imam Jafar al-Sadiq (Jafari law); permits muta, no Aul Majority of Indian Shias Shia Ismaili (Bohras, Khojas) Distinct inheritance customs among Khojas Gujarat, Maharashtra Shia Zaidi Zaid bin Ali Yemen, small in India Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937. Section 2: in intestate succession, special property of females (inherited or contractual), marriage, dissolution (talaq, ila, zihar, lian, khula, mubarat), maintenance, dower, guardianship, gifts, trusts and trust properties, and wakfs, the rule of decision for Muslims is Muslim personal law, notwithstanding custom. The original Act excluded adoption, wills and legacies unless a person made a declaration under Section 3 (the Act’s 1943 amendment dealt with agricultural land). This is why a Muslim’s will and adoption are not ‘Shariat Act’ matters and why the JJ Act applies to adoption.

p: Sources and Schools of Family Law · Family Law
x: Christians: Indian Christian Marriage Act 1872; Indian Divorce Act 1869 (amended 2001); Indian Succession Act 1925; Guardians and Wards Act 1890; plus customary and canon-law elements. English common law doctrines applied through justice, equity and good conscience. Parsis: Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act 1936 (amended 1988); Indian Succession Act 1925 (special rules in Part V Chapter III); customs of Parsi Panchayat; marriage must be by ‘Ashirvad’ ceremony before a priest and two witnesses. Jews: largely uncodified (Cochin and Bene Israel communities); Jewish customs, Indian Succession Act, and the Special Marriage Act for civil marriage. Anglo-Indians, tribals: tribal customs retained in the Fifth and Sixth Schedules and Article 371A and similar provisions; Section 2(2) HSA and Section 2(2) HMA exclude Scheduled Tribes.

p: Sources and Schools of Family Law · Family Law
x: Article 13: are personal laws ‘laws in force’? State of Bombay v Narasu Appa Mali (1952) held personal law is outside ‘law’ for Article 13; this is still criticised and was not decided in Shayara Bano (2017), where the majority tested the 1937 Act’s recognition of talaq-e-biddat under Article 14. Articles 14, 15, 21: equality, non-discrimination, personal liberty and privacy; Article 15(3) allows special provisions for women and children. Article 25–26: freedom of religion; ‘essential religious practice’ doctrine (Shirur Mutt, 1954). Article 44: UCC as a Directive Principle (see topic 10 ). Entry 5, List III (above). Articles 141 and 142: precedent binding; ‘complete justice’ power used for divorces.

t: Overview: Sources and Schools of Family Law
p: Sources and Schools of Family Law · Family Law
x: Core idea: India has no single family law. Each religious community is governed by its own personal law, partly codified and partly uncodified, under the constitutional umbrella of Entry 5 of the Concurrent List (marriage and divorce; infants and minors; adoption; wills, intestacy and succession; joint family and partition; all matters for which parties were subject to personal law immediately before the Constitution). Because it is a Concurrent List entry, both Parliament and State legislatures can legislate, subject to Article 254 (repugnancy and Presidential assent). That is why a State UCC is constitutionally arguable.

t: Memory Capsule: Sources and Schools of Family Law
p: Sources and Schools of Family Law · Family Law
x: Dayabhaga is the school of Bengal and Assam, not Mithila. ‘Mitakshara’ is a commentary on Yajnavalkya Smriti; ‘Dayabhaga’ is a digest, not a commentary on one Smriti. The Shariat Act, 1937 does not cover wills, adoption (original text) or agricultural land (original text). Ijma and Qiyas are independent sources; istihsan is Hanafi, not Shafi’i. Fatwa is not law (Vishwa Lochan Madan v Union of India, 2014: Sharia courts and fatwas have no legal sanction).

t: Analysis Angle: Sources and Schools of Family Law
p: Sources and Schools of Family Law · Family Law
x: Recent trend box: The Supreme Court (Supriyo, 2023) refused to recognise a fundamental right to marry or to read down the Special Marriage Act for same-sex couples, and the review was dismissed in 2025 (verify). Questions now test the interplay between personal law and fundamental rights rather than just listing sources.

p: Marriage and Dissolution of Marriage · Family Law
x: Section 5: conditions for a valid marriage Monogamy: neither party has a spouse living at the time (5(i)). Sound mind: at the time of marriage neither party is incapable of giving valid consent through unsoundness of mind, or though capable of consent is suffering from a mental disorder of such kind or extent as to be unfit for marriage and procreation of children, or has been subject to recurrent attacks of insanity (5(ii), as amended by the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Act 1999; earlier ‘idiot or lunatic’). Age: bridegroom 21, bride 18 (5(iii)). Penalty under Section 18 HMA is now dominated by the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006 (PCMA). Prohibited degrees: not within degrees of prohibited relationship unless custom permits (5(iv)); defined in Section 3(g). Sapinda: not sapindas of each other unless custom permits (5(v)); sapinda relationship extends up to five degrees in the line of ascent through the father and three through the mother (Section 3(f)). Clause (vi) (guardian’s consent) was omitted in 1978. Section 7: ceremonies. A Hindu marriage may be solemnised in accordance with the customary rites and ceremonies of either party. Where the rites include the saptapadi (seven steps taken jointly before the sacred fire), the marriage becomes complete and binding when the seventh step is taken. Case law: Bhaurao Shankar Lokhande v State of Maharashtra (1965: ‘solemnise’ means to celebrate with proper ceremonies; Hindu marriage needs essential rites); Priya Bala Ghosh v Suresh Chandra Ghosh (1971). In Dolly Rani v Manish Kumar Chanchal (2024) the Supreme Court held that a Hindu marriage without the requisite ceremonies is not valid merely because a certificate was issued, and a registration under Section 8 does not by itself confer validity (it is evidence of marriage). Section 8: registration. State Governments may make rules for registration of Hindu marriages; failure to register does not invalidate the marriage (8(5)). Seema v Ashwani Kumar (2006) directed compulsory registration of marriages of all persons of all religions in India. Section 9–18 (remedies, covered in topic 3 ). Void and voidable marriages: Type Section Grounds Who may petition and limits Void (void ab initio) 11 Bigamy (5(i)); within prohibited degrees (5(iv)); sapindas (5(v)) Either party (even a third party in some cases); no time limit; decree of nullity is declaratory Voidable 12 (a) Respondent’s impotence leading to non-consummation; (b) breach of 5(ii) (mental disorder); (c) consent obtained by force or fraud (as to nature of the ceremony or any material fact about the respondent); (d) respondent was pregnant by another person at marriage Only the aggrieved party. Section 12(2): fraud or force petitions within 1 year of discovery or cessation of force and no cohabitation afterward; pregnancy ground within 1 year of marriage and no marital intercourse since discovery Not a ground for nullity: underage marriage (it is not void under HMA; it may be voidable under PCMA at the child’s option). Section 16: legitimacy of children. Children of void marriages (under Section 11) and of annulled voidable marriages are legitimate. Section 16(3): they have rights only to the property of their parents, not to any other relative’s property. Parayankandiyal Eravath Kanapravan Kalliani Amma v K. Devi (1996) said property rights of such children are confined to the parents’ self-acquired property; Jinia Keotin v Kumar Sitaram Manjhi (2003) similar; Revanasiddappa v Mallikarjun (2023, three-judge bench) held such children are entitled to a share in the parents’ property, self-acquired and ancestral, to the extent of the parents’ share, even in a Hindu joint family. Bigamy. Section 17 HMA: punishable under IPC 494 and 495, now BNS Section 82. Sarla Mudgal v Union of India (1995) and Lily Thomas v Union of India (2000): conversion to Islam to contract a second marriage does not dissolve the first Hindu marriage; the second marriage is void and an offence. Yamunabai Anantrao Adhav v Anantrao (1988): a woman in a bigamous (void) marriage cannot claim maintenance under Section 125 CrPC; later, Badshah v Urmila Badshah Godse (2014) tempered this where the wife entered marriage in good faith (verify exact holding before using in an examination).

p: Marriage and Dissolution of Marriage · Family Law
x: Section 4: conditions: monogamy, sound mind (same test as HMA), age 21/18, not within prohibited degrees (unless custom permits for both). Notice: 30 days’ notice of intended marriage to the Marriage Officer (Section 5), objections within 30 days (Section 7), solemnisation within 3 months of notice (Section 14). Allahabad High Court in Safiya Sultana v State of UP (2021) held that publication of notice is optional and directory at the option of the parties (verify current practice). Section 15–18: registration of marriages celebrated in other forms; Section 19: the marriage under the Act of a member of an undivided family who professes the Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh or Jain religion is deemed to sever him from that family. Section 21: succession governed by Indian Succession Act 1925 (except for Hindus, Buddhists, Sikhs and Jains who are governed by Section 21A: succession under the Hindu Succession Act). Divorce: Section 27 (fault grounds), Section 28 (mutual consent: 1 year separation), Section 29 (no petition within 1 year of marriage); Section 36–37 alimony; Section 38 custody. Relevance: inter-religious and inter-caste couples; protected by Article 21 ( Lata Singh v State of UP , 2006; Shakti Vahini v Union of India , 2018; Shafin Jahan v Asokan , 2018: right to marry a person of choice).

p: Marriage and Dissolution of Marriage · Family Law
x: Nature: a civil contract ( aqd ) with religious sanctity. Essentials: (1) proposal (ijab) by one party and acceptance (qubul) by the other in the same meeting; (2) free consent; (3) capacity: sound mind and puberty (presumed at 15 under Hanafi law; majority at 18 under the Indian Majority Act; marriage of a Muslim girl who has attained puberty has been upheld by some High Courts, but the interaction with PCMA 2006 is contested and the Supreme Court issued enforcement guidelines for PCMA in 2024 without settling it: verify); (4) two male Sunni witnesses (or one male and two females); Shia law does not require witnesses; (5) mahr is a consequence, not a condition of validity. Classification (Sunni): valid (sahih), irregular (fasid), void (batil). Shia: valid or void only. Prohibition Examples Effect Absolute Consanguinity (mother, daughter, sister, aunt, niece); affinity (wife’s mother or daughter after consummation); fosterage (milk relations) Void Relative Unlawful conjunction (two sisters at once); fifth wife (void in Sunni; temporary bar until one of the four is divorced in some views); marriage during iddat (irregular in Sunni; void in Shia); absence of witnesses (irregular, Hanafi); difference of religion (Muslim man with kitabia is irregular; Muslim woman with non-Muslim void); marriage during pilgrimage (ihram) Irregular or void as stated Muta (temporary marriage) is recognised in Ithna Ashari Shia law only: fixed period, fixed mahr, no maintenance, no mutual inheritance, issue legitimate; iddat is two menstrual courses (about 45 days) after expiry; for widow, four months and ten days. Polygamy: up to four wives at one time, with equal treatment; courts treat polygamy as not an ‘essential’ practice for Article 25 purposes in some decisions; Uttarakhand UCC Act 2024 bans it for residents (see topic 10 ). Legitimacy and presumption. Child born at least six months after marriage and within two years (Hanafi), four years (Shafi’i) or ten months (Shia) after dissolution or death is presumed legitimate. Section 112 Indian Evidence Act (now Section 116 BSA 2023): birth during marriage or within 280 days after dissolution while the mother is unmarried is conclusive proof of legitimacy.

p: Marriage and Dissolution of Marriage · Family Law
x: Mode Initiator Key features Talaq-ul-sunnat: Ahsan Husband Single pronouncement in tuhr (period of purity) and abstinence through iddat; most approved; revocable in iddat Talaq-ul-sunnat: Hasan Husband Three pronouncements in three successive tuhrs; final pronouncement makes it irrevocable Talaq-ul-biddat Husband Triple talaq in one sentence or single irrevocable pronouncement; sinful but effective before 2017; now void Ila Husband Vow of abstinence for four months; becomes irrevocable if not resumed Zihar Husband Comparing wife to prohibited relative; wife can seek judicial dissolution unless husband performs expiation (kaffara) within four months Talaq-i-tafwiz Delegated by husband Husband delegates power to wife or third person (recognised in Indian case law) Khula Wife Offer to release husband on consideration; consent of husband needed in Hanafi law; Zohara Khatoon v Mohd. Ibrahim (1981) Mubarat Both Mutual release; aversion on both sides; offer by either; no compensation necessarily Lian Husband accuses wife of adultery without witnesses Wife can obtain dissolution by court Judicial divorce Wife Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939, Section 2 Shayara Bano v Union of India (2017). Five-judge bench held talaq-e-biddat unconstitutional by 3:2. Justices Nariman and Lalit: manifestly arbitrary, violates Article 14 and is not protected by Article 25; Justice Kurian Joseph: against the Quran, hence not part of Shariat; Chief Justice Khehar and Justice Nazeer (dissent): practice is protected personal law under Article 25 but Parliament should legislate. Earlier: Shamim Ara v State of UP (2002) held talaq must be for a reasonable cause, preceded by an attempt at reconciliation, and proved in court; a talaq pleaded in a written statement is not itself a valid pronouncement. Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act 2019. Talaq-e-biddat void and illegal (Section 3); imprisonment up to three years and fine (Section 4); offence cognizable only on information from the married woman or her blood or marriage relatives (Section 7); compoundable by the Magistrate on the woman’s application; bail only after hearing the wife; subsistence allowance (Section 5); custody of minor children (Section 6). Applies only to pronouncement of talaq-e-biddat; other forms remain valid. Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939, Section 2 grounds for a wife: Whereabouts of husband not known for four years. Failure of husband to maintain her for two years. Husband sentenced to imprisonment for seven years or more. Husband failed to perform marital obligations for three years without reasonable cause. Husband impotent at marriage and continuing to be so. Husband insane for two years or suffering from virulent venereal disease (leprosy was removed by the Personal Laws (Amendment) Act 2019: verify). Repudiation of marriage (option of puberty) by a girl married before 15 and who repudiates before 18, marriage not consummated. Cruelty: habitual assault or making life miserable; associating with women of evil repute; forcing to lead an immoral life; disposing of her property or preventing her from exercising legal rights; obstructing religious practice; unequal treatment of co-wives. Any other ground recognised as valid for dissolution under Muslim law. Section 4: wife’s renunciation of Islam or conversion does not by itself dissolve her marriage (she may seek dissolution on other grounds if she was a Muslim by birth who reverts); Section 5 protects her dower rights.

p: Marriage and Dissolution of Marriage · Family Law
x: Indian Christian Marriage Act 1872: applies where one or both parties are Christian. Section 4–5: marriage solemnised by a clergyman of Church of England, Church of Scotland, a minister of another Church licensed, or a Marriage Registrar; Section 60: conditions (monogamy, age 21/18, consent of the father or guardian if either is a minor); time: between 6 a.m. and 7 p.m. (Section 9 with exceptions); notice and registration provisions. Indian Divorce Act 1869: Section 10 grounds after the 2001 amendment: adultery, conversion, unsound mind for two years, venereal disease, wilful refusal to consummate, desertion for two years, cruelty (introduced 2001), and parity between husband and wife; mutual consent divorce under Section 10A after two years of separation (not one). Nullity under Section 19 (impotence, prohibited degrees, prior spouse, unsoundness of mind).

p: Marriage and Dissolution of Marriage · Family Law
x: Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act 1936: ‘Ashirvad’ ceremony performed by a Parsi priest in the presence of two Parsi witnesses (Section 3); prohibited degrees (Schedule I); monogamy (a bigamous Parsi marriage is void and punishable); age 21/18; registration (Section 6). Divorce under Section 32 : wilful refusal to consummate within one year; unsound mind; pregnancy by another; adultery, bigamy, rape or unnatural offence; hurt; cruelty; desertion; imprisonment for seven years; non-compliance with decree of restitution; conversion; Section 32B mutual consent after one year separation. Courts are special Parsi Chief Matrimonial Courts and District Matrimonial Courts (with delegates assisting).
