t: 10.4 Uttarakhand Uniform Civil Code Act 2024 (first State UCC)
p: Uniform Civil Code (UCC) · Family Law
x: Process: committee headed by Justice (retd.) Ranjana Prakash Desai; Bill passed by the State Assembly in February 2024 ; Presidential assent in March 2024 ; brought into force in January 2025 after rules were notified (reported; verify exact dates). Scope: applies to residents of Uttarakhand (also residents living outside the State) and excludes Scheduled Tribes and persons whose customary rights are protected by the Constitution; covers marriage and divorce, succession (wills and intestate), live-in relationships, and miscellaneous provisions. Key features: equal marriage age (21 for men, 18 for women); monogamy (bigamy prohibited); mandatory registration of marriages and divorces; equal grounds of divorce for men and women; prohibition of practices such as triple talaq, halala and iddat; marriages and divorces by religious customs allowed as to ceremonies but not to substance; equal inheritance rights for sons and daughters; children of void or voidable marriages and live-in relationships treated as legitimate; adopted and biological children treated alike; live-in relationships to be registered and terminated with notice. Challenge: petitions have been filed in the High Court against the live-in registration and other provisions (verify status).

t: 10.5 Gujarat Uniform Civil Code 2026 (second State UCC)
p: Uniform Civil Code (UCC) · Family Law
x: Process: committee chaired by Justice (retd.) Ranjana Prakash Desai; Bill introduced on 24 March 2026 , passed the same day by the Gujarat Assembly after about seven and a half hours’ debate; Presidential assent reported in early October 2026 ; the State must notify rules before it comes into force (reported; verify). Scope: Marriage and divorce, succession and live-in relationships; applies to residents of Gujarat and to Gujarat residents living outside the State; excludes Scheduled Tribes and groups whose customary rights are protected by the Constitution. Reported features: registration of live-in relationships and of their termination; prohibition of bigamy (a marriage is valid only if neither party has a living spouse); all separations must be through civil courts (reportedly ending extra-judicial or customary divorce); compulsory registration of marriages; common succession framework. Opposition: concerns that it is politically driven and may infringe religious freedom and fundamental rights.

p: Uniform Civil Code (UCC) · Family Law

Narasu Appa Mali (1952) and the question whether personal laws are subject to fundamental rights (unsettled). Reform by consent vs imposition: the UCC can be enacted by Parliament under Entry 5, List III or Article 44 as a directive; no deadline.

p: Uniform Civil Code (UCC) · Family Law
x: Core idea: Article 44 (Directive Principle, Part IV) says: ‘The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.’ It is non-justiciable (Article 37). The debate is between equality and gender justice (Articles 14, 15) and religious freedom and cultural pluralism (Articles 25–29). As of 2026 there is still no national UCC; Goa has a historic common code, and Uttarakhand (2024) and Gujarat (2026) have enacted State UCCs.

p: Uniform Civil Code (UCC) · Family Law
x: Article 44 is in Part IV (DPSP), not Part III; it is not enforceable. Uttarakhand was the first State to enact a UCC post-Independence; Goa’s code is a continuation of a pre-Independence Portuguese law. The Law Commission (2018) said UCC was neither necessary nor desirable at this stage ; the 22nd Commission started fresh consultation in 2023. State UCCs exclude Scheduled Tribes . Shah Bano, Sarla Mudgal, John Vallamattom each urged the government to enact a UCC; none ordered it.

t: 11.5 Frequent confusions (MCQ traps in one place)
p: Revision Toolkit: Cases, Numbers, Timelines and Traps · Family Law
x: Void vs voidable: HMA Sections 11 (void) and 12 (voidable); child is legitimate in both (Section 16). Judicial separation vs divorce: marriage subsists after judicial separation. Mutual consent vs irretrievable breakdown: 13B is statutory; irretrievable breakdown is Article 142 only. Dower vs dowry; mahr vs mutah (gift on divorce) vs muta (temporary marriage). Hizanat (custody) vs wilayat (guardianship): mother has hizanat; father has wilayat. Guardian and Wards Act (secular) vs HMGA (Hindu). Hiba (gift) vs wasiyat (will): hiba effective immediately with delivery; wasiyat after death. Aul vs Radd: Aul reduces shares; Radd returns the surplus. Wakf vs trust: ownership in God; mutawalli is not owner. Section 125 CrPC vs Section 144 BNSS: same subject; do not confuse with Section 144 CrPC (prohibitory orders). Natural guardian of a married Hindu girl: her husband.

t: 0.1 BNS at a glance: high-yield numbers
p: Scope, Law Used and Exam Pattern · Law of Crimes
x: 358 sections in 20 Chapters; the IPC had 511 sections in 23 Chapters. Chapter I = preliminary and definitions (s.1-3; s.2 is the definitions section); Chapter II = punishments (s.4-13); Chapter III = general exceptions (s.14-44); Chapter IV = abetment, criminal conspiracy and attempt (s.45-62); Chapter V = offences against women and children (s.63-99); Chapter VI = offences affecting the human body (s.100-146); Chapter VII = offences against the State (s.147-158); Chapter VIII = offences relating to the Army, Navy and Air Force (s.159-168); Chapter IX = offences relating to elections (s.169-177); Chapter X = coin, bank notes, currency notes and Government stamps (s.178-188); Chapter XI = offences against public tranquillity (s.189-197); Chapter XVII = offences against property (s.303-334). New offences added: organised crime (s.111) , petty organised crime (s.112) , terrorist act (s.113) , mob lynching (s.103(2)) , snatching (s.304) , hit and run (s.106(2)) , sexual intercourse by deceitful means or false promise of marriage (s.69) , and acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India (s.152) . Removed or dropped: sedition (IPC 124A) (replaced in substance by s.152), adultery (IPC 497) (already struck down in Joseph Shine v. Union of India , 2018), unnatural offences (IPC 377) (consensual part read down in Navtej Singh Johar , 2018; BNS has no equivalent), and attempt to commit suicide (IPC 309) (replaced by a narrow s.226, attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain a public servant, punished with community service). Community service is a new punishment (s.4(f)), provided for small offences such as petty theft, defamation, attempted suicide to coerce a public servant and public intoxication. Rape (s.63) is still a male-offender, female-victim offence; the age of consent stays at 18 years.

t: Overview: Scope, Law Used and Exam Pattern
p: Scope, Law Used and Exam Pattern · Law of Crimes
x: The criminal substantive law of India is now the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) , in force from 1 July 2024 ; it replaced the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC). Procedure moved to the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) (replacing CrPC 1973) and evidence to the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) (replacing the Evidence Act 1872). Every topic below gives the BNS section first and the old IPC section in brackets, because UGC NET options still mix both numbering systems and almost all case law was decided under the IPC.

p: General Principles of Criminal Liability · Law of Crimes
x: Human being under a legal duty to act or abstain (a juristic person such as a company is also a "person", BNS s.2(26); IPC s.11). Mens rea : the guilty mind. Actus reus : the prohibited conduct, its circumstances and its result. Injury to another or to society, recognised by law.

p: General Principles of Criminal Liability · Law of Crimes
x: Meaning : the external, physical part of a crime: the act or illegal omission, the surrounding circumstances and (for result crimes) the consequence. The act must be voluntary (a reflex, sleepwalking or a seizure is not an act in law). Types : conduct crimes (offence complete on doing the act, e.g., perjury), result crimes (need a consequence, e.g., murder needs death), and state-of-affairs crimes (possession offences, e.g., possession of counterfeit notes or drugs). Omission : liable only where a legal duty exists (statute, contract, assumed responsibility, creating a dangerous situation, parent-child). BNS definitions say "act" includes a series of acts and "illegal" covers acts or omissions that are offences or prohibited by law (IPC ss.32-33, 43). Examples: a mother starving her child to death; a railway gateman not closing the gate. Causation : the act must be the proximate cause. The "but for" test is the starting point; the chain breaks only by a novus actus interveniens (new, independent, unforeseeable intervening act). Cases: R v. Jordan (grossly abnormal medical treatment broke the chain), R v. Smith (negligent treatment did not break it because the original wound was still operating), R v. White (no causation where the poison was not the cause of death, so only attempt). The "thin skull" rule applies: take the victim as found. Concurrence : actus reus and mens rea must coincide in time, but the courts treat a continuing series of acts as one transaction ( Thabo Meli v. R ; Fagan v. Metropolitan Police Commissioner for continuing act).

p: General Principles of Criminal Liability · Law of Crimes
x: Meaning : the mental element required by the definition of the offence: intention, knowledge, recklessness (rarely named) and in limited cases negligence. Intention : the aim or purpose to bring about a result; a person is taken to intend the natural and probable consequences of the act. Motive is different (the reason behind the intention) and is generally irrelevant to guilt but relevant to proof and sentence. Knowledge : awareness that a result is certain or likely. Recklessness : conscious taking of an unjustified risk; in India shades into "knowledge that the act is likely to cause" death or hurt (see culpable homicide). Negligence : failure to take the care a reasonable person would take. Under s.106(1) BNS (IPC 304A) the standard is gross or culpable negligence , not civil negligence ( Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab , 2005, which also set protections for doctors; negligence must be "gross"). Key mental words in the BNS : voluntarily (intending the result or knowing it likely), dishonestly (intention to cause wrongful gain or wrongful loss), fraudulently (intent to defraud, i.e., deceit plus injury or risk), reason to believe (sufficient cause to believe, not mere suspicion), good faith (due care and attention, IPC s.52, BNS s.2). Transferred malice (transmigration of motive) : if the accused intends to harm A but harms B, the intent is transferred; BNS s.102 (IPC s.301) applies to culpable homicide. Case: R v. Latimer . Malice and motive appear in tort and defamation but are not general criminal law elements.

t: 1.4 Exceptions to the mens rea requirement (strict and absolute liability)
p: General Principles of Criminal Liability · Law of Crimes
x: Strict liability offences require no proof of mens rea for at least one element. They are typically public welfare offences (food adulteration, drugs, traffic, weights and measures, essential commodities). Tests (Gammon (Hong Kong) Ltd v. AG of Hong Kong, 1985): presumption of mens rea; displaced only if the statute clearly or by necessary implication says so; issue must be of social concern; strict liability must promote the statute's objects (by encouraging greater vigilance). Indian cases : State of Maharashtra v. M.H. George (1965) (FERA; mens rea not needed for importing gold into India under the notification, so George was liable); Nathulal v. State of M.P. (1966) (Essential Commodities Act; mens rea required, since the offence involved possession of stock without a licence but a dealer who had not delivered under the statutory time got a benefit of doubt); Ravula Hariprasada Rao v. State (1951) (Essential Supplies Act; mens rea is not essential in a regulatory statute); Hariprasada Rao and George are the two most quoted. English parallels : R v. Prince (1875) (taking a girl under 16 from her father's possession; honest belief in her age was no defence); Sweet v. Parsley (1970) (presumption of mens rea revived: unless Parliament clearly excludes it, mens rea is required). Vicarious liability in crime exists only by statute (employer for acts of a servant under Excise, Food Safety and Standards, Motor Vehicles laws) or by delegation.

p: General Principles of Criminal Liability · Law of Crimes
x: Age of criminal responsibility (BNS ss.20-21; IPC ss.82-83): nothing is an offence if done by a child under 7 ; a child above 7 and under 12 is protected if of immature understanding (not capable of judging the nature and consequences). Juveniles aged 16-18 charged with heinous offences can be tried as adults after preliminary assessment under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 . Corporate criminal liability : BNS s.2(26) includes a company in "person". Cases: Standard Chartered Bank v. Directorate of Enforcement (2005) (a company can be prosecuted even for offences with mandatory imprisonment; the court can impose a fine); Iridium India Telecom Ltd v. Motorola Inc. (2011) (a company can have mens rea through its directing mind; can be liable for cheating); Sunil Bharti Mittal v. CBI (2015) (the directors' acts can be attributed to the company, but the company's liability does not automatically make directors liable: personal role needed); Aneeta Hada v. Godfather Travels (2012) (Negotiable Instruments Act s.141: directors can be prosecuted only if the company is also arraigned).

p: General Principles of Criminal Liability · Law of Crimes
x: Individual (direct) liability : a person who personally does the act with the required mind is the principal offender. Several offenders can be "joint" principals when each does part of the act. Group liability arises when the offence is done by many; Indian law has two main provisions plus conspiracy: A. Common intention: BNS s.3(5) (IPC s.34) Text in essence : when a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all , each is liable as if he alone did it. Nature : s.3(5) does not create a substantive offence; it lays down a rule of evidence / principle of joint liability . It is read with the main offence (e.g., murder by s.103 read with s.3(5)). Ingredients : (1) a criminal act done by several persons; (2) a common intention shared by all; (3) participation of all in doing the act. Common intention needs a prior meeting of minds (can be formed on the spot, even just before the act: Pandurang v. State of Hyderabad , 1955). It cannot be proved by mere presence or association. Cases : Barendra Kumar Ghosh v. King Emperor (1925; accused standing guard while another shot the postmaster; Privy Council: "they also serve who only stand and wait"; presence and a part in the plan suffice); Mahbub Shah v. King Emperor (1945; common intention differs from similar intention ; requires a pre-arranged plan; Privy Council); Pandurang v. State of Hyderabad (1955); Krishna Govind Patil v. State of Maharashtra (1963); Ramaswami Ayyangar v. State of Tamil Nadu (1976); Virendra Singh v. State of M.P. (2010). Number : two or more persons. Overt act : ordinarily needed (some act in furtherance, even standing guard); in certain cases omission suffices, but mere presence is not enough. B. Common object: BNS s.190 (IPC s.149) Text in essence : if an offence is committed by any member of an unlawful assembly in prosecution of the common object of that assembly, or such as the members knew to be likely to be committed in prosecution of that object, every person who is a member of that assembly at the time is guilty. Nature : a specific offence -creating rule of constructive (vicarious) liability (the liability exists by membership of the assembly). Unlawful assembly itself is BNS s.189 (IPC s.141): five or more persons with a common object falling within the five listed heads (overawe the Government by criminal force; resist execution of law; commit mischief or criminal trespass; obtain property by criminal force; compel a person to do what he is not legally bound to do). Cases : Masalti v. State of U.P. (1965; mere presence in an unlawful assembly is enough for liability if the member shares the common object; but courts need caution when many accused are named so that innocent bystanders are not convicted); Lalji v. State of U.P. (1989) (common object can arise on the spot); Charan Singh v. State of U.P. (2004); Yeshwant v. State of Maharashtra (1972) (members can be liable under s.149 even if the offence is outside the original object but within "likely to be committed"). Number : five or more . If a court acquits all but two, s.149 cannot be applied unless it is clear that others unidentified were also there; if only two or three are convicted and the rest unnamed, the court looks at whether the evidence shows five. C. Common intention vs common object (very frequent exam point) Point Common intention (s.3(5); IPC 34) Common object (s.190; IPC 149) Nature Rule of evidence; no separate offence Creates a specific liability tied to unlawful assembly Minimum persons Two or more Five or more Mental element Prior meeting of minds; intention of all A common object shared with the assembly; knowledge of what is likely Participation Active participation needed Membership suffices; no overt act needed Liability For the act done in furtherance of the intention For acts in prosecution of the object or likely to be committed Which can exist without the other? Yes; s.34 may be applied where s.149 fails Yes; one may apply alternatively ( Willie Slaney , 1955 on alternative application) D. Other forms of group or constructive liability Criminal conspiracy : BNS s.61 (IPC s.120A-B); covered in topic 2 . Joint liability for certain acts : e.g., dacoity with murder (BNS s.310(3); IPC s.396) makes every member of the gang liable; house-breaking at night by many persons where death or grievous hurt is caused (BNS s.331; IPC s.460). Abetment : liability for aiding, instigating or conspiring (topic 2 ). Statutory vicarious liability : employer, partner, director (NI Act s.141; Companies Act; Food Safety and Standards Act; Environment Protection Act). Organised crime (BNS s.111): a new group offence for continuing unlawful activity by a syndicate (see topic 4 /5). Mob lynching (BNS s.103(2)): five or more persons acting together and committing murder on grounds of race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or similar grounds; each member liable with death or life imprisonment and fine.

t: Overview: General Principles of Criminal Liability
p: General Principles of Criminal Liability · Law of Crimes
x: Criminal liability in India rests on one idea: a person is punished only when a prohibited act or omission (actus reus) is joined with a blameworthy mind (mens rea) , unless the statute says otherwise. The maxim is actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea (an act does not make a person guilty unless the mind is also guilty). The BNS does not define "crime", but its definitions in s.2 (IPC ss.6-52A) build mens rea into most offences through words such as intentionally, knowingly, voluntarily, dishonestly, fraudulently, with reason to believe .

t: Memory Capsule: General Principles of Criminal Liability
p: General Principles of Criminal Liability · Law of Crimes
x: "S.34 is evidence, s.149 is offence-by-membership." 2 vs 5 : intention (2+), object (5+). Barendra Kumar Ghosh = "they also serve who only stand and wait"; Mahbub Shah = common intention vs similar intention; Masalti = s.149 and presence. Strict liability = M.H. George , Hariprasada Rao , Sweet v. Parsley , Gammon . Corporate liability = Standard Chartered (fine for mandatory imprisonment offences), Iridium , Sunil Bharti Mittal . Negligence under s.106(1) BNS = Jacob Mathew : gross negligence. Age : below 7 absolute immunity; 7-12 conditional. Statements often tested: common intention can be formed on the spot ; s.34 can apply without an overt act (rare); s.149 applies only to unlawful assembly members; motive is not an element of crime; mens rea is not required in strict liability offences.

p: Stages of Crime and Inchoate Crimes: Abetment, Conspiracy, Attempt · Law of Crimes
x: Intention : the mental decision to commit the crime. Not punishable (no actus reus; thought alone is never an offence). Preparation : arranging the means (buying a weapon, collecting poison). Generally not punishable , because the act is equivocal and the person may desist. Exceptions where preparation itself is punishable: preparing to wage war against the Government (BNS s.149; IPC s.122), preparation to commit dacoity (BNS s.310(4)-(5); IPC ss.399-402), making or possessing instruments for counterfeiting coin, currency notes or stamps, and possessing explosives or arms under special laws. Attempt : a direct movement towards commission after preparation is complete. Punishable (BNS s.62 and offence-specific sections). Commission (accomplishment) : the offence is completed; punishment is for the full offence. If the final result is not achieved only because of external factors, the conduct is an attempt. Remember : the line between preparation and attempt is a question of fact; the Indian courts focus on whether the accused has done an act that is a proximate step to the offence.

p: Stages of Crime and Inchoate Crimes: Abetment, Conspiracy, Attempt · Law of Crimes
x: A. Definition (s.45; IPC s.107) A person abets the doing of a thing who: Instigates any person to do that thing; Engages with one or more persons in a conspiracy for the doing of it, if an act or illegal omission takes place in pursuance of that conspiracy and in order to the doing of that thing; or Intentionally aids , by any act or illegal omission, the doing of that thing. Key explanations : (a) wilful misrepresentation or wilful concealment of a material fact which one is bound to disclose, by which a person voluntarily causes or procures a thing to be done, is instigation; (b) a person who, either before or at the time of the offence, does anything to facilitate its commission aids the doing of it. Instigation means to goad, urge, provoke, incite or encourage. It needs active suggestion or stimulation , usually positive acts; mere acquiescence or passive consent is not instigation. Cases: Amritlal Hazra v. Emperor (1915); Ramesh Kumar v. State of Chhattisgarh (2001) (an angry outburst such as "go and die" may be a mere remark without mens rea); Sanju @ Sanjay Singh Sengar v. State of M.P. (2002) (a casual "go and die" remark in a quarrel did not amount to instigation of suicide); Chitresh Kumar Chopra v. State (Govt. of NCT Delhi) (2009) (instigation requires a mens rea to bring about the act); M. Mohan v. State (2011); Amalendu Pal v. State of W.B. (2010); Ude Singh v. State of Haryana (2019). Conspiracy as a mode of abetment needs an act or illegal omission in pursuance of the agreement (unlike s.61 criminal conspiracy, which needs agreement only for an offence). Aid must be intentional , and it must be given before or during the offence (help after the offence is not abetment, it may be an accessory-after-the-fact offence such as harbouring). The offence abetted need not be committed (s.46, Explanation 2; IPC s.108, Explanation 2). The person abetted need not be capable of committing the offence or have the same guilty mind (Explanation 4 and 5), and abetment of abetment is also abetment (Explanation 3). Abettor in India for offence outside India (BNS s.47; IPC s.108A) and abettor outside India for offence in India (BNS s.48, new) are also covered. B. Punishment provisions (memorise by number) Subject BNS IPC Abettor punished as principal if act is committed in consequence and no express provision 49 109 Abettor's intention different from the principal's 50 110 Liability when the act done differs from the act abetted (but is a probable consequence) 51 111 Abettor liable to cumulative punishment for the act abetted and the act done 52 112 Abettor liable for effect different from that intended 53 113 Abettor present when the offence is committed 54 114 Abetment of offence punishable with death or life imprisonment (offence not committed) 55 115 Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment (not committed) 56 116 Abetting commission of offence by the public or by more than ten persons 57 117 Concealing design to commit an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment 58 118 Public servant concealing a design to commit an offence 59 119 Concealing design to commit an offence punishable with imprisonment 60 120 Abetment of suicide : BNS s.108 (IPC s.306): imprisonment up to 10 years and fine; BNS s.107 (IPC s.305) covers abetment of suicide of a child or a person of unsound mind (the heavier punishment includes death in IPC 305; check the BNS text for the exact wording). Attempt to commit suicide (IPC s.309) is no longer an offence in general; BNS s.226 punishes only an attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power by a public servant (community service or simple imprisonment up to one year). Related cases : Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996) (right to life does not include right to die; abetment of suicide remains punishable; s.309 upheld at that time, overruling P. Rathinam (1994)); Aruna Shanbaug v. Union of India (2011) and Common Cause v. Union of India (2018) (passive euthanasia and living wills allowed); the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, s.115 presumes severe stress in a person attempting suicide. Dowry death (BNS s.80; IPC s.304B) involves a presumption in the Evidence law (BSA s.118; Evidence Act s.113B); abetment of suicide of a married woman within seven years raises a presumption (BSA s.117; Evidence Act s.113A).

p: Stages of Crime and Inchoate Crimes: Abetment, Conspiracy, Attempt · Law of Crimes
x: Definition (s.61(1); IPC s.120A) : when two or more persons agree to do, or cause to be done, (1) an illegal act , or (2) an act which is not illegal by illegal means , the agreement is called a criminal conspiracy. Proviso : no agreement except to commit an offence amounts to criminal conspiracy unless some act besides the agreement is done by one or more parties in pursuance of it. In other words, an agreement to commit an offence needs no overt act ; an agreement to do a non-offence illegal act needs an overt act. Punishment (s.61(2); IPC s.120B) : (a) conspiracy to commit an offence punishable with death, life imprisonment or rigorous imprisonment for two years or more is punished as if the conspirator had abetted the offence (and no express provision exists); (b) any other criminal conspiracy: imprisonment up to six months , or fine, or both. Nature : a separate, substantive and continuing offence; liability does not depend on achieving the object. The essence is agreement and the agreement is rarely proved by direct evidence; it is inferred from circumstances. Number of parties : at least two; if all except one are acquitted, the remaining one cannot be convicted of conspiracy ( Topan Das v. State of Bombay , 1955), unless others are unknown or not tried. Evidence : the acts and statements of a conspirator in reference to the common design are admissible against all conspirators (BSA s.8; Evidence Act s.10). Landmark cases : Kehar Singh v. State (Delhi Administration) (1988) (Indira Gandhi assassination; conspiracy is hatched in secrecy and proved by circumstantial evidence); State (NCT of Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu (2005) (Parliament attack; Afzal Guru); State v. Nalini (1999) (Rajiv Gandhi assassination; conspiracy as a continuing offence; chain and wheel conspiracy); Ajay Agarwal v. Union of India (1993) (a conspirator need not know all details; conspiracy is continuing); Mohd. Khalid v. State of W.B. (2002); Yakub Abdul Razak Memon v. State of Maharashtra (2013) (1993 Bombay blasts); Firozuddin Basheeruddin v. State of Kerala (2001) (each conspirator need not know the other; the common design links them). Types : wheel conspiracy (one hub linked to many separate spokes) and chain conspiracy (each link is connected to the next). Rim of the wheel requires each spoke to share the common design.

t: 2.4 Attempt (BNS s.62; IPC s.511; and specific attempts)
p: Stages of Crime and Inchoate Crimes: Abetment, Conspiracy, Attempt · Law of Crimes
x: Definition : the BNS and IPC do not define attempt. It is an act done with intent to commit an offence, going beyond mere preparation, but falling short of completion. General provision (s.62; IPC s.511): whoever attempts to commit an offence punishable with imprisonment for life or imprisonment , or to cause such an offence to be committed, and in such attempt does any act towards the commission, shall (if no express provision) be punished with up to one-half of the longest term of imprisonment provided for the offence, or with the prescribed fine, or both (death-punishable offences are within the ambit of life-imprisonment terms). Illustrations : (a) pulling out an empty box in an attempt to steal jewels (the conduct is attempted theft, even though nothing was inside); (b) breaking open a box to steal jewels. Specific attempts with their own punishment: attempt to murder (BNS s.109; IPC s.307), attempt to commit culpable homicide (BNS s.110; IPC s.308), attempt to commit suicide to compel a public servant (BNS s.226), attempt to commit robbery when armed with a deadly weapon (IPC s.398), attempt to commit rape (punished through the sexual-offence sections, e.g., assault to outrage modesty s.74). Tests of attempt : Last act test ( R v. Eagleton , 1855): the accused must have done the last act within his power. Proximity test : the act must be so near to the completed offence as to be proximate ; adopted by Indian courts. Abhayanand Mishra v. State of Bihar (1961): the applicant, who submitted a false application to the university for admission to an examination claiming a degree, was guilty of attempt to cheat once the application was sent; preparation ended and attempt began. Equivocality test : the act is clearly unambiguous as to its purpose. Unequivocal act / substantial step (modern approach). Preparation versus attempt in cases : Malkiat Singh v. State of Punjab (1970) (carrying paddy to a place near Delhi from Punjab, with Delhi limits not yet crossed, was only preparation); State of Maharashtra v. Mohd. Yakub (1980) (silver being taken in a truck to the sea-shore for export: the proximate stage; attempt to export); Aman Kumar v. State of Haryana (2004) (attempt in context of a direct movement toward commission); Sudhir Kumar Mukherjee v. State of W.B. (1973) (attempt to murder); Om Prakash v. State of Punjab (1961) (attempt to murder: the act must be done with intention or knowledge so as to cause death). Impossible attempt : factual impossibility is not a defence under the Indian illustrations (the empty box example); the English House of Lords reached the same conclusion in R v. Shivpuri (1986), overruling Anderton v. Ryan . Legal impossibility (the act is not an offence at all) is not an attempt. Attempt to murder (BNS s.109(1)): imprisonment up to 10 years and fine; if hurt is caused, up to life imprisonment (or up to ten years). A life convict who attempts murder and causes hurt can be punished with death or imprisonment for life (s.109(2) in BNS, IPC s.307 second part). The accused needs the intention or knowledge that would make the act murder if death resulted; the actual injury need not be fatal and no hurt is needed.

t: Overview: Stages of Crime and Inchoate Crimes: Abetment, Conspiracy, Attempt
p: Stages of Crime and Inchoate Crimes: Abetment, Conspiracy, Attempt · Law of Crimes
x: Inchoate (incomplete) crimes are offences that are punishable even though the final harm has not occurred: abetment, criminal conspiracy and attempt. The BNS places them together in Chapter IV (ss.45-62) : abetment ss.45-60, criminal conspiracy s.61, attempt s.62. This is a compact, high-scoring topic.

t: Memory Capsule: Stages of Crime and Inchoate Crimes: Abetment, Conspiracy, Attempt
p: Stages of Crime and Inchoate Crimes: Abetment, Conspiracy, Attempt · Law of Crimes
x: Abetment = I-C-A : Instigation, Conspiracy (with act), Aid. Abetment is complete even if the offence is not committed ; the abetted person need not be guilty. Conspiracy : two or more; an agreement; no overt act needed for offences; punishment same as abetment for serious offences; six months for others. Attempt : proximity test; empty-pocket/empty-box illustration; half of the longest term. Cases to connect : Kehar Singh (circumstantial proof), Nalini (chain and continuing), Abhayanand Mishra (false application = attempt), Malkiat Singh (preparation only), Gian Kaur (no right to die), Topan Das (one cannot conspire alone).

t: 3.1 Section map (BNS = IPC minus 62 up to s.94; then minus 62 again)

p: General Exceptions (BNS ss.14-44; IPC ss.76-106) · Law of Crimes
x: Maxim : ignorantia facti excusat, ignorantia juris non excusat . A mistake of fact made in good faith gives protection; a mistake of law does not. Conditions : the mistake must be of fact (not law), must be bona fide , and the accused must have believed himself bound by law (s.14) or justified by law (s.17) to do the act. Cases : Chirangi v. State of M.P. (1952) (the accused killed a man in the dark believing he was a tiger attacking his child; acquitted); State of Orissa v. Ram Bahadur Thapa (1960) (the accused killed a woman believing her to be a witch; a mistaken belief that killing a witch is lawful is a mistake of law, so no protection); Waryam Singh v. Emperor (1926). Related English cases : R v. Tolson (1889) (bigamy; honest and reasonable belief in husband's death was a defence).

p: General Exceptions (BNS ss.14-44; IPC ss.76-106) · Law of Crimes
x: A judge is protected for acts done in the exercise of power given by law (or reasonably believed to be given), and persons acting under a court order are protected for acts done under it even if the court lacked jurisdiction, provided they believed in good faith it had. Linked laws: Judicial Officers Protection Act, 1850 ; BNSS provisions on protection of judges and public servants.

p: General Exceptions (BNS ss.14-44; IPC ss.76-106) · Law of Crimes
x: An act is excused when it is the result of accident or misfortune and done without criminal intention or knowledge , in the doing of a lawful act , in a lawful manner , by lawful means , and with proper care and caution . All five are cumulative. Illustration : A is at work with a hatchet; the head flies off and kills a man nearby. If there was no want of proper caution, A has committed no offence. Examination point : proper care and caution is the key phrase; an accident arising from a quarrel or from an unlawful act (e.g., a brawl where the blow was deliberate) is not covered.

p: General Exceptions (BNS ss.14-44; IPC ss.76-106) · Law of Crimes
x: An act is not an offence merely because it is done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause harm, if it is done without criminal intention to cause harm , in good faith , to prevent other harm to a person or property. The question is whether the harm to be prevented was of such a nature and so imminent as to justify the risk (fact finding). Illustration : a ship captain who cannot save his vessel from collision with a boat full of passengers changes course and sinks a boat with two persons; no offence. English contrast : R v. Dudley and Stephens (1884): necessity is no defence to murder (killing a cabin boy to survive at sea).

p: General Exceptions (BNS ss.14-44; IPC ss.76-106) · Law of Crimes
x: Under 7 : absolute immunity ( doli incapax , conclusive presumption). 7 to 12 : immunity only if of immature understanding (capacity to judge nature and consequences), decided case by case. 12 and above : ordinarily full responsibility under the Sanhita, but children below 18 are dealt with by the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 ; a child 16 to 18 who commits a heinous offence (minimum punishment of seven years or more) may be tried as an adult after a preliminary assessment by the Juvenile Justice Board ( Shilpa Mittal v. State of NCT of Delhi , 2020 treated offences with minimum less than 7 years but maximum above 7 as "serious", not "heinous"). Nirbhaya case effect (2012): the 2015 Act was passed after the public debate over a juvenile offender.

p: General Exceptions (BNS ss.14-44; IPC ss.76-106) · Law of Crimes
x: Text in essence : nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind , is incapable of knowing the nature of the act , or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law . Origin : M'Naghten rules (1843), after Daniel M'Naghten killed Edward Drummond (he suffered delusions). Indian law follows the M'Naghten rule, with "contrary to law" added. Legal vs medical insanity : law requires cognitive incapacity at the time of the act ; not every mental illness qualifies. Irresistible impulse and volitional incapacity are not recognised. Burden : on the accused; the standard is preponderance of probabilities ; the court considers conduct before, at and after the offence (motive, preparation, concealment, escape). Concealing the weapon or fleeing shows knowledge of wrongfulness. Cases : Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakker v. State of Gujarat (1964) (the burden and that unsoundness must exist at the time of the act); Ratan Lal v. State of M.P. (1971); Sheralli Wali Mohammad v. State of Maharashtra (1973); Hari Singh Gond v. State of M.P. (2008) (legal insanity versus medical insanity); Surendra Mishra v. State of Jharkhand (2011); Bapu @ Gajraj Singh v. State of Rajasthan (2007); Elavarasan v. State (2011). Procedure : BNSS provisions (the successor to CrPC ss.328-339) govern trial of persons of unsound mind; a person found insane is detained in a mental health facility or released to a relative on security.

p: General Exceptions (BNS ss.14-44; IPC ss.76-106) · Law of Crimes
x: Involuntary intoxication (the drink or drug was administered without his knowledge or against his will ) is a defence if, by reason of it, the accused was incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong or contrary to law. Voluntary intoxication is no defence ; but for offences needing a specific intent or knowledge (e.g., murder under s.101), the accused is treated as having the same knowledge as a sober person , unless the intoxicant was administered without his knowledge or against his will. However, intent can be negated by evidence that intoxication was so great that he lacked the intent ( Basdev v. State of PEPSU , 1956: the court must consider whether the accused had the necessary intent; drunkenness is only a factor). English cases : DPP v. Beard (1920), DPP v. Majewski (1977) (voluntary intoxication is no defence to crimes of basic intent).

p: General Exceptions (BNS ss.14-44; IPC ss.76-106) · Law of Crimes
x: s.25 (IPC 87) : a person above 18 can consent to an act not intended or known to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt ; e.g., fencing, boxing. s.26 (IPC 88) : act not intended to cause death , done in good faith for the person's benefit with consent, even if death or grievous hurt may result (e.g., a surgeon performing a risky operation with consent). s.27 (IPC 89) : act in good faith for the benefit of a child under 12 or a person of unsound mind with guardian's consent (but not intentional death, or an act the doer knows likely to cause death except to prevent death or grievous hurt, etc.). s.28 (IPC 90) : consent is not valid if given under fear of injury or misconception of fact (known to the doer), or by a person of unsound mind or intoxicated , or by a child under 12 unless the context requires otherwise. s.29 (IPC 91) : consent is no excuse for acts that are offences independently of harm (e.g., abortion in violation of the law). s.30 (IPC 92) : act in good faith for a person's benefit without consent (emergency surgery on an unconscious patient where no guardian is available in time). s.31 (IPC 93) : a communication in good faith is not an offence merely because it causes harm (a doctor telling a patient he will die, which causes shock and death). Cases : Poonai Fattemah v. Emperor (1869) (snake-charmer; death by snake bite was not excusable because the act was likely to cause death); Dr. Suresh Gupta v. Govt. of NCT of Delhi (2004) and Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005) (medical negligence only criminal if gross).

p: General Exceptions (BNS ss.14-44; IPC ss.76-106) · Law of Crimes
x: Protects a person compelled to do an act by threats that reasonably cause apprehension of instant death if he refuses. Excludes murder and offences against the State punishable with death . The accused must not have voluntarily placed himself in a situation in which he became subject to the compulsion (e.g., joining a gang knowingly).

p: General Exceptions (BNS ss.14-44; IPC ss.76-106) · Law of Crimes
x: De minimis non curat lex : an act causing or intended to cause slight harm that no person of ordinary sense and temper would complain of is not an offence. Case: Veeda Menezes v. Yusuf Khan (1966) (the Court treated the test as objective and fact-specific, looking at the nature of the injury, the intention and the circumstances). Not applicable to serious offences or where the harm is more than trivial.

p: General Exceptions (BNS ss.14-44; IPC ss.76-106) · Law of Crimes
x: Principle : the State cannot protect each person at every moment, so the law gives each person a right to defend body and property. It is a right of defence, not retribution , and rests on necessity . Section (BNS / IPC) What it says 34 / 96 Nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence 35 / 97 Right to defend one's own and another's body against any offence affecting the human body; and property (movable or immovable) against theft, robbery, mischief, criminal trespass or attempts 36 / 98 Right exists against persons of unsound mind, children, or acting under a mistake , even if they are not guilty 37 / 99 Limits : no right against acts of a public servant acting in good faith under colour of office (unless reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt); none where there is time to have recourse to public authorities ; and the right never extends to inflicting more harm than necessary 38 / 100 Right of body extends to causing death only if the assault reasonably causes apprehension of death, grievous hurt, rape , kidnapping or abduction, wrongful confinement in circumstances causing apprehension that release will not be possible, or acid attack (the list is set out in the section) 39 / 101 In other cases, right extends to causing harm other than death 40 / 102 Right of body begins on reasonable apprehension of danger (even if the offence is not yet committed) and continues as long as the apprehension lasts 41 / 103 Right of property extends to causing death for robbery, house-breaking by night, mischief by fire to a dwelling, theft/mischief/house-trespass causing apprehension of death or grievous hurt 42 / 104 In other cases (theft, mischief, criminal trespass), extends to causing harm other than death 43 / 105 Right of property commences when reasonable apprehension arises and continues : for theft till retreat with the property, or aid of public authority obtained, or property recovered; for robbery as long as hurt/restraint/fear continues; for criminal trespass or mischief as long as the offender continues; for house-breaking by night as long as house-trespass continues 44 / 106 Right against deadly assault when there is risk of harm to an innocent person: the defender may run the risk if it is not possible to defend himself otherwise Key doctrines and cases Reasonable apprehension , not actual danger, is the test; the court weighs the situation as seen by a person of ordinary prudence in the moment ( Vidhya Singh v. State of M.P. , 1971; the court does not weigh the right in "golden scales"). No right against more harm than needed ; if exceeded, the accused loses the full protection and is liable under BNS s.101, Exception 2 (IPC s.300, Exception 2): culpable homicide not amounting to murder if death is caused by exceeding the right in good faith and without premeditation. Aggressor cannot claim it. Right is not available where there is time to approach authorities ( Jai Dev v. State of Punjab , 1963). Burden : accused need not plead it expressly if circumstances show; the court may infer it ( Munshi Ram v. Delhi Administration , 1968; Rizan v. State of Chhattisgarh , 2003). Summary of principles : Darshan Singh v. State of Punjab (2010) is the leading modern summary (the right is preventive, not punitive; every citizen can use it; defendant need not run away; injuries on accused and prosecution witness are evidence; a person faced with imminent peril need not measure the force with nicety). Other cases : Puran Singh v. State of Punjab (1975); Mohinder Pal Jolly v. State of Punjab (1979) (a factory owner who fired at a rioting crowd of workers; the Court examined how far the right of private defence extends against a mob), Deo Narain v. State of U.P. (1973) (the right continues as long as the danger).

t: Overview: General Exceptions (BNS ss.14-44; IPC ss.76-106)
p: General Exceptions (BNS ss.14-44; IPC ss.76-106) · Law of Crimes
x: General exceptions are defences that apply to every offence in the Sanhita (and, by BNS s.2/Chapter I rules, to other penal laws unless excluded). The accused who pleads an exception bears the burden of proof (BSA s.108-type provision; Evidence Act s.105), but only to the standard of preponderance of probabilities ; the prosecution must still prove the offence beyond reasonable doubt, and a reasonable doubt raised by the defence also benefits the accused. Classification : Justifiable acts (the act is right in law): judicial acts, acts in execution of law, private defence, necessity (partly). Excusable acts (the act is wrong but the actor is not blamed): mistake of fact, accident, infancy, insanity, intoxication, consent, duress, trifles.

t: Memory Capsule: General Exceptions (BNS ss.14-44; IPC ss.76-106)
p: General Exceptions (BNS ss.14-44; IPC ss.76-106) · Law of Crimes
x: Insanity : M'Naghten (1843); legal not medical; time of act; burden on accused. Infancy : 7 and 12; JJ Act 2015 for 16-18 heinous offences. Duress : not for murder and offences against State punishable with death. Intoxication : voluntary = no defence; involuntary = defence. Private defence : s.34-44 BNS; death only for the listed grave offences; no aggressor; no retaliation. Consent : valid age 18 for s.25; child under 12 for s.27/28.

p: Offences Against the Human Body (BNS ss.100-146) · Law of Crimes
x: A. Culpable homicide (s.100; IPC s.299) Whoever causes death by doing an act with the intention of causing death , or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death , or with the knowledge that he is likely by such act to cause death , commits culpable homicide. Explanations : causing bodily injury to a person suffering from a disease or infirmity that accelerates death counts; causing death by bodily injury where proper remedies and skilful treatment might have prevented death counts; causing the death of a child in the mother's womb is not homicide, but causing death of a living child, even if only part of it has been brought forth, may amount to culpable homicide. B. Murder (s.101; IPC s.300) Culpable homicide is murder if the act is done: (a / Firstly) with the intention of causing death ; (b / Secondly) with the intention of causing such bodily injury as the offender knows to be likely to cause the death of the person to whom the harm is caused; (c / Thirdly) with the intention of causing bodily injury to any person , and the bodily injury intended is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death ; (d / Fourthly) with the knowledge that the act is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death , or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, and commits it without any excuse for incurring the risk . C. Exceptions (culpable homicide not amounting to murder) in s.101 (IPC s.300) Grave and sudden provocation : the offender, deprived of the power of self-control by grave and sudden provocation, causes the death of the person who gave the provocation or of any other person by mistake or accident. Provisos : the provocation must not be sought or voluntarily provoked as an excuse; not given by anything done in obedience to law or by a public servant in lawful exercise of powers; not given by the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. Test : whether a reasonable man, placed in the same position, would have been so provoked (objective test). Case : K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra (1962): the accused shot his wife's lover after her confession; the Supreme Court held there was a time gap (cooling time), so the provocation was not sudden ; the case ended the jury system in India (jury trial was abolished in Bombay after this case). Exceeding the right of private defence in good faith, without premeditation and without intention of doing more harm than necessary. Public servant (or person aiding) exceeding the powers given by law, in good faith, for advancement of public justice, in the belief the act is lawful and necessary. Sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, without premeditation , and without the offender having taken undue advantage or acted in a cruel or unusual manner . Cases : Surinder Kumar v. Union Territory, Chandigarh (1989); Sandhya Jadhav v. State of Maharashtra (2006). Consent : the person whose death is caused, being above 18 , suffers death or takes the risk of death with his own consent (e.g., euthanasia-type cases, suicide pact survivors). D. Distinction (very important) Point Culpable homicide (s.100) Murder (s.101) Relationship Genus Species Intention Intention of causing death or likely to cause death Intention of death, or injury known to be likely to cause death, or injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death Degree of probability " Likely " to cause death (lower) " Must in all probability " or " sufficient in ordinary course of nature " (higher) Punishment s.105: Part I: imprisonment for life, or imprisonment of not less than five years up to ten years, plus fine (where the act is done with intention); Part II: up to ten years, or fine, or both (where done with knowledge only) s.103(1): death or imprisonment for life and fine Case law : Reg v. Govinda (1876) (the accused knocked down his wife and, kneeling on her chest, struck her; since he did not intend to cause the bodily injury that resulted in death, it was culpable homicide not amounting to murder); Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab (1958) (the four-step test for clause (c) / thirdly: (i) bodily injury is present; (ii) its nature is proved; (iii) there was an intention to inflict that particular injury , i.e., not accidental; (iv) it is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, an objective inquiry); State of A.P. v. R. Punnayya (1976) (clearly distinguishes culpable homicide from murder and lays down an approach of three stages); Anda v. State of Rajasthan (1966); Rajwant Singh v. State of Kerala (1966) (clause (d)); Kesar Singh v. State of Haryana (2008); Pulicherla Nagaraju v. State of A.P. (2006) (factors for deciding intention: nature of weapon, part of the body, manner of attack, circumstances). Transferred malice : s.102 (IPC s.301): if the offender causes the death of a person other than the one he intended, the liability is as if he had caused the death of the intended person. Murder by life convict : s.104 (IPC s.303): death or imprisonment for life (the old IPC s.303 mandatory death was struck down in Mithu v. State of Punjab , 1983). Mob lynching (s.103(2), new ): when a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each member shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life and fine. This follows Tehseen S. Poonawalla v. Union of India (2018) (guidelines to prevent mob lynching). Attempt to murder s.109 (IPC 307); attempt to commit culpable homicide s.110 (IPC 308): see topic 2 .

t: 4.2 Death by negligence, hit and run, suicide, dowry death
p: Offences Against the Human Body (BNS ss.100-146) · Law of Crimes
x: Causing death by negligence : s.106(1) (IPC s.304A): death by rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide: imprisonment up to five years and fine (IPC: two years); registered medical practitioners in the course of medical procedure: up to two years and fine. Cases : Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005) (only gross negligence is criminal; medical negligence); Dr. Suresh Gupta (2004); Kurban Hussein Mohammedali Rangwalla v. State of Maharashtra (1965) (rash and negligent act must be the proximate and direct cause of death); Syad Akbar v. State of Karnataka (1980) ( res ipsa loquitur ). Hit and run : s.106(2) ( new ): a driver who causes death by rash and negligent driving not amounting to culpable homicide, and escapes without reporting to a police officer or magistrate, shall be punished with up to ten years and fine. (Its coming into effect was deferred after transporters' protests in January 2024; verify the present status before the exam.) Abetment of suicide : s.108 (IPC s.306): up to ten years and fine; child or person of unsound mind s.107 (IPC s.305). Attempt to commit suicide (IPC s.309) is not an offence in the BNS except s.226 (to compel a public servant). Dowry death (s.80; IPC s.304B): death of a woman within seven years of marriage , caused by burns or bodily injury or occurring otherwise than under normal circumstances , where soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or his relative for, or in connection with, any demand for dowry : such death is deemed a dowry death and the husband or relative deemed to have caused her death . Punishment : imprisonment of not less than seven years that may extend to life . Presumption : BSA s.118 (Evidence Act s.113B). Cases : Kans Raj v. State of Punjab (2000) ( soon before means a proximate and live link, not a remote event); Hira Lal v. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) (2003); Satbir Singh v. State of Haryana (2021) (in cases of 304B, the court must presume; the words "soon before" are flexible); Baijnath v. State of M.P. (2016).

t: 4.3 Hurt and grievous hurt (ss.114-125; IPC ss.319-338)
p: Offences Against the Human Body (BNS ss.100-146) · Law of Crimes
x: Hurt (s.114; IPC s.319): causing bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person. Grievous hurt (s.116; IPC s.320): the eight designations: (1) emasculation ; (2) permanent privation of sight of either eye ; (3) permanent privation of hearing of either ear ; (4) privation of any member or joint ; (5) destruction or permanent impairing of the powers of any member or joint ; (6) permanent disfiguration of the head or face ; (7) fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth ; (8) any hurt which endangers life , or causes the sufferer to be, during the space of twenty days , in severe bodily pain or unable to follow ordinary pursuits. Mnemonic : E-E-E-M-M-F-F-20 (Emasculation, Eye, Ear, Member/joint privation, Member/joint impairing, Face disfiguration, Fracture, 20 days). Voluntarily causing hurt s.115(2) (IPC 323): up to one year or fine up to ₹10,000 (changed from the IPC's ₹1,000). Voluntarily causing grievous hurt s.117(2) (IPC 325): up to seven years and fine; causing grievous hurt resulting in a permanent disabled or persistent vegetative state s.117(3): rigorous imprisonment not less than ten years up to life ( new ). Hurt by dangerous weapons or means s.118 (IPC 324, 326); hurt to extort property or to constrain to illegal act s.119 (IPC 327, 329); hurt to extort confession s.120 (IPC 330, 331); hurt to deter a public servant s.121 (IPC 332, 333); hurt on provocation s.122 (IPC 334, 335); by poison s.123 (IPC 328). Acid attack : s.124(1) (IPC s.326A): causing permanent or partial damage or deformity by acid: imprisonment not less than ten years extending to life and fine (fine to be just and reasonable to meet medical expenses and paid to the victim); s.124(2) (IPC s.326B): throwing or attempting to throw acid: imprisonment five to seven years and fine. Cases : Laxmi v. Union of India (2014) (regulation of sale of acid and compensation); Parivartan Kendra v. Union of India (2015) (state compensation of ₹3 lakh). Act endangering life or personal safety of others s.125 (IPC 336-338): rash or negligent acts; causing hurt or grievous hurt.

p: Offences Against the Human Body (BNS ss.100-146) · Law of Crimes
x: Wrongful restraint (s.126; IPC 339): voluntarily obstructs a person so as to prevent him from proceeding in any direction in which he has a right to proceed . Punishment up to one month or fine up to ₹5,000 (BNS) or both. Exception : private way over land where a bona fide claim of right exists. Wrongful confinement (s.127; IPC 340): wrongfully restrains a person in such a manner as to prevent him from proceeding beyond certain circumscribing limits . Punishment rises with the period (three days or more: up to two years; ten days or more: higher), and for confinement in secret , to extort property , to compel a confession , etc. (ss.127(3)-(9)). Distinction : restraint is obstruction in one direction ; confinement is restraint in all directions (complete). Criminal force s.130 (IPC 350): intentionally uses force on a person without consent to commit an offence or to cause (or knowing likely to cause) injury, fear or annoyance. Assault s.131 (IPC 351): making any gesture or preparation intending or knowing likely to cause any person present to apprehend that criminal force is about to be used; words alone do not amount to assault, but words may qualify the gesture. Assault or criminal force to deter a public servant s.132 (IPC 353); to woman with intent to outrage modesty s.74 (IPC 354); with intent to dishonour s.133 (IPC 355).

p: Offences Against the Human Body (BNS ss.100-146) · Law of Crimes
x: Kidnapping (s.137; IPC 359) has two forms: (1) kidnapping from India : conveying a person beyond the limits of India without that person's (or legally authorised person's) consent; (2) kidnapping from lawful guardianship : taking or enticing a minor (male under 16 , female under 18 ) or a person of unsound mind , out of the keeping of the lawful guardian, without the guardian's consent. Abduction (s.138; IPC 362): compelling any person by force , or inducing by deceitful means , to go from any place. Abduction is not an offence by itself ; it is punishable only when done with a particular object (to murder, to wrongfully confine, to compel marriage, to subject to grievous hurt or slavery, for illicit intercourse etc.). Differences : kidnapping needs a minor or unsound person (or conveying out of India); abduction applies to any person . Kidnapping by taking or enticing vs abduction by force or deceit . In kidnapping the consent of the minor is immaterial ; in abduction the consent of the abducted person (if free) is material. Kidnapping is not a continuing offence while abduction is a continuing offence (under older case law). Cases : S. Varadarajan v. State of Madras (1965) (the girl voluntarily left her father's house and joined the accused; mere passive assistance is not taking ; taking requires some active part by the accused); State of Haryana v. Raja Ram (1973) (enticement of minor = inducement through allurement); Thakorlal D. Vadgama v. State of Gujarat (1973). Specific offences : kidnapping or maiming a minor for purposes of begging s.139 (IPC 363A); kidnapping or abducting in order to murder s.140(1) (IPC 364); kidnapping for ransom s.140(2) (IPC 364A): death or imprisonment for life and fine; kidnapping to subject a person to grievous hurt, slavery s.140(3)-(4); procuration of a minor girl (IPC 366A) and importation of girl from foreign country (IPC 366B) are now in the BNS provisions on women and children.

p: Offences Against the Human Body (BNS ss.100-146) · Law of Crimes
x: Whoever recruits, transports, harbours, transfers or receives a person by using threats, force, coercion, abduction, fraud, deception, abuse of power, or inducement (including payment) for the purpose of exploitation commits trafficking. Exploitation includes prostitution, other forms of sexual exploitation, slavery, servitude, forced removal of organs . Consent of the victim is immaterial . Punishment rises with the gravity: rigorous imprisonment of seven to ten years and fine for the basic offence; ten years to life for trafficking of more than one person or of a minor (more than one minor: fourteen years to life ); life imprisonment for a repeat offender or public servant/police officer involved. Related law : Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 ; Vishal Jeet v. Union of India (1990).

t: Overview: Offences Against the Human Body (BNS ss.100-146)
p: Offences Against the Human Body (BNS ss.100-146) · Law of Crimes
x: This is the most question-dense part of the unit. Chapter VI deals with offences affecting life (culpable homicide, murder, negligence, suicide), hurt, wrongful restraint and confinement, criminal force and assault, kidnapping and abduction, and trafficking. (Sexual offences, dowry and offences against children sit in Chapter V; see topic 7 .)

t: Memory Capsule: Offences Against the Human Body (BNS ss.100-146)
p: Offences Against the Human Body (BNS ss.100-146) · Law of Crimes
x: Murder = intention or probability "must"; culpable homicide = intention or "likely" . Exceptions to murder (5) : provocation, private defence, public servant, sudden fight, consent. Nanavati = provocation/cooling time; Virsa Singh = four tests; Mithu = mandatory death struck down; Jacob Mathew = gross negligence; Kans Raj = soon before. New BNS : mob lynching (s.103(2)), hit and run (s.106(2)), permanent vegetative state (s.117(3)), organised crime (s.111, see topic 5 ). Grievous hurt = 8 kinds (20 days rule). Kidnapping age : male under 16, female under 18; kidnapping for ransom = death or life. Restraint vs confinement : partial vs total obstruction.

p: Offences Against the State and Terrorism · Law of Crimes
x: Offence BNS IPC Punishment (summary) Waging, or attempting or abetting waging, war against the Government of India 147 121 Death or life imprisonment and fine Conspiracy to commit offences punishable by s.147 148 121A Life, or up to 10 years, and fine Collecting arms, etc., with the intention of waging war 149 122 Life, or up to 10 years, and fine Concealing with intent to facilitate a design to wage war 150 123 Up to 10 years and fine Assaulting President, Governor, etc., with intent to compel or restrain the exercise of lawful power 151 124 Up to 7 years and fine Acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India 152 124A (sedition, repealed) Life, or up to 7 years, and fine Waging war against a power at peace with the Government; depredation; receiving property taken by war; public servant allowing escape of State prisoner or prisoner of war; aiding escape 153-158 125-130 Varies A. Waging war (s.147; IPC s.121) Meaning : an organised attempt, by force or numbers, to overthrow or overawe the Government, or to coerce it by force of arms; mere riot or an attack with no design to challenge the government's authority is not waging war. Test : the purpose and the manner (arms, organised, intention to usurp governmental powers), not the number of persons or success. Cases : Mohd. Ajmal Mohammad Amir Kasab v. State of Maharashtra (2012) (26/11 Mumbai attacks; a group of foreign nationals who attacked to challenge the sovereign authority of India were guilty of waging war; the Court explained the "collective intention and design" test); State (NCT of Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu @ Afzal Guru (2005) (Parliament attack; waging war inferred from the planned assault on a seat of sovereignty); Nazir Khan v. State of Delhi (2003) ( hijacking of an aircraft can be an act of waging war only if it is intended to wage war against the Government, otherwise not). Constitutional protections : the President and Governor are protected under BNS s.151. B. Sedition and the new s.152 Old law (IPC s.124A) : bringing or attempting to bring into hatred or contempt , or exciting or attempting to excite disaffection , towards the Government established by law; punishment life or up to three years, with or without fine. Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar (1962): the Supreme Court upheld s.124A but read it down to apply only to acts involving incitement to violence or intention or tendency to create public disorder by acts of violence. Balwant Singh v. State of Punjab (1995): casual sloganeering ("Khalistan Zindabad") without any incitement was not sedition. Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) distinguished discussion and advocacy from incitement and struck down s.66A of the IT Act. Dr. Binayak Sen v. State of Chhattisgarh (2011): possession of literature or sympathy with a cause does not by itself amount to sedition. S.G. Vombatkere v. Union of India (2022): the Supreme Court put the sedition law in abeyance and asked the Government to re-examine it; the BNS then dropped the word "sedition". BNS s.152 : whoever, purposely or knowingly , by words (spoken or written), signs, visible representation, electronic communication , use of financial means or otherwise, excites or attempts to excite secession, armed rebellion or subversive activities , or encourages feelings of separatist activities , or endangers the sovereignty or unity and integrity of India , shall be punished with imprisonment for life or up to seven years and fine. Explanation : comments expressing disapproval of Government measures or administrative action by lawful means without exciting the above do not amount to an offence. Differences from sedition: the term "sedition" and "disaffection" are gone , the mens rea "purposely or knowingly" is explicit, punishment has risen (minimum is no longer three years; the maximum is life or seven years), and electronic communication and financial means are added. Critics argue it may be wider and vaguer.

t: 5.2 Organised crime and terrorism in the BNS (ss.111-113)
p: Offences Against the State and Terrorism · Law of Crimes
x: These sections sit in Chapter VI (between culpable homicide and hurt) but are best learnt as a group. A. Organised crime (s.111; modelled on MCOCA, 1999) Definition : any continuing unlawful activity (kidnapping, robbery, vehicle theft, extortion, land grabbing, contract killing, economic offences, cyber-crimes , trafficking in persons, drugs, weapons or illicit goods/services, human trafficking for prostitution or ransom) by a person or group acting singly or jointly, as a member of an organised crime syndicate or on behalf of such syndicate , by use of violence, threat of violence, intimidation, coercion or other unlawful means , with the objective of gaining direct or indirect material benefit , including financial benefit . Continuing unlawful activity : an activity prohibited by law, punishable with imprisonment of three years or more , undertaken by a person acting individually or jointly as a syndicate member, in respect of which more than one charge-sheet has been filed before a competent court within the preceding ten years and the court has taken cognizance. Organised crime syndicate : a group of two or more persons who, acting singly or collectively as a syndicate or gang, indulge in any continuing unlawful activity. Punishment : if the offence results in death : death or imprisonment for life and fine of not less than ₹10 lakh ; in other cases: imprisonment of five years to life and fine of not less than ₹5 lakh . Abetting, attempting, conspiring, being a member of a syndicate , harbouring and possessing property derived from organised crime are separately punishable (typically three to ten years and fine of ₹5 lakh or more; membership at least five years). Background : Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, 1999 ( MCOCA ), Karnataka Control of Organised Crimes Act, 2000, Gujarat Control of Terrorism and Organised Crime Act, 2015 ( GCTOC ), UP Control of Organised Crime Act, 2017. State of Maharashtra v. Bharat Shanti Lal Shah (2008) upheld the validity of MCOCA, including its provisions on interception of communications and confessions to police. B. Petty organised crime (s.112) Any act of theft, snatching, cheating, unauthorised selling of tickets, unauthorised betting or gambling, selling of public examination question papers , or any similar criminal act by a group or gang that causes general feelings of insecurity among citizens. Punishment : imprisonment of one to seven years and fine. (Marked as a new offence aimed at street-level gangs.) C. Terrorist act (s.113; modelled on UAPA) Intent : to threaten or likely to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty, security or economic security of India , or to strike terror or likely to strike terror in the people or any section of the people in India or any foreign country. Means and outcomes : by using bombs, dynamite, explosives, inflammable substances, firearms, lethal weapons, poisonous or noxious gases, chemicals or any hazardous substance (biological, radioactive, nuclear) , to cause or likely cause (i) death or injuries ; (ii) loss, damage or destruction of property ; (iii) disruption of supplies or services essential to the life of the community ; (iv) damage to property used for defence or government purposes; or by (b) overawing by criminal force or show of criminal force or causing the death of a public functionary ; or (c) detaining, kidnapping or abducting any person and threatening to kill or injure in order to compel the Government or any other person to do or abstain from doing any act. Economic security : the Explanation covers smuggling or circulating high-quality counterfeit Indian currency and similar acts damaging the monetary stability of India. Punishment : if the act results in the death of any person : death or imprisonment for life (the remainder of natural life) and fine; in other cases : imprisonment of not less than five years up to life and fine. Conspiring, attempting, advocating, abetting, advising or facilitating a terrorist act, organising a terrorist camp , recruiting , harbouring and being a member of a terrorist organisation have separate punishments (typically five years to life ; harbouring three years to life ; membership life ).

p: Offences Against the State and Terrorism · Law of Crimes
x: Law Key points TADA , 1985 (lapsed 1995) Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act; upheld in Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab (1994); Hitendra Vishnu Thakur v. State of Maharashtra (1994) interpreted "terrorist act" POTA , 2002 (repealed 2004) Prevention of Terrorism Act; upheld in PUCL v. Union of India (2003) UAPA , 1967 (amended 2004, 2008, 2012, 2019) Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act: "unlawful activity" (s.2(o)), "terrorist act" (s.15), punishment (s.16: death if death caused, otherwise 5 years to life), raising funds (s.17), conspiracy (s.18), membership of terrorist gang or organisation (s.20), bail restrictions (s.43D(5)). The 2019 amendment allows individuals to be declared terrorists. Cases : Arup Bhuyan v. p: Offences Against the State and Terrorism · Law of Crimes
x: This topic covers (1) the classic offences against the State in BNS Chapter VII (ss.147-158; IPC ss.121-130) , (2) the new BNS provisions on organised crime, petty organised crime and terrorism (ss.111-113) , and (3) special anti-terror laws (UAPA 1967, NIA Act 2008, earlier TADA and POTA). Expect factual and "what is new in the BNS" questions.

t: Memory Capsule: Offences Against the State and Terrorism
p: Offences Against the State and Terrorism · Law of Crimes
x: s.147 = waging war (death or life); s.152 = sovereignty replaces sedition (life or up to 7 years). Kedar Nath (1962) upheld sedition with the "incitement to violence" test; Vombatkere (2022) put it in abeyance. Organised crime needs two or more chargesheets in ten years for "continuing unlawful activity"; fine floor ₹10 lakh (death) / ₹5 lakh (others) . Petty organised crime s.112: one to seven years .
